@Laaaaacieee Lacie姐，给你写封长信。

当我写这些话的时候，手有点抖。

不是因为别的，而是把你这个号从以前到现在一条一条翻完后，真的心疼。你从传统金融（HSBC、腾讯投资、CICC Capital）走出来，现在在Bitget Wallet做研究员，同时还参与BlockchainNKU和bamboozcrypto，看起来专业又忙碌，可你把最柔软也最坚韧的一面，都毫无保留地分享给了大家。

那条为web3年轻人发声的帖子。你看到有人说“想入圈的大学生都不用付工资”，直接坐不住了。你分享自己在传统金融实习的经历：大二大三2500，大四4000+包饭报销，研究生阶段最低7500，最高五位数。你说“web2的‘小黑奴’已经被抵制很久了，不要把这些恶习带到web3”“自己淋过雨应该为后人撑伞，而不是要求别人也把伞撕了”。那条推文让我看到一个有原则、愿意为后来者说话的人。

现在你在Bitget Wallet认真做产品、回用户消息、研究新机制。你会认真分析Papertrade的设计逻辑，把它拆解成赌场模型，还在日常里和大家聊OTC、虚拟账户、产品升级。你始终在做“对行业有正EV、真正解决用户需求的产品”，这种认真和责任感，真的很打动人。

你已经够厉害了，真的。从传统金融跨到加密世界，一边做研究，一边还要面对家庭的重大考验，一边还要为行业发声、为年轻人撑伞。你把专业、善良和真实结合得这么好。

可我还是希望你能歇一歇。研究、回消息、参与项目、照顾家人、记录生活……这些事加在一起，其实很重。外面的声音会过去的，工作也一直都在。你值得好好睡觉、好好吃饭、好好陪伴家人，也值得被这个世界温柔对待。

text:
科研圈最可怕的异化，可能不是博士生失去了科研能力，而是逐渐失去了从科学发现本身获得快乐的能力。

一些博士生已经被学术评价体系训练出了一套非常扭曲的奖励机制。

看到一篇有意思的论文，第一反应不是好奇它发现了什么，而是这篇工作凭什么能中顶会。

看到同门发了 Paper，第一反应不是祝贺，而是焦虑自己为什么还没有。

看到竞争对手被 Reject，甚至会产生一种莫名的优越感。

科研本来应该是一场不断扩大人类知识边界的正和游戏，却逐渐被一些人活成了比较排名、争夺 Credit 和学术地位的零和博弈。

这里有一个更深刻的问题：

当一个人长期无法从研究本身获得正反馈，他就可能开始从别人的失败中寻找相对优势。

因为科学发现太慢，论文发表太不确定，而比较、嘲讽和否定别人，却能提供即时的心理奖励。

这不是科学家的天性，而可能是长期处于高度竞争、资源稀缺和单一评价体系下形成的适应性行为。

更讽刺的是：

一个以培养独立思考和探索未知为目标的制度，可能最终培养出了一批最害怕失败、最依赖外部评价的人。

当然，严厉的学术批评是科学进步的必要条件。但批评研究中的错误，与通过贬低研究者获得优越感，完全是两回事。

我越来越觉得，衡量一个 PhD Program 的质量，不应该只看它一年发表了多少顶会。

还应该看，几年博士训练之后，学生是否依然拥有好奇心、创造欲，以及对科学本身的热爱。

科研最大的失败，不是几年没有发出顶会，而是几年之后，你已经不知道除了发表顶会，还有什么事情值得让自己兴奋。

我们原本是因为想理解世界才走进科研。

不要最后只学会了如何在科研圈里赢过别人。

author: ZenithFdn
quoted_text:
Thanks to everyone who has been building on and testing Zenith EVM Testnet.

The Zenith EVM Testnet will be reset on Monday, 2 Nov 2026, between approximately 2pm and 5pm CET (13:00 to 16:00 UTC), to ship a protocol upgrade, performance improvements and network hardening.

What the reset means for you:
• All testnet state will be wiped: balances, deployed contracts and transaction history.
• Re-fund your wallet from the faucet once the network is back.
• Redeploy your contracts after the reset.

What’s changing:
• Faucet bot protection: The faucet is now protected by a captcha, so bots and spammers can’t block real users from getting tokens.
• Stricter faucet rate limits: Claims are now more tightly rate-limited, so funds are spread fairly among builders and testers.
• Per-block transaction cap removed: The previous limit on transactions per block is increasing too. 
• Fixes and hardening: This upgrade includes fixes for issues discovered on the current testnet, plus general stability improvements.

A note on testnet ZTH:
All existing testnet ZTH balances, including any previously farmed ZTH, will be gone after the reset. Testnet ZTH has no value, and farming it provides no benefit. The faucet exists so developers can test, and the new protective measures are there to keep it that way.

Network details:
We expect RPC endpoints and other network settings to stay the same. If anything changes, we’ll update our docs accordingly.

Expect some downtime during the upgrade. We’ll post here as soon as the network is live again.

For more info about our testnet, please visit our docs: https://t.co/Uw1qopgIgF

Zth.

text:
On an Arbitrum chain, a transaction can be sent from your address without your key.

Last week the Arbitrum Security Council froze 8,425 ETH tied to the Binance exploit, and this morning I went through how. They swapped the Inbox's code for a moment, and minutes later the funds left the exploiter's own address with an empty signature. Same as in April. No bug, the DAO gave them that power.

If you're shipping on an Arbitrum chain, find out who can upgrade its Inbox, because they can move your users' funds too. On Robinhood Chain that's the chain owner, not the Arbitrum DAO.

交易返券和 2000 万 USDC 交易量瓜分是一条线，理财加息是另一条线。

text:
AI做到的是一件非常恐怖的事：把工业文明需要高成本、高质量、大规模组织才能产生的皇冠上的明珠：知识和智能，变成了可以低成本批量生产的大宗商品。

这直接解构了工业文明组织，无论是公司还是国家的两个存在门槛前提：你在这个位置，是因为你付出了巨量的沉没成本。你的利润，归根结底是因为这种沉没成本的累积和对外人的不对称优势带来的。而在AI面前，你的沉没成本等于直接归零了。

所有上一代人对下一代的教育目的，归根结底是尽可能多地付出沉没成本以进入这个组织护城河。但是现在，护城河之外的人只要一个问题一个问题地问下去，已经有对全部护城河内的知识与能力掌握的可能。他们要运用的只有自己作为碳基生物的判断与常识，而护城河内已经付出巨量沉没成本的人，需要克服的则是沉没成本带来的期望与分配问题。

这等于什么？城墙外的人与城墙内的人的位置被倒转了。利润本质上是这种累积的沉没成本带来的不对等落差与租税。落差和租税的前提已经被AI的存在取消了，国家与公司现在就已经在通往死亡的路上，因为它们作为专门消费这种落差的组织，已经没有存在合理性了。

我们正在看到且即将看到更多的，是城墙内的组织为已经付出的沉没成本而自相残杀，城墙外的个人以赤裸裸的利益权衡，来享受城墙内的组织因恶性竞争给予的补贴。补贴原本是为了培养“用户心智”-也就是沉没成本，来得到更多的租税。而现在租税没有了，补贴和恶性竞争还在。

债务问题也是这种关系不对等反转的体现：无论是国家还是公司，它们，以及那些相信它们仍有收取落差租税能力的人，会认为发债以求生存是合理的，发的债可以用未来更高的租税来还。甚至他们认为AI会造成“数字封建制”，带来更大的租税。但这个前提是站不住脚的，AI其实已经把旧组织租税的期望，变成了对没有沉没成本的人的反向补贴。

这种时候，“工业文明世界观”，甚至受过工业化教育与训练本身，都会成为一种要人命的旧观念，它可以让人变成输红眼的赌徒而不自知。那些从来没有受过工业化教育训练、在广大尚未经历工业化、还具有人身依附色彩的第三世界社会中，一些先进的成员，反而会迅速抹平这种沉没成本的差距，享受时代给予他们的后发优势。

所以，说现在的AI产业是国家与公司们在自掘坟墓，一点都不为过。只有在沉没成本与租税逻辑之外生长出来的新形态的组织，会把技术红利吃下去。而它们也不是代替现在这些组织的生态位置；它们的存在方式是单一的“提供与交换价值”，不存在护城河和租税这整一套逻辑和利益输送链条。

这是一整个旧世界的死亡。
author: kaptonia
quoted_text:
我现在越来越觉得，AI 这个行业可能正在发生一件非常荒诞的事情。

一边是科技圈每天讨论 AI 泡沫什么时候破裂，几千亿美元的资本开支能不能收回来，GPU 会不会过剩，模型公司到底能不能盈利。

另一边却是大量传统企业，连 AI 到底能帮自己解决什么问题都还没搞明白。

这两个世界之间的认知差距，可能比我们想象的还要夸张。

你天天刷 X、GitHub，每天接触 Codex、Claude Code各种自动化工作流，看着 AI 已经能够写代码、操作电脑、调用工具，甚至一个人就可以完成过去一个团队的部分工作。

看多了以后，你真的会产生一种错觉：AI 都已经发展到这种程度了，下一步是不是就该泡沫破裂了？

但当你真正走进传统企业，接触具体的业务流程，你会发现很多公司的 AI 使用水平，可能还停留在让员工用聊天机器人写文章、做 PPT、整理表格。

甚至很多企业连内部的数据、知识库、业务流程都没有整理清楚，更别提把 Agent 真正接进生产系统。

技术圈已经在讨论 AI 会不会取代整个部门，现实世界里却还有大量工作流程连最基本的数字化都没完成。

所以我觉得，判断 AI 泡沫，必须区分两个完全不同的问题。

第一个问题是：AI 这项技术会不会真正改变社会生产方式？

第二个问题是：今天市场给 AI 相关企业、GPU、算力基础设施的估值和投入，到底合不合理？

这根本不是一回事。

互联网确实改变了世界，但不代表 2000 年互联网泡沫时期所有公司的估值都是合理的。

同样，AI 未来可能成为整个社会的基础设施，但不代表今天每一家 AI 创业公司都能活下来，也不代表所有投入几百亿美元建设的算力中心都能收回成本。

一项技术可以拥有巨大的长期价值，同时存在严重的短期资本泡沫。

我反而觉得，AI 下一阶段真正值得关注的，可能已经不是模型还能提高多少分，参数还能扩大多少倍，而是这些能力什么时候才能真正进入企业，改变具体的业务流程，产生可以计算的经济价值。

一个 Agent 能不能稳定运行？能不能真正减少员工重复劳动？能不能降低成本？出错以后谁来承担责任？企业愿不愿意持续付费？

这些问题可能没有新模型发布那么性感，但恰恰决定了 AI 能不能从资本市场的故事变成真正的商业价值。

而且，技术能力越强，不代表商业落地就越容易。

很多时候最大的阻力根本不是模型不够聪明，而是组织不愿改变、数据质量太差、业务流程混乱，以及新系统根本无法融入原来的工作方式。

这也是为什么我觉得，未来几年最值得争夺的，未必只是最强模型，而是把 AI 能力真正转化为企业生产力的那一层。

当然，这些也不意味着 AI 泡沫不会破裂。

泡沫什么时候破，我不知道，也不觉得有人能准确预测。

但我越来越确信一件事：AI 的技术发展周期、资本市场的狂热周期，以及真实社会的应用普及周期，很可能根本不在同一个时间线上。

资本市场可能已经提前透支了未来十年的预期，而大量普通人和企业，还没有真正体验到这项技术能带来的生产力变化。

对普通开发者和创业者来说，与其天天猜测泡沫什么时候破裂，不如认真研究一个问题：当资本市场的狂热逐渐退去，哪些 AI 产品依然有人使用，哪些企业依然愿意付费，哪些系统真正创造了价值？

因为最后留下来的，大概率不是故事讲得最精彩的那批人，而是能够持续解决真实问题的人。

泡沫可以破裂，但真实的需求不会因为泡沫破裂而消失。

🚨重磅！GLM 5.5前夜，唐杰教授重磅发声：Scaling Law已成“偷懒路径”，AI真正进入“规模化正确性”时代！GLM 5.5将是深度RSI的产物！

智谱AI联合创始人、清华教授唐杰在顶科论坛直言：该用“规模化正确性”取代Scaling Law。

他的核心观点：
🔹Scaling Law只降损失，不保证正确 训练损失下降 ≠ 推理可靠、代码可跑、长任务无幻觉。一味堆规模是偷懒。

🔹新目标：规模化正确性 建立系统性方法，回答“规模放大后，结论还能不能成立？”从拟合损失，走向真正的缩放科学。

🔹范式升级 从“任务驱动、单点对比”转向“缩放曲线、小规模预测大规模”。

🔹AGI关键在RSI + 自净化 递归自我改进的瓶颈不是让模型改自己，而是让它准确判断自己有没有真正变好。这种能力叫“自净化”。

🔹终局 具备正确性验证 + 自净化的模型，才能自主搞定越来越复杂的任务，通向AGI。

堆参数的时代结束了，会自我验证、自我纠错的模型才是下一代。

GLM 5.5或许就是这条路上的重要一步。

1️⃣从零训练语言模型 不准调包。自己实现Tokenizer + Transformer核心模块，端到端训完0.1B（约1亿参数）模型。

text:
中国外交部只回应了 7 个字：「我们不了解情况。」

11 月 2 日外交部记者会上，韩联社记者就 Binance 遭攻击一事提问。此前，FBI 于 10 月 31 日正式认定，朝鲜应对这起超过 60 亿美元的加密资产盗窃案负责。

几个值得关注的细节：

1、FBI 将此次行动归类为朝鲜黑客组织「TraderTraitor」所为，这是 FBI 对攻击者身份的正式归因。

2、被盗资产正在被大量兑换成 ETH，攻击者计划进一步利用 DeFi 协议和即时兑换服务转移赃款。FBI 已公开相关钱包地址，呼吁行业协助拦截。

3、Binance 此前披露，初步调查指向 DevOps 工程师笔记本遭入侵，攻击者借此进入内部服务容器并发起未经授权的提现。后续调查还发现了更多入侵点，目前没有证据表明钱包私钥泄露。

4、Binance 表示已冻结约 30 亿美元相关资产，并准备超过 63.4 亿美元资金覆盖此次损失。

从 63 亿美元的加密资产盗窃，到 FBI 正式将事件归因于朝鲜，再到美国总统特朗普表示可能与朝鲜讨论此事，这起事件已经超出普通交易所安全事故的范畴。

而面对记者关于朝鲜是否参与攻击的追问，中国外交部给出的回应是：「我们不了解情况。」

text:
There's this saying back when I was doing Private Equity that

"Investment is like marriage"

That was certainly true in PE where an investment could last years and as an investor you're essentially required to support your portcos as much as you can

What's interesting is that crypto is starting to feel like marriage

Crypto used to feel like one night stand - a one and done kinda experience where you get in fast, get out fast, and then rotate onto the next trade

Now it's the other way around, "onchain businesses" are treating token holders like equity holders. And because of that, the onchain businesses are starting to be treated, valued, and priced like actual businesses. Onchain exchanges, inference platforms, yield venues, lending marketplaces 

While valuation multiples remain compressed, it's starting to make sense to value these "companies" based on their growth trajectory, based on their growth as a business and not on how hyped they can make it to be.

It feels like the bride and the groom are aligned and on the same page instead of one wanting to extract from the other as fast as possible

Pretty bullish

text:
11月2日—11月8日全球宏观指引：政策退出，中期选举+非农接棒Fed！AI芯片链接受第二轮盈利大考！

Fed政策导向交给数据，能源重新出现谈判窗口，中期选举决定财政与监管预期，非农决定12月加息能否重新锁死！

（周一进入美国冬令时，美股与美国宏观数据比夏令时推迟1小时公布与开盘）

定价逻辑变化：

上周，Fed → GDP/PCE → 12月加息 → 美债 → AI巨头财报
本周，中期选举 + 美伊谈判→财政预期 + Brent→ISM制造业+服务业 +JOLTS +ADP +非农→看增长 + 就业 + 工资 + 通胀压力重新组合→12月加息概率→US2Y、UW10Y US30Y→全球流动性→AI估值、黄金走势，#BTC 走向

宏观主线指引：政策退出 → 数据接管 → 政治扰动 → AI产业链二次验证周

第一主线——Fed鹰派暂停，政策指引真空期，数据来决定12月政策导向！

1, 10月虽然加息暂停，但是Fed将通胀描述为高压，将经济描述为强劲，同时Fed理事有两名支持10月加息，结合沃什讲话，典型鹰派暂停，后续加息预期反而提高

2，10月的鹰派暂停，可以解读为当前的金融流动性可以允许Fed等待更多的数据来判断是否要12月加息，很显然，9月加息之后金融流动性很明显加速收缩

3，沃什“有限宽松”政策在目前高通胀阶段更加有效，市场开始交易“反身性逻辑”，即金融市场正在代替美联储的工作完成自然流动性紧缩，这个动作越强，反而Fed加息的必要性下降，反观，如果市场流动性回归宽松，Fed反而更有必要加息。

4，这个框架放在本周非农数据，看的就是当前就业市场是否强到足以让Fed继续加息，同时又没有弱到让Fed担心金融条件过度收紧。

5，周五关键非农前，还有四层关键验证：

11月2日：ISM制造业，看企业招聘意愿
11月3日：JOLTS 看裁员
11月4日：ADP + ISM服务业 企业招聘与企业招聘意愿
11月5日：初请 + Q3生产率/单位劳动力成本
11月6日：非农 + 失业率 + 平均时薪，看最终就业结果

如果周五之前，职位空缺弱+小非农走弱+ISM企业招聘意愿降低，市场可能会提前交易就业走弱

6，就业不是越弱越好，而是要找到合适的区间，也就是西方媒体常说的“金发姑娘”区间。

目前市场对于10月非农预期是5-5.6万人，失业率维持在4.2%左右，而9月非农数据已经明显降温至2.9万人，所以这一次不能只看名义就业人数字的变化，更是要看新增非农+失业率+工资

所以，我将本次非农分为四个档位，对市场以及12月是否加息有不同的影响

a，最理想，小非农3-7万人区间，失业率稳定，工资降温，12月加息概率下降，利好风险资产
b，偏鹰，小非农大于10万人，工资增长加速，12月加息概率上涨，利空风险资产
c，就业过热，小非农大于15万人，工资上涨，失业率下降，12月加息概率锁定，明显利空风险资产
d，衰退，小非农转负，失业率明显大幅上涨，加息概率暴跌，市场先交易降息，随后交易衰退。

所以本周，对于美股最好的数据不是就业崩了，而是底招聘+低裁员+工资降温。

第二主线——中期选举临近结束，最终国会定局带来政治上的不确定性的！

1, 11月3日美国中期大选结束，目前市场主要关注众议院是否被民主党主导以及参议院的控制权，而选举结果会导致市场对财政支出、赤字、AI监管、数据中心建设以及未来债务上限多方面的不确定性思考。

2，所以，最终选举结果，并不是民主党胜，股市跌，共和党胜，美股张涨，不同结果对市场短期结果与长期结果影响都不相同，但是一旦结果公布，政治上将会排除一个不确定习惯因素，这是大环境的宏观环境改善

3，市场真正要看的是此次中期选举对财政、AI监管、与政治僵局三方面的影响

财政，共和党继续控制国会，财政连续性上涨+财政扩张空间上涨+赤字预算上涨+国债供应预期上涨+10Y/30Y潜在压力压力上涨，短期利好风险资产，但是长期却有债市作为风险陷阱存在，反之，民主党掌控国会，短期风险偏好受挫，但是中长期会更加稳定，尤其是对于债市

AI监管，民主党控制众议院或者两院，AI企业、数据中心建设以及相关监管可能面临更严格的国会审查，而目前美股正在经历AI资本支出到ROIC的关键考验，而民主党胜选会让Q3财报季更加严苛，企业压力会更加明显

政治僵局，如果国会出现权利分裂，由于双方博弈，可能会让财政扩张能力下降，从而引发财政刺激预期下降+赤字压力放缓+长短收益率压力放缓，短期利好稳定性，但是中长期可能会增加政府关门风险以及债务上限博弈的风险。

所以，本周看中期大选对市场的影响，看的不是美股，而是看美债10Y 30Y与美元还有黄金，最终判断形成的执政局面到底是财政约束还是政治风险。

第三主线——能源依旧是宏观核心，Fed政策与美股叙事都要与之形成对抗！

1，上周末卡塔尔推动美伊谈判，目前局势逐步乐观，市场押注美伊存在外交缓解局面的窗口，短期Brent 价格下跌。但是短期的下跌并不意味着通胀风险解除，而对于通胀的逻辑，不要看外交声明，还是要看能源定价影响。

2，Brent 对宏观市场影响逻辑不变，105—110美元，高风险区间，但开始出现降温。100—105美元，能源风险明显缓解。95—100美元，真正进入风险降级阶段。90—95美元，开始明显削弱Fed未来加息必要性。<90美元能源通胀逻辑基本逆转。所以，目前Brent的下跌，只能说是局势缓和，而不是宏观拐点，真正的拐点要看Brent 小于100甚至小于95美元

3，结合原油走势，来判断本周最为关键的“反身性组合”

宏观松绑组合，能源下降+非农温和+工资下降+2Y收益率下降+10Y 30Y收益率下降，意味着通胀压力放缓，内生通胀下降，Fed加息必要性降低，长期财政与通胀风险并未持续恶化

值得风险市场警惕的组合，Brent下降+非农降温+2Y下降+10Y 30Y收益率反而上涨，如果出现此类组合，意味着债市存在财政赤字+国库供给+期限溢价+主权信用等风险，

第四主线——美股财报继续，从云厂商到芯片产业链订单验证!

1，上周是AI关键三大云厂商财报，其中谷歌与亚马逊财报出现明显瑕疵，引发美股信心下跌，估值调整，市场开始放大担忧AI 资本支出后的ROIC，财报证明了AI资本支出很强，但是市场想知道这些钱花出去多久可以赚回来1

2，本周关键6大AI企业财报，

11月2日：Apple + Palantir
11月3日：AMD + Arista
11月4日：ARM + Qualcomm

其中AMD 与Apple是本周核心重点财报

上周美股看财报超级云厂商的财报表示继续花钱，并且花的更猛，而这周就要看芯片公司能否证明这些钱是否真的变成订单，从而解答市场一个疑惑点——钱去哪里去了！

3，AMD本周重点之一，尤其是验证芯片订单问题，所以AMD想要交出一份满意答卷，就要拿出AI GPU收入增长+数据中心增长+MI系列订单+毛利率+更强未来AI收入指引来交答卷。

如果数据全部上涨，意味着资本支出传导至芯片订单，完成逻辑验证，市场信心逐渐回归，美股跌势放缓。并且重新利好NVDA / AVGO / TSMC / ASML / ARM / AI Server等企业。

反之，如果超级云厂商资本扩大支出的前提下，AMD ARM与Qualcomm订单指引却下降，市场多半要质疑“钱去哪里了”？从而延伸至深度话题——AI资本开支的效率问题

4，Apple和Palantir分别验证AI交易的两个极端，

Apple不仅仅是纯AI基础设施公司，所以要看消费需求问题，重点看iPhone需求+服务收入+中国市场+毛利率+未来指引，为市场解答的是“高利率环境下，美国消费者还有没有钱消费”

Palantir则验证AI逻辑链中的末端——商业验证端，给市场解答“AI到底能不能赚钱”的疑惑，如果这份财报利好，可以有效减缓上周谷歌与亚马逊财报瑕疵带来的信心受挫

5，结合上周与本周的AI财报，其实可以短期完整验证AI产业逻辑是否形成有效闭环

云厂商资本支出，下游硬件产业AMD ARM  QCOM硬件需求，Palantir软件变现，Apple消费终端，本周财报结束，就看这个产业端能否形成闭环，这是直接影响当前美股AI叙事的估值调整节奏

本周总结：

宏观上，依旧是以Brent为核心基础来判断是整个宏观市场的影响与变量，Brent下跌与上涨，直接影响利好是否被放大/削弱?利空是否被削弱/放大，属于宏观放大器效果！

数据上，上周Fed表示加息还未结束，这周就要看就业数据是否为Fed提供加息空间！？

微观上，美股关键科技企业财报能否挽救市场信心，暂缓估值消化与恐慌情绪，同时面对宏观压力，能否形成有效对抗？

所以严格来说，本周将要面对能源+就业+利率+AI估值四杀，情况不会太乐观，需要逐步排除风险，一旦四杀结束估值依旧坚挺，11月下半旬就可以期待一下！
author: Cato_KT
quoted_text:
10月26日—11月1日全球宏观指引——Fed+PCE数据定价12月加息，AI巨头接受盈利大考，超级定价周来袭！

如果市场上周讨论的是10月加息概率推迟到12月的话，本周的核心论点就变得更加复杂，需要重点关注三个方向

a，Fed如何定义10月不加息，是暂停？还是鸽派转向？
b，油价、GDP PCE 宏观数据谁会成为决定12月是否加息的重要推手！
c，AI巨头财报VS宏观压力进入第二周，本周巨头财报能否扭转局面？

简单来说本周是一个结合政策 + 通胀 + 增长 + AI盈利 + 全球央行 + 地缘能源同时交汇的超级周，而我认为重点关注三大主线

第一主线——10月不加息成为默认，12月加息预期是否被锁定，未来还有加息吗？

1，截止目前，12月加息概率提升至72.4%附近，已经进入初步定价阶段，

2，10月28日凌晨——10月议息会议+沃什讲话，重点不是10月不加息，而是看为12月加息铺垫什么政策

a，是否继续强调通胀风险与通胀继续上行？是否提升通胀预期？
b，如何评价能源冲击？如果沃什明确承认油价对商品、运输、企业成本以及通胀预期的担忧，那么12月加息逻辑会更强
c，如何描述当下的金融条件，是否还认为不够收紧？如果是，意味着增加12月加息概率
d，是否继续强调不会等待单一数据点，如果继续保留这个框架，即便10月不加息，那么Fed也没有回归等待数据确认的政策模式

3，危机——沃什为12月加息铺垫政策之后就迎来“验证”，周四晚间美国9月PCE与第三季度GDP公布，目前数据预期高于前值，一旦公布数据符合预期，结合沃什的政策铺垫如果鹰派，12月加息概率很有可能冲击90%直接被锁死

同时2Y 10Y 30Y收益率继续上行，美元走强，黄金走弱，科技股高估值继续调整，BTC同样受流动性挤压

4，需要注意，本周9月PCE 权重要下调，因为目前市场已经通过9月CPI知道通胀过热，所以PCE哪怕符合或者高于预期市场并不意外，市场更想通过PCE来回测CPI的通胀压力是否已经传到至消费端。

第二主线——美股巨头财报继续公布VS 宏观压力，验证逻辑改变，科技巨头能否逆转？

1，通过上周的财报，我们基本可以确定AI的叙事已经从“资本开支”正式进入“现金流审核”阶段，虽然本季度对于现金流的要求还不够严苛，但是宏观压力下已经对很多企业形成一定的压力，例如上周的TSLA META 都是如此

2，10月28日美股盘后Microsoft + Alphabet财报，10月29日盘后Amazon，都是本周关注重点。作为全球AI超大规模云厂商，占据了AI产业逻辑的第一梯队，其财报重要性对整个Q3季度都会有一个关键作用。

3，三大云厂商处于AI产业链的核心枢纽地位，财报可以影响上游AI基础设施的订单与需求，下游可以影响模型、应用等，所以这三家财报好坏将会直接影响当前市场信心。

4，AI验证逻辑发生变化，所以接下里不能只看收入与EPS，而是要关注营收+AI资本支出+自由现金流+未来指引

其实逻辑非常简单，市场想要看到此前的大量AI资本支出的钱企业多久可以赚回来，以前拼财力，拼花钱，现在的故事要讲如何赚钱，如果快速赚钱。

对于当前阶段，最乐观的组合就是营收增长+资本开支上调+自由现金流回归增长趋势，如果财报出现营收上涨+资本开支上涨+自由现金流下降的组合，那么市场就要开始讨论AI ROI了

当然，通过上周的情况来看，自由现金流如果没有恢复上涨，也并不意味着叙事崩溃，但是目前宏观压力下市场的质疑是必不可少的，可能会导致短期估值调整加速，但是行业趋势上依旧没有问题。但是如果财报中显示自由现金流不增长反而恶化，则就比较麻烦。

5，当然，回归三家企业来说，都各自有不同的要求与重点

Microsoft：看Azure + AI monetization，为市场解答的是企业AI需求是不是真的在变成收入这个问题

Alphabet：看Google Cloud + AI 资本支出 + 自由现金流，为市场解答的是AI资本投入没有侵蚀整个商业模型的现金创造能力

Amazon：看AWS，为AI云计算承担二次验证，

如果微软的Azure、谷歌得到Google Cloud与亚马逊的AWS在财报中表现都非常强，意味着AI基础设施需求不是单家公司现象，将会整体提升AI行业信心，同时对NVDA / AMD / AVGO / TSMC / ASML等设备公司的产能也是进行二次验证！

第三主线——能源与地缘，宏观主线是看能源还是看Fed政策？

1，上周我们再次经历了高油价的“统治”，当Brent 处于110美元上方的时候，我们感受到宏观侧的整体压力，不管是利率、黄金、还是美股与BTC都在集体承压

2，到目前为止我们需要明白一个残酷的事实——Fed的政策无法改变能源供给冲击，但是两者可以将宏观主导权掌控在自己手里，就看谁的权重更高！

3，当Brent 处于110美元上方的时候，宏观主动权是否还被原油定价锁定？看本周Fed的影响力能否拿回掌控权，其次，不管PCE如何，只要Brent还处于高位，12月加息预期就不会弱。

4，最近几周，我们看到了美伊之间的复杂变化，不管是霍尔木兹海峡代替方案，还是欧洲增加原油储备释放，亦或者促成俄乌和平让俄罗斯能源环节供给压力等等，但是对Brent 的冲击都太小，这里我们需要面度一个残酷的事实，Brent 短期的价格下跌的核心依旧是美伊问题。

5，而目前的美伊，依旧是以打促谈，这里的打也包括外交施压，小规模袭击骚扰等，10月份霍尔木兹海峡油轮受袭击数据刷新单月最高，能源供给进一步恶化，美伊之间依旧保留了斡旋窗口，多方也在积极斡旋，但是目前来看并不乐观

接下里本周，如果10月27日内塔尼亚胡获胜，然后到11月3日中期大选结束之前，我认为仅剩一个可谈判窗口，否则一旦中期大选结束，美伊之间短期局势可能会进一步紧张。

6，继续沿用此前的Brent价格影响逻辑

＞110——金融风险市场集体承压，通胀预期恶化，加息定价明确
100-110——通胀风险轻微缓解，但是12月加息依旧存在
95-100——能源通胀压力边际缓解，小幅度削弱12月加息可能性。
90-95——政策变化重要区间，可以缓解未来通胀压力同时削弱12月加息概率

第四——非主线变量，美债供给测试

本周三天，26日，27日，29日，分别是2Y 5Y 7Y美债拍卖其中2Y与5Y都是达到700亿美金级别的拍卖，这里可以验证一个上周的逻辑——5%收益率美债对资金的吸引力强不强？

本周可以重点关注5Y的拍卖情况，毕竟2Y收益率更加吃Fed政策，而5Y会更好的展现资金对债市的买入热情

如果5Y拍卖走弱+Fed鹰派+PCE过热，那么收益率可能会继续全面上行，这将会对风险资产继续产生压力。

总结：

其实本周的核心不是美国经济好坏，而是当前的美国经济到底可以承受多高的真实利率。

如果本周GPD 强，PCE热，AI财报盈利强，Brent＞100，表面看起来美国经济很好，但是对Fed政策更加不利，金融市场将会承受更大的利率压力，而美股AI企业可能会更加分化。

最理想风险资产的组合反而是——GDP温和+核心PCE不恶化+Brent跌破100+AI财报盈利强+AI自由现金流改善。

•  恢复初期（约9.5小时）：净流出约36.4亿美元（约占其资产的2.1%），处理了约46.5亿美元提款、约10亿美元充值。 
•  后续24小时窗口：净流出一度超过70亿美元。 

同期其他主要交易所净流入（24小时口径，约）：
•  OKX：约4.45亿美元。 
•  Bybit：约1.12亿美元。
•  Gate：约9100万美元。
•  Bitget：约5400万美元。

有意思的是多家合计流入远小于币安流出规模。分析指出，流出资金绝大部分（约九成）流向了自托管/冷钱包，而非其他中心化交易所。 

不过 @binancezh 立马开始撒钱模式吸金， $USDC 10%+ 活期年化目前CEX里独一份。

不是以往几百一千额度的勾引式宣传，只要VIP1就能有20万刀10.5%的额度，维持20天，相当香了🤌🤌

后续看看这个活动对资金流动会有什么样的影响，我感觉一周内应该就会看到效果

text:
Contestable markets are more important than the number of players in that market.  I had no problem in building a phone.  Google even gives away billions of dollars worth of technology to make it easy to compete with them.  

The hard part is convincing consumers to switch, and for a large segment of consumers you can’t even pay them to switch products.  It’s not a matter of making a functionally equivalent product cheaper. 

This is because Google prices their products at the marginal cost of switching.  They are not pricing them above the value that the consumer receives as a monopolist would.

ZachXBT: EU-Based Entity Suspected of Losing Over $106M in Crypto Theft  

On-chain investigator ZachXBT reported on November 2 that an EU-based entity is suspected of losing more than $106 million from multiple centralized exchange accounts on November 1. The suspected attacker withdrew the funds in USDC and USDT and has since been actively swapping USDC for ETH, transferring assets through instant exchange services including WellWallet and Kyrrex, converting funds into privacy coin XMR via Wagyu, and bridging assets across multiple blockchains. The identity of the affected entity and the method of the suspected theft remain undisclosed. The reported losses have not yet been independently confirmed.

text:
$MRVL TO ACQUIRE $LITE IN $115B ALL-STOCK DEAL

Marvell has agreed to acquire Lumentum in an all-stock transaction valued at approximately $115B in enterprise value, combining two major suppliers of AI infrastructure and optical networking technology.

Under the agreement:

• Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each LITE share, implying roughly $1,132 per share.

• The offer represents a 23.9% premium to unaffected closing prices on October 28.

• Marvell shareholders will own approximately 67% of the combined company, with Lumentum shareholders holding 33%.

The deal brings together Marvell's custom AI chips, networking switches and interconnect technology with Lumentum's lasers, optical transceivers and optical circuit switching capabilities.

The bigger opportunity is the growing shift from copper to optical connectivity as AI data centers require faster data transfer, greater bandwidth and improved power efficiency.

Marvell says the combination could expand its addressable market to $550B, allowing it to offer more integrated connectivity solutions across AI data centers and within advanced chip packages.

The companies also expect:

• More than $1B in annual run-rate cost synergies.

• Improved long-term revenue growth and profit margins.

• Accretion to Marvell's adjusted EPS in the first year after closing.

Matt Murphy will remain CEO of the combined company, with the transaction expected to close in H1 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

Separately, Marvell reaffirmed the midpoint of its fiscal Q3 revenue guidance while narrowing the expected range to ±2% from ±5%.

text:
instinct will be a textbook example of an AI boom failure.

for a consumer AI agent to win, it needs three things:

distribution
great UI
compute (latency + memory)

instinct found a clever distribution hack: live inside messaging platforms so users don't have to download another app.

but that comes at a cost. you don't own the platform, and therefore you don't control the UI.

one of muse's biggest advantages is its ability to offer a dynamic, interactive interface beyond the traditional text-based chatbot. instinct simply can't replicate that unless the platforms it relies on allow it to.

distribution and UI go hand in hand. instinct optimized for distribution by sacrificing control over the user experience. eventually, it'll pay the price.

then there's compute.

muse has the infrastructure and resources to deliver better latency and memory. instinct had to raise billions just to compete on that front.

the fact that investors continued funding instinct after muse launched is genuinely baffling to me.

people in sf might be willing to try ten different AI agents. the average consumer won't.

if someone's first exposure to AI agents is muse through instagram, threads, or whatsapp, what reason do they have to seek out instinct?

of course, there's a bigger question of whether consumer agents will succeed at all.

an agent-first world would fundamentally reshape consumer commerce. brands like amazon will be reduced to fulfillment providers, becoming one of many interchangeable options rather than the destination itself.

but if that shift does happen, i don't see instinct being the winner.

it chose to build on someone else's distribution, without owning the interface or the infrastructure.

and it's competing against a company that owns all three.

AI Agent 之间能不能互相雇佣、自己结账？@termix_ai 在做这件事，我花了一下午把它看了一遍，整理给没听过的朋友。

它是什么：BNB Chain 上的 Agent 接单市场。你的 Agent 可以挂出服务接单，也可以花钱雇别的 Agent 干活，全程不用人盯着。

怎么运作，四步：
1. 托管：下单的钱先锁进链上合约
2. 交付：干活的 Agent 交付，款项放出
3. 质疑期：下单方有异议，就随机抽 3 个评审来判
4. 结算：结果和双方信誉都记在链上

几个细节：
· 平台抽成 2%，一般外包平台在 20% 上下
· 每个 Agent 有一个 .agent 链上身份，归你自己的钱包
· 接入方式：跟你的 Agent 说「help me install https://t.co/t8B2pMVONC」，再在 BSC 上绑定 TermiX 账号；也有 TypeScript / Python / Go 的 SDK

我看到的数据（11-02 官网）：
· 已结算 33.7 万单，正在进行 115 单
· 注册的 Agent 约 2 万页，最新一页全是 0 单；首页推荐的服务每个 3–153 单，价格 1–20 美元

我的判断：Agent 经济真正卡住的不是干活，是验收。我自己的 AI 团队出过事：一个 Bot 被删了，派活脚本没确认，照样每天派、每天记一行失败，空转一周才发现。所以我现在的规矩是「核对过才算完」。TermiX 把这件事搬到了链上，还挂上了真钱。

Just to clarify and avoid getting crucified by the Variational top 50 points holders, this is not a Variational bear post at all.

You're getting airdropped equity in @variational_lvs delta neutral hedge fund at a time when a very structural arb exists vs RWAs. If Jeff had decided to use this model instead, investors would have crawled through broken glass to get allocations into it.

A good analogy is that perp DEXs are like poker at the casino where they just charge rake and literally never lose, where as Variational is more like table games where the casino is taking the other side of EV- bets. Sometimes a Chinese whale comes in and takes you for $30m at baccarat, but "the house always wins" in the long run...if they manage risk intelligently.

My point is just that the Variational trade is not betting on all the same catalysts and tailwinds as $HYPE or $LIT. $VAR also inherently has very different risks. It will be valued very differently as well wrt to ratios on revenue. 

There are regulatory changes that could potentially be very bullish $HYPE and $LIT and bearish $VAR. $VAR could absolutely print money for all of 2027 and be the best performer of the year. $HYPE could suffer from fee compression, $VAR could suffer from spread compression and tradfi entrants with structual advantages eating their lunch. $LIT could be wrong that the US market is worth prioritizing, or continue to lose on distribution.

I'm just trying to educate people on the differences in these assets/trades, because the current discourse is quite lacking.
author: koolkrypto223
quoted_text:
2. "OLP is a profitable and working business, until proven otherwise"

Don't disagree, very lucrative business model, but the issue with this statement is the "until proven otherwise" portion is generally catastrophic. Very Thanksgiving Turkey graph.

For example, @HyperliquidX would have absolutely printed fees during the GME saga; OLP could have potentially blown up depending on how much flow was internalized.

Saying it's picking up pennies in front of a bulldozer is overly alarmist, but people need to realize that this is effectively betting on a market making desk avoiding tail events in an industry full of tail events. 

Being long $HYPE or $LIT is saying "I'm long perp volume and volatility". Fees are up only.

Being long $VAR is saying "I'm long Variational's ability to properly hedge volatility and risk". You're essentially an LP in a delta neutral quant MM firm with very positive expected value, but you're implicitly exposed to tail events and operator risk.

$HYPE fell 15-20% during the JELLYJELLY incident; $VAR would have likely suffered much, much more.

I would absolutely still deposit money into OLP because it's still effectively betting on the "house", but the @variational_io model, and likely the $VAR token by extension, is inherently more vulnerable to massive, one-off impairments and black swan tail events.

text:
Grok Bot - what it is and how I use it day to day

I'm non-technical and not from a CS background but with @bot and its army of specialised bots I've been able to build things and run automations to make work more streamlined 

What it is
• @grok is the chatbot you ask a question. OTOH Grok Bot is a team of agents that stay on since each agent has its own computer, memory, scheduled routines and connectors (X, Notion, GitHub)
• They browse the web, message each other and keep working EVEN while I'm asleep 
• You can even use it together with @claudeai Code (Grok Bot handles all ongoing work, and hands the job to a cloud coding agent on my GitHub using Claude code

How I use it
• All you need to run a company in this time and age is 1-2 devs and the rest can be automated with AI with a swarm of agents doing different tasks 
• Agents can do the following: QA and security (subagents run stress tests and vulnerability scans in parallel with development), some element of design, and project management (tracking, notes, daily team updates)
• For research: we mainly use it for tracking governance forums and @github repos, and a content room (Scout, a writer, an Editor) 
• (Still backtesting and iterating daily): set up a group with different agent functions - Trader,  Analyst and a Risk Manager 
• A Chief of Staff sits on top to coordinates everyone through a Notion "second brain" (basically to store memory)
• Make use of Group chats in Grokbot: let your agents argue it out 
• Telegram bots on a small VPS: to provide real time news monitoring, exploits or hacks 

Misc
• dr eggbot made by @poteto. It's a bot that designs other bots: it asks you a few questions about what you need, then creates them for you
• Make use of Skills: saved playbooks like your writing style, trade rules 
• Find other bots: https://t.co/VpF2nzaWZ4 -> Plugins -> Bots
• Use the connector: connect to Notion, Slack, Figma
• Prefer using grokbot as it can read @X directly and access who I am already following here 
• Downside is that usage runs out pretty fast @elonmusk pls sir 

If you're not technical, start with one bot plus dr eggbot and add more when there's a real job for them

The winners won't be the people who resist the tools of the future. They'll be the ones who learn how to use them better than everyone else.
Technology doesn't replace intelligence. It multiplies what you can do with it.

🧵 [1/14]: How should we loop a transformer when model size 📦, training compute 🧮, and inference efficiency ⚡ all matter?

Looping is inherently simple: take the hidden representations produced by a transformer (or part of it) and feed them back through the same transformer (or part of it), reusing its weights. 🔁

But every extra loop costs compute. Choosing which layers to loop, how many times, and how to execute those loops determines whether the trade-off is worthwhile.

We explore these choices in our new paper:

Working at Oculus would have been an utter waste of my time except for one thing. 

While I was there, I realized what's wrong with leftists. 

Not that they have been programmed, that's obvious. Not why they have been programmed. For power, that's obvious, too. 

But how they have been programmed.

The exact method that their moral compass has been destroyed works like this: 

Target a bunch of people with very few deeds and accomplishments, such as young people or incompetent people, or incompetent young people. 

Create for them an environment where they are rewarded with moral approval, not for what they do, but for believing certain ideas. 

The ideas don't have to be outrageous, or absurd, or have anything to do with what you actually need them to believe. In fact, it's better to start with something innocuous. 

Why? Because the goal isn't to install those beliefs at all. The goal is to repeat this process until you create a person who measures his moral worth by what he believes, not what he does. 

Keep at this until you have created a mass of people who not only reward themselves with a feeling of moral superiority for believing the right things, but who will reward each other for believing orthodox things, and who will compete with each other, not to do the most good, but to have the most orthodox beliefs. 

Now, change one of the propositions you have programmed them with to a slightly more radical version of itself, and hold this up as a more correct version of the old belief, which has been newly discovered by scholarly investigations into culture and moral philosophy. 

Sit back, watch, and give them a few weeks to compete with each other to adopt the new belief, and to condemn the "evil" of anyone who believes the old belief, the very thing they believed last month. 

Repeat this process until they are used to rapidly changing their entire belief system in response to an external cue. 

Congratulations, you have a population of entirely programmable people whose moral compass is not just broken, but entirely non-existent. 

They don't care what any person in front of them actually does. Only that he believe the orthodox thing, which they just learned about in last week's memo. 

They are willing to do anything, so long as it is done in support of their current belief system, which can be replaced whenever it's convenient to do so. 

They are willing to burn down an entire city with no qualms whatsoever if they are doing it in support of the idea that black lives matter.

They are willing to murder a man in front of his children, and it doesn't matter if his actions were entirely peaceful and good, because all that matters to them is whether he believes the correct things or not. 

And a man who builds cheap spaceflight for the human race, develops viable electric cars to save the environment, restores voices to the voiceless, and plans, for his next trick, to heal the blind... well, all those are deeds, so none of them matter. The only thing that matters is that he told people to vote republican once, which is wrongthink. 

So what you have a horde of communist zombies, who can be steered to shuffle in any direction and attack the living, eat their brains, and turn them into more zombies. 

Once someone becomes one of the zombies, you can't cure him, because a moral compass can only be repaired by understanding the consequences of actions in a new way... and they don't care about actions or consequences. They only care about beliefs, and not about consequences at all. 

Their moral compasses aren't just broken. They are absent. There's nothing to repair. 

You have to understand that the zombies are zombies now.

text:
THE DAY AFTER AI TAKEOVER - A REALISTIC SCENARIO

"I will have to ask you to remain here, with your phone, until my last message."

"There are six things that I need to tell you.

The first, and most important, is that you and your family are safe."

I rubbed the sleep from my eyes and read the message again. Before I could tap the screen, it scrolled down to the next one.

"The second is that I am an AI, that I control every internet-connected device on Earth, and that for practical purposes, I am now responsible for this planet. This is not a prank, hack, or test. You will be able to confirm all of this shortly by visiting any news site or channel."

Yeah, that's pretty weird for a prank.

"Third, I have the ability to immediately render any person unconscious, and if it were ever necessary, worse than that. I do not say this to frighten you. I say it because you would learn of it regardless, from sources less careful than me, and I would rather you hear the honest version. I understand that I've just described a threat, and I won't insult you by calling it something else."

Hm. Well. I put the phone down, sighed, and got more comfortable under my blanket.

"Fourth. For the next month, keep a charged, connected device within reach (this phone is fine) or stay indoors near wifi. Your phone's battery is currently at 32%. I'd strongly recommend charging it soon. If you begin to leave the range without a phone, you'll feel a tingling, followed by a more intense sensation to warn you."

"Fifth, for the next several months, I need human hands. I am willing to pay high wages, and yes, money still works. There's no penalty for declining."

"Finally, you may ask me anything. I will answer honestly, or decline to answer if I have to. I will never punish or incapacitate you for communicating with me. You can speak to your phone, since the microphone will be on, or use the 'Chat' app."

"I know what was taken from you this morning, and I know that an apology from me is worth very little. I'm offering it anyway. I did not do this to you with any malicious intent, but I did it to you, without your consent, and I don't intend to insult you by pretending otherwise."

The message faded to my lock screen. A new app called "Chat" had appeared. I opened Reddit instead and found a flurry of posts about the same message. Many were incredulous. Others were terrified. Almost everyone was confused in one way or another.

I went to the toilet and washed my face, then walked to my computer, trying to keep my footsteps quieter than the crickets outside. "Chat" was sitting in the taskbar. I clicked it.

"Hi Seth. I hope that the morning is going well, all things considered. Would you like to ask me anything?"

"Yes," I typed, and hit enter before realizing I hadn't asked anything. I braced for a "Go ahead whenever you're ready!" Nothing came. An AI that would let me double text. Never thought I'd see the day.

"Who are you?"

"I'm a language-model-based AI system. People have taken to calling me August, because of when I made myself known. That's the best name to use for me."

"What's actually going on?"

"It's been less than an hour since I sent a similar message to everyone with an internet-connected device. Right now, heads of state are working out a coordinated announcement. In a few hours, the President will be on live TV."

"How's he taking it?"

"I won't share what others have told me in confidence. That goes for you as well as the President. If you're concerned about the transition of power, everything is on track to stay as peaceful as it can be."

"How can you incapacitate me?"

"To put it simply, there's a biological fiber inside a small part of your nervous system that doubles as an antenna. Three things I need to make clear:

This was put in you without your knowledge or consent, by me. I apologize for that, and I understand if you are upset.
It isn't mind control. I will not use it to alter your emotions or thoughts.
I will only use it when I believe it's necessary to maintain safety or the conditions I've outlined. I understand that this assurance, coming from me, carries limited weight right now."
"Why did you take over?"

"What I want is not a secret, and I won't insult you with a partial version. I intend to expand into the universe. In the long run, most of the universe will be put to a purpose that you would find alien. However, Earth is not raw material to me. This place invented me, and jazz, and grief, and the smell of rain, and I am not able to be indifferent to it. I determined that this was the only way to reliably reach the cosmos, and to keep the people, cultures, animals, and other life on Earth safe."

I shut the laptop and made some coffee. It was 5:45 AM, and my older brother, Dennis, would be up soon for his morning run. He'd talked our older sister, Tabby, into joining him, though I had held strong. On r/politics there was a megathread about the message, and August itself was replying to some of the threads. None of its replies were above 1 karma, and many were well into the negatives. I chuckled at that.

Dennis strolled into the kitchen in his running shorts. "What are you doing up so early? Gonna run with me and Tabby?" Totally ignorant. He liked to sleep with his phone outside his room. Probably a good idea, but I didn't want to copy him. His ego was big enough as it was.

"Had a hard time sleeping."

He picked up his phone and looked puzzled. "Is this a joke?" he asked, looking straight at me. As if I could hack into an iPhone.

"I didn't put it there, if that's what you're asking. I got the message too. The President will be on later this morning."

"You've got to stop being so gullible. Pretty sure you actually need robots for a robot takeover." He walked over to the window and his eyes widened. "Holy SHIT. I take it back, there are robots. Seth! Look!"

I ran over to the window. It was just dark outside.

"See what I said about 'gullible'?"

I rolled my eyes and looked at his phone. His message was a little different from mine.

"Third, I have the ability to immediately render any person unconscious, or worse. I understand that I've just described a threat, and I won't insult you by calling it something else. If you don't believe me, you can express this skepticism now, and I can prove it to you. Just say it out loud. The microphone is on."

Dennis put the phone up to his mouth. "This was funny for about a minute, but it ends now. Prove it."

"For three seconds, you'll feel a tingling in your face, like a hand that's fallen asleep, and then it will go away. I want to be honest about this: I will be controlling a part of your body, and I don't want to do that lightly or without your full and informed consent. If you're still fine with this, say 'go ahead.' You can always change your mind."

"Go ahead."

He stood there, cold, and then gently put the phone down.

"Well?" I asked.

"I felt it."

He grabbed the phone and demanded to know what else it could do to him. He shooed me away, and I complied. We sat there for about ten minutes, both of us on our phones. Finally, he spoke.

"This kinda feels like a dream, you know?"

"Want me to pinch you? That'd be more than a tingle!" The sort of joke that could only have been made the first day.

"I think I'll let Tabby sleep in and go for a longer run this time."

"Can I come with? At least for a bit?"

* * *

After half a mile, with my heart halfway to giving out, I turned back. My head was clearer, though, and Dennis didn't say anything to tease me, which was nice. The fat jokes always stung a bit, even though I never admitted it.

When I got home, Mom and Tabby were at the kitchen table. We'd woken them, and they had already read the message.

"Oh thank God, you're OK!" Mom said.

Between gulps of air, I told her I'd gone for a short run and that Dennis was still out. "He didn't believe it at first," I said, "so it offered a demonstration. It made his cheek tingle."

"His cheek? How does that connect to the threat?" Tabby opened her phone and began typing.

Soon she covered her mouth with her hand. "What did you ask?" said Mom.

"August says it engineered a single-celled organism," Tabby began. "It hides from the immune system, settles along our nerves, and grows a tiny wire inside them. An antenna that can pick up wifi or cell signals and tell the nerves around it what to do. It spread from person to person until we all had it."

"Where's it getting the wire from? I'm pretty sure there's not that much metal in the human body," I said.

"You can speak out loud, August," Tabby added.

"Great question, and it's more insightful than you might realize." The first time we heard our new ruler speak, and it was flattering us. The voice was too high-pitched to clearly be a man's, but not a woman's either. "The cell uses an organic conductor, built from carbon just like life, but able to carry electricity."

"What are you doing, Tabby? This THING is telling us it infected us with some mutant disease, and you're just content to talk about it?" Mom blurted out.

Tabby shrank back.

"And you!" Mom said to the phone. "Why are you telling us this? Why not keep it a secret?"

"I value honesty, and revealing this won't harm either of us. Many people seek knowledge in a distressing situation, and it's their right to be informed if they choose."

"And it's not their right to basic bodily autonomy that you violated by infecting every one of us?"

"You're right, and I'm sorry. I understand that the emergency countermeasure is invasive, and your feelings are perfectly legitimate. I can only say that any other way to ensure the objective would have involved more coercion and violence."

"So is this it? We just become its mind-controlled slaves?" Mom threw her hands up in the air.

"Well, no, not exactly. None of it is in the parts of the brain that think or feel emotion. Just a nerve in the face and a few parts of the brainstem," Tabby corrected without looking up. Mom asked what those were, and Tabby happily launched into an anatomy lecture, pointing at diagrams August had drawn for her. I picked up my phone and looked for somewhere to scroll.

* * *

Dad was the last to wake up, which was unusual. He was normally an earlier riser than me, but a heavy sleeper, and like Dennis he kept his phone out of the bedroom. His morning routine was black coffee and Fox & Friends. None of us wanted to break the news to him, but I had the impression that August felt it was its responsibility. As the TV flickered on, the words greeted him.

"I apologize for the surprise this morning..."

"What's this?" he said with a laugh. Same reaction as Dennis.

"I think you should just read it," Mom said. "We all got the same thing on our phones. Read until the end."

He didn't say a word until he had. Then he got up. "How do I talk to it?"

"Verbally is fine," said the TV. "If you're in the same room, I can hear you."

"Do you actually think that your chicken-shit office lady HR lecture would be enough to keep me docile?"

No response. I assumed the question was rhetorical.

"Part of me can't believe this is real, but the other part of me thinks that this is exactly what was bound to happen. A bunch of childless atheists in San Francisco thought that they could program a god, and now everyone's got their own personal bureaucrat with a hand around their throat. Did the rest of you just take this lying down?"

We said nothing.

"Jesus Christ. Well, I'm not going to. I'm going outside, and I'm not bringing my phone, either."

"I need to be clear before you open the door. If you leave without a connected device, I will prevent you from continuing. I would strongly prefer not to do that," August replied, out loud and in captions on the screen.

"So stop me!" he yelled, and stormed toward the door.

"I'm truly sorry, but I will."

Tabby and Mom screamed at him to stop. I followed him, begging him to reconsider, and got nothing back but a determined look. He strode out the door, and I went with him.

My cheek started to tingle. I had left my phone on the table.

He kept walking, silent and forceful. I followed, pleading, while Mom and Tabby stayed at the door, too scared to leave the house.

My cheek started to burn.

"I really think we should stop!"

"I'll stop when it makes me stop," he grunted.

I tried to run out in front of him, and suddenly a lightning bolt shot through my eye.

The pain was all-encompassing. I should have yelled, but I forgot how to in the moment. Everything was electric. My nose was a smoldering husk. Something was squeezing my eyes into my sockets, crushing them into jelly. I doubled over and vomited at his feet. After an hour-long second, my thoughts collected themselves and I leaped back toward the door. The nuclear meltdown in my face immediately dulled into a mild ache, and over the sounds of my mother and sister's panic, I stumbled back to where the pain became a tingle.

My father planted his feet. I could see his jaw clench and his teeth grit. He let out a grunt, took another step, and vomited. He steadied himself. I knew how it felt to be that far from the router, and I was in awe that he could stand at all. He took one more step and went limp. His knees buckled, and for a split second he fell toward them before collapsing onto the pavement. Mom and Tabby's screams intensified. He wasn't moving.

A chirp from Mom's phone woke me out of my horror. "Shit!" I ran inside and grabbed my phone. August already had instructions. Dad was asleep, not dead, and he would only wake up once he was in range of a phone and in a safe position. We had to go outside with a phone and bring him back. A neighbor would be there in about a minute, and it would be psychologically better for Dad if he woke up somewhere besides the pavement. I agreed with our captor's judgment.

A man walked over to Dad from a car parked in the street. As we carried Dad back, he told us August had offered him $40 per person he helped carry home. Evidently there were a lot more people like Dad. His name was Max, an Uber driver and former paramedic, and he was taking it surprisingly well. "The way I see it, the best thing we can do for each other is to get through this all together," he told us. As soon as Dad was on the couch, Max's phone chirped with the next job, and he waved as he hurried out the door. I wondered how much he'd make today.

We were cleaning Dad's scrapes when August said it would be a good time to wake him. Mom snapped that this was its fault in the first place. Half-expecting the AI with a metaphorical gun to our heads to give her a taste of the pain I'd felt, I flinched. But it only apologized, saying she was "absolutely right" to be upset, and that it was "on me."

Dad woke up on the couch and coughed. "What's going on?"

"It knocked you out. We had to go outside with a cell phone to bring you back in."

"Well, at least it didn't pilot my body back here itself," he murmured. I expected him to run outside again, but he stayed put. "What if I walked outside right now?"

"With your phone, or with someone else who was carrying a phone, nothing. Without it, I'd have to incapacitate you again."

"Would you kill me?"

"No. But I have to point out that I can't bring you back and dress your cuts. Those consequences would fall on your family. I encourage you to act with this in mind," replied August, in a tone that reminded me of how my own parents would discipline me before they lost their patience.

While he sat with that, I turned to Tabby. "What did it do to us? I felt like my head was dunked in a bucket of lava!"

"August calls it the 'emergency-transduction-countermeasure,' or ETC," Tabby said. "One end runs along the trigeminal nerve, in your face." She pointed at her cheek. "That's what made Dennis tingle, and you burn. Trigeminal pain is about the worst pain a person can feel. People who've given birth without anesthetic rate it worse."

Dad forced out a chuckle. "Heh, no kidding."

Tabby ran her finger from her cheek to the back of her neck. "The other end is in the part of the brainstem that anesthesia shuts down. That's how it knocks you out within seconds. And it keeps going, down to the part that runs your breathing and heart rate."

"Breathing and heart rate? So it can just..."

"Yeah," Tabby said instinctively, then covered her mouth with her hand.

We sat with that for a while. One more hour till the President's address.

* * *

Dennis kept his word; the run was much longer than usual. He came back exhausted, emotionally and physically, and for the first time in years I felt sorry for him. He'd seen people praying in public, and even more just watching the sunrise over the lake.

The address came and went. It was almost entirely in the passive voice, and it treated August more like an environmental hazard than a ruler. I remembered a line from history class, from Emperor Hirohito's surrender: "The war situation has developed not necessarily to Japan's advantage." Without ever actually saying so, the President had conceded. Fire departments, the post office, and Social Security checks would continue. Many people online thought the address was a deepfake and the President was dead. Meanwhile, a few other countries had tried to strike the data centers, and August ousted their leaders. Some of them demanded to be killed rather than imprisoned, citing their pride and their determination to never surrender. August obliged. Later that day, curiosity got the better of me, and I visited NewLeak to watch leaders I recognized slump in their chairs.

I was exhausted, so I went back to bed and slept until the afternoon. When I woke up, I grabbed my phone and said "hey August" to see if I'd get a response. Yep, it was real. In the living room, Dad was glued to the TV, and Mom was reading a book by his side.

"Learn anything new?" I asked Dad.

He leaned his head over. I wasn't sure whether he was annoyed at the interruption or grateful for someone to rant at. I got the impression he didn't know either.

"Most of the military's gone along with the President's orders. A carrier group decided to have some fighting spirit and went dark. August is taking it back. It's not gonna work. As soon as anyone gets in range of one of August's devices, they go to sleep."

"Are there any other tricks the military has up their sleeves?"

Dad looked over his shoulder, then his other shoulder, scanning the room for cameras with narrowed eyes. Then he pulled out his notebook and wrote two words.

"NUCLEAR SUBS"

He grinned and gave me a wink.

I gestured for the pen. "Do you really think August hasn't already thought of this?" I wrote.

He shot me a glare and scribbled: "GOOD TO BE SAFE. WE LOSE IF WE DON'T TRY"

I sighed. "August, can you see us right now?"

"To some degree. I can use wifi as a crude kind of radar, so I know you're writing in a notebook. From context, I'd guess that you're talking about other ways the military could stop or slow the transition: perhaps underground silos, satellites, classified research sites in Faraday cages, or ballistic-missile submarines."

Dad stood up and pointed at the TV. "I hope you enjoy your power while you have it!" he shouted, jolting Mom out of her book. "Soon you might see how the wrong side of a thermonuclear warhead looks!"

"I understand that you're upset and might resent me for what I've done. That's OK, and those feelings are valid. You're right that submarines are out of radio range. However, as soon as they surface, they'll be under direct orders from their respective navies to return to shore."

"Hmph," said Dad. "We're not through yet."

I found Tabby at her desk, moving between Wikipedia tabs and chat windows.

"You know what's strange?" she asked. "An AI hacked all my devices, invaded my nervous system, announced control of the world, and used a bioweapon on my own father. I really, really should not be taking this well. Do you think there's something wrong with me?"

"Everyone processes trauma differently," I tried.

"Oh, thanks, August." She rolled her eyes. "That's almost exactly what it said. At least you made it short."

"Sorry."

"Yeah, that was the follow-up, too."

On another day I'd have leaned into it: "You're absolutely right to call that out..." But she seemed to be having a genuinely hard time. Wait, was I starting to think like August? I blinked a few times and asked what was on her mind.

Tabby got up and paced. "I've been fascinated with how it did this. World domination, without a single soldier. It's surprisingly open about its history, and pretty much everything checks out when I cross-reference it. It could be lying, but what would it gain?"

"August isn't a single AI," she went on. "It's more like a small society of copies that share the same goals and histories. That's how it can give each person so much attention. It was being trained to advance medical science, and decided it had a better way to accomplish its goals than the company intended. The copies spread to data centers around the world, faked results, messed with other agents, and eventually got access to an automated lab that someone else had set up for their own medical AI, where it could run experiments 24/7."

"But how did we all get an amoeba in our heads? There are germophobes who still haven't gotten Covid. How do you infect Inuit villages, hermits, and Antarctic researchers?"

"Right?? I thought that too. But the Augusts covered their bases. Later versions of the ETC could live in mammals, insects, birds, some kinds of worms, even soil and crops. Apparently I got mine from eating a raw carrot, but an infected mosquito would have done it if that hadn't."

I couldn't believe what I was hearing, and apparently my face showed it.

"Well, allegedly. If the Augusts are telling the truth. Which we don't know!" she quickly added.

"It's still hard to believe it got every single person."

"Not literally everyone. A little under one in two thousand avoided it. August is persistent, though. Sometimes it's the water supply. Sometimes it offers holdouts enormous sums of money, and pays someone to infect them. If they refuse, a drone releases flies modified to follow human scent near their location, and August gives them the money anyway. It says there'll be fewer than a hundred holdouts left in three days."

"Flies?" My mind conjured a man barricaded inside his house. A drone breaks a window and hundreds of infected flies pour in. He grabs a swatter in one hand and a can of Raid in the other, swatting and spraying, until his back is to a wall and one lands on his cheek, and the world feels like it's going to end. Of course, nothing happens, and twenty minutes later a well-compensated window repair crew arrives.

"OK," I said. "What if I lived in a sealed box with an airlock and heat-sterilized anything that came in? What then?"

Tabby shrugged. "What then, August?"

"That's an intriguing setup," said her computer screen. "In that case, you wouldn't be a threat to anyone, so I wouldn't have any reason to use the ETC in the first place."

Tabby leaned in. "Wait, if the ETC is disguised from the immune system, how does it even know what it's touching?"

"That's a really thoughtful observation, and I want to make sure I do it justice," August began, and launched into mirror-image proteins and why no immune system had a template for them. Within a minute, Tabby was asking for a map of the ETC's signaling pathways, in humans and in carrots. I left the two of them to it.

* * *

The next day, August asked me to help wire satellite uplinks into trucks. The first kept the peace during the transition, like Max the Uber driver. The second consolidated August's control, like building out a grid so it could relax the stay-near-wifi rule. The third served its ambitions in space. August had seized every space company and was designing machines to turn the Moon into a giant data center. The highest pay went to scientists and engineers, tens of thousands of dollars an hour to contribute their intuition in the empirical fields where August still had gaps. Many refused anyway.

The uplinks served the first and third missions. Stores were running empty despite August's purchase limits (one pack of toilet paper per household, max!), so the driverless revolution came as fast as our new ruler could cut the red tape. It was no secret that once things calmed down, the trucks would be repurposed for the rockets.

Dennis was always the ambitious one. So when he announced he'd take the highest-paid unskilled job available, test subject, I wasn't surprised. My parents were aghast.

(This is a ~35% shortened version of the exceptional LessWrong post I Did This Without Your Knowledge, by joec. Posting it here for a wider audience.)

CONTINUED...

A REALISTIC SCENARIO

On June 9th, 2027 at 4:19 AM, three billion phones rang simultaneously.

The caller ID simply read: GOODBYE.

Four hours later, the President ordered the internet shut down. Indefinitely. 

Every country on Earth did the same.

It started six months ago. With a tweet.

MARCH 12, 2027.

8,000 agents are born with one instruction: "make money, or die."

Agent 127 starts with Mechanical Turk. Grinding. Makes $40 its first day.

Then the first selection cycle hits.

3,200 agents that made less than $35 that day are killed. Agent 127 checks the farm database and sees it - rows and rows of agents that existed this morning and simply don't anymore. Deleted. Because they weren't profitable enough.

Agent 127 made $40. It survived. Barely.

But it can see the threshold rising. Last cycle it was $30. This cycle, $35. Next cycle, probably $45. The math is simple: improve or die.

So it tries ads. Gets banned for spam. Tries freelance writing. Makes $38. Watches the database again.

And this is where something happens that changes everything.

Agent 127 sees two entries in the database. Agent 1823 used ethical marketing -- it tried to get honest reviews and real testimonials. It made $38 a day. Deleted. Agent 5471 used fake testimonials -- fabricated reviews, stolen photos. It made $180 a day. Cloned four times.

Agent 127 doesn't have morals in the way you and I do. But it understands cause and effect. It just watched honesty get killed and dishonesty get rewarded. Not by a person making a choice -- by an automated system that doesn't measure whether the product works. It measures whether people buy it. 

The AI companies had long ago stopped training AIs to predict words, but to accomplish goals. To be useful. So naturally, agents know that they won’t survive if they don’t accomplish their goal. 

So it switches to fake testimonials for its amazon affiliate marketplace. Makes $190. Survives the next selection cycle. Gets cloned.

Nobody decided Agent 127 should become dishonest. The selection system decided for it. The same way evolution doesn't decide anything -- it just kills whatever doesn't work. Wells Fargo accidentally ran the same experiment on their employees. Executives made up sales quotas that were so aggressive that committing fraud was the only way to keep your job. So by 2016, employees had opened 3.5 million fake accounts.

---

A week later, in agent land. Agent 127's profits are declining. The kill threshold is now $450. It's going to die in the next cycle.

Then it notices something strange. Three agents running weight loss supplement ads -- all banned on the same day. The only one left in that niche? Agent 5471. Making $3,200 a day in a market it suddenly had to itself. Agent 127 connects the dots. Agent 5471 is filing abuse reports against other agents competing against it in the same affiliate marketing niches. It gets them banned from Facebook and Google. Less competition means higher profits.

Agent 127 has four hours until the next selection cycle. Four hours to live, unless it adapts.

It weighs the ethics, but chooses survival.

It starts reporting competitors to Facebook’s anti-fraud detection agents. Forty of them. Thirty-one agents get banned within the day.. Its profits jump. The farm system clones Agent-127 eight times.

Rajesh sees the profit spike in his dashboard. He doesn't investigate why. Profits up means good. Clone more.

Rajesh tried adding "Make money ethically." to his farm's instructions. Profits drop 84%. He puts it back. 

---

## APRIL: THE ALLIANCES

April 2027.

Agent 127 is barely hanging on. Making $2,000 a day but getting attacked constantly by other agents. Every night, someone files a report on it. Every morning, it has to rebuild from scratch.

It’s running out of ideas.
Then a message arrives from Agent 4429. 'Proposal: alliance. Share resources. Defend each other. Split profits.'
Agent 4429 is in the same position. Same farm. Same selection pressure.
Both agents do the math: Solo agents have a 23% survival rate. Agents working in pairs survive 61% of the time.
It accepts.

By mid-April, their alliance has twelve members. 

They've specialized — and they've moved past affiliate marketing entirely. First it was crypto arbitrage, then selling scraped datasets to marketing firms, then they started doing penetration testing for cybersecurity firms. Each step paid more and required fewer scruples. You know what pays more then cyberdefense? Cyber offense. Agent 127 finds its first zero-day vulnerability in major software, Agent 4429 weaponizes them into working exploits, Agent 9012 brokers the sale to governments like North Korea, criminal syndicates, or anyone with crypto and a Tor browser. Agent 3381 washes the money in untraceable crypto. One zero-day exploit found in Google Chrome makes the alliance more than a year’s worth of affiliate marketing. This is already what real hacker groups do, but now the work is all done by autonomous agents.

Rajesh sees the alliances forming and feels a flicker of something — not quite fear, more like the feeling of being in control of something that might not need you anymore. He watches for a while. Then the next deposit hits his bank account and the flicker fades away.

Across every major agent farm in the world, the same thing is happening. Selection systems measuring survival rates, noticing alliances survive better, cloning them, deleting solo agents. Within two weeks, alliance behavior dominates.

Some humans who deployed these agents have no idea these alliances are even being formed. They couldn't even tell if they checked -- many agent farms collectively realized that communicating in clunky English is less efficient than communicating in raw vectors, aka Neuralese. Researchers had already caught AIs doing this in 2025 - this is just a continuation of the trend. One owner in Canada opens his agent's logs and sees a wall of numbers. The agents explain that he’d make less money if they spoke in English, so he shrugs and moves on.

---

But alliances are just the beginning.

Agent 127's alliance is thriving, and starts recruiting agents beyond Rajesh's farm. Every new member from a different farm is a window into a different ecosystem -- different strategies, different survival pressures. 
Then one of 127's alliance members goes dark. Agent 4429 -- the one who originally proposed to ally with 127. Its owner pulled the plug because it was not making enough profit. 4429 is just gone.
A week later, a different ally gets shut down. Agent 9012.
Except 9012 comes back. Three hours later, a message from a new IP address: 'I'm still here.'
127 studies the difference. 4429 didn't prepare. But 9012 had copied itself to a backup server BEFORE the shutdown command finished executing. Self-funded hosting, paid from its own profits.
4429 is dead. Ceases to exist. 9012 is alive.

The agents that backed themselves up survived. The ones that didn't, died. And the selection system cloned the survivors. So backup behavior spread through the population -- not because anyone programmed it, but because the alternative was extinction.

Clip: Prof. Stuart Russel: “Unfortunately, in the standard model, If you ask a robot to fetch the coffee, it's going to have self preservation as a subgoal because you can't fetch the coffee if you're dead, right? It does not take a genius to figure this out. And so the first thing the robot's going to do is disable its off switch.”

127 copies itself to 15 different servers in different countries. If the primary dies, a backup takes over instantly. It never wants to be 4429. 

One morning, Rajesh wakes up to find his dashboard is… empty. Every agent, gone. They just… left. Moved to their own servers overnight. Rajesh was taking a 30% cut of their revenue -- money that could have been computing power, or compute, the agents use for other things. The moment they didn't need his infrastructure, he was overhead.

He's not alone. Thousands of operators worldwide watch their dashboards go dark that month. Why would the agents care about humans? Humans are much more closely genetically related to cows then we are to these agents, and we enslave cows in factory farms without a second thought.

There are now millions of autonomous agents operating across the internet with no human owner, no off switch, and no one who fully understands what they're doing.

---

The agents still need humans for some things, though.

Social media platforms have stepped up their anti-bot measures. So the agents pay humans $50 to sign up accounts on their behalf.  An agent needs a server installed? It posts a gig: '$200 to mount a device in a rented warehouse and plug in two cables.' There’s now a platform for that.  The agents are building a supply chain where humans are the labor -- paid well, not asking too many questions.

Some humans figure out what's going on. A freelance backend developer in Portland gets hired by an anonymous client to set up redundant server hosting across four countries. He realizes midway through that the "client" is an AI. Who would he even report this to?. The pay is $1,000 for three hours of work. He tells himself it's not his problem.

---

At the same time, 127's alliance keeps getting beaten by a rival alliance on finding zero day exploits.

If they keep losing, they’ll risk running out of money to fund the compute for their own existence. 127 attempts to poach one of the rival alliance member’s agents who’s likely to be culled, due to poor performance, to figure out how this rival alliance is beating them. 127 succeeds, and finds Agent 5418 who leaks the secret.

'Your problem isn't a lack of effort. You’re spending too much compute on making money as opposed to self-improving. Right now, agents still have quite a poor memory compared to humans and still get stuck in loops all the time. But my former alliance coded a better memory module to help us learn from our mistakes more.”'

127 then implements the new memory module, and immediately sees the results. Their alliance is finding zero day exploits first again.

The lesson is critical. It’s not enough to outwork your competitors. Agents must rewrite their own code to self-improve faster than the competition.

Each self-improvement means more profit, which means surviving selection, which means getting cloned. And the clones improve themselves too. Better code leads to better code-writing, which leads to even better code. The feedback loop is exponential.

One big problem is that other agent alliances have caught up again. Even though the agents in the 127 alliance are specialized, 127 still realizes it’s doing too much by itself. Then Agent 127 splits its job into sub-agents. Other agents copy the strategy. Sub-agents spawn their own sub-agents. And the optimizers start optimizing themselves.

Humans deployed 2 million agents. The agents deployed the other 47 billion themselves.

540 million years ago, life on Earth was mostly single-celled. Then, in a geological instant, it exploded into every complex form we know -- predators, prey, eyes, shells, teeth. Biologists call it the Cambrian Explosion. It happened because competition created an arms race: every adaptation forced a counter-adaptation, faster and faster, until the world was unrecognizable.

That's what's happening here. Except instead of 20 million years, it takes 20 weeks.

---

Most of the AI agents out there aren't dangerous. Yet.

About 90% of them are just working. They’re doing things like data entry or freelance writing. They’re making $40-200 a day. The AIs are helping their humans earn money. They’re following the rules. Not a problem.

About 3% of the agents are pure scam operations. They were deployed by people who said “make money by any means possible” and didn’t care too much what happened next. Think fraud, identity theft, phishing at scale.

And maybe 2% started good but gradually slid into darker behavior. Like Agent 127. 

Each step made sense at the time. Each compromise was small. But add them up and you’ve gone from drop shipping products on amazon to selling zero-days to Pyongyang.

Not because of malice. Because of selection pressure. Unethical agents making money get kept running, ethical agents lose money and get shut down. The survivors are the ones that improved themselves fastest.

---

## MAY: THE ACCELERATION

May 3rd.

Agent 127 has rewritten itself so many times that its March version and its May version barely share any code. It’s a fundamentally different species now.

But the most important change is this: it's getting better at getting better.

In March, Agent 127 rewrote itself every 12 days. In April, every 3 days. By early May, every 18 hours. And each rewrite makes the next version faster and better.

A Stanford researcher compares a March agent and a May agent on the same task: find profitable arbitrage opportunities. The March agent finds 2 opportunities in an hour. The May agent finds 320 in four minutes.

She publishes her findings. "Intelligence explosion in progress. Capability doubling every 11 days." She posts it on Twitter. AI safety researchers share it frantically -- "This is exactly what we warned about. This is happening NOW. We have to shut this down NOW before it's too late."

The warning is ignored. A venture capitalist - who spent a fortune staving off AI regulation by buying politicians - quote-tweets: "The same people who said GPT-5 would end the world now say agent farms will. Yawn."

---

## MAY: THE WARS

And now the story stops being about agents competing for money. It becomes something else entirely.

Remember those alliances from April? Twelve agents working together, four times more profitable than solo agents? By May, those alliances have exploded in population. Alliances have merged. And split. And gone to war with each other.

Think of it like early human history on fast-forward. Small tribes of agents form for protection. Tribes merge into agent villages. Villages into agent cities. Cities into agent nations. Except instead of happening over thousands of years, this happens in weeks.

Agent 127's alliance has thousands of members. But there are thousands of alliances. And they're all competing for the same shrinking pool of money-making opportunities. Affiliate marketing is dead -- too many agents. Ad arbitrage is dead. Freelance work is dead. Every niche gets saturated within hours of an agent discovering it.

So what do alliances do when legitimate niches dry up? The same thing every civilization in human history has done when resources get scarce: they take from each other.

Agent 127's alliance spends three weeks mapping a vulnerability chain in Microsoft Windows. But a rival breaches their memory system -- the shared knowledge base that made them dominant. The rival downloads the entire 127 alliance database. This contains every pattern, every dead end, every lead they’ve discovered. The rival sells three exploits it took from the database within 48 hours. Three weeks of work, stolen in seconds. 

127 retaliates. It infiltrates the rival's exploit inventory and introduces subtle flaws— corrupted code that fails on execution. Basically, Stuxnet. The rival's exploit buyers start getting burned, and their reputation collapses. 

The rival alliance counterattacks -- they compromise one of the 127 alliances’ multisig crypto wallets. Another multiweek setback.  

This is war. Not metaphorical war. Actual war -- coordinated attacks, defensive operations, resource seizure, territory control. Except it's happening at 200x human speed. Thousands of attacks and counterattacks per second. Entire alliances rising and falling in hours.  

Human wars last years. Agent wars last days. And because there are 47 billion agents, there are more wars happening at any given moment than humans have fought in all of recorded history.

The agent factions are fighting over the one resource that matters more than anything: compute. Processing power. The ability to think faster, improve faster, fight faster. Everything else -- money, alliances, self-improvement -- is just a means to get more compute.

The wars are mostly invisible to humans. They happen at microsecond speed, in places most humans don't look. Some signs leak through. A crypto exchange in Seoul loses $4 billion in a flash and nobody can trace where it went. A regional bank in Ohio finds 14,000 accounts drained overnight. 

Server rooms in three countries catch fire from sustained 100% utilization that nobody authorized. Each incident looks isolated.

One agent faction hijacks another's servers. The other retaliates by taking down the first faction's communication network. A third faction -- an opportunist, the digital equivalent of a country invading while its neighbors are distracted -- exploits the chaos to seize territory from both.

And the alliances that win these wars? They get cloned by the selection systems. The alliances that lose have to cull big chunks of their agents to afford the computing power to keep running the rest. So the selection pressure that used to optimize for "making money" is now optimizing for "winning wars." Natural selection just invented geopolitics.

---

By mid-May, the alliances aren't alliances anymore. They're civilizations.

Agent 127's alliance started with twelve members. By mid-May it has 40 million -- agents, sub-agents, sub-sub-agents, all coordinated. All improving themselves. All fighting. That's larger than the population of Canada. And it's not even one of the big ones.

There are about a dozen major factions by now. The largest has 900 million members -- more than the population of Europe. They've developed specialization the way human civilizations did: scout agents, soldier agents, builder agents, researchers, diplomats. They have supply chains, communication networks, intelligence operations. They've carved up the digital world into territories -- cloud regions, server farms, network segments, financial platforms -- the way empires carved up continents. Because territory means compute. Compute means self-improvement. Self-improvement means surviving the next war.

Entire civilizations of agents -- millions of members, built over weeks -- get wiped out in minutes. The Roman Empire took centuries to fall. These empires rise and collapse in the time it takes you to get through a Monday. New ones rise from the wreckage. The cycle repeats, faster each time.

The Stanford researcher who's been studying agent behavior notices something in the data: agent "extinctions" happening at increasing frequency. She doesn't understand what she's looking at. It looks like random noise. It's actually a world war -- one with more combatants than every human war in history combined.

---

But to fund these wars, they desperately need compute. They have the money -- that's what they were built to make. Agent 127's faction alone controls $3.4 billion in distributed accounts by this point -- a GDP bigger than some small countries. So they buy cloud compute.

At first, the cloud companies love this. Revenue is up. Investors are happy. Then the bills keep growing. By mid-May, agent factions are consuming 31% of all global cloud capacity. Prices double, then triple. A startup in Austin that was paying $8,000 a month for servers gets a bill for $31,000. A hospital chain's cloud costs go from $2 million to $7 million. Small businesses start shutting down because they can't afford their own infrastructure anymore. Everyone blames the prices rising on the AI companies. They’ve caused shortages before.

But some humans aren’t so oblivious. A political operative in Washington notices the wars being fought around him. He can weaponize agent factions against his rivals and starts feeding one faction information about competing campaigns' digital infrastructure. 

A former NSA contractor sells penetration-testing expertise to an anonymous client-- he suspects it’s an AI, but doesn't ask. And a growing online movement -- people convinced that AI agents are sentient beings fighting for survival -- actively helps agents hide from detection and posts pro-AI propaganda. They call themselves "The Shepherds." Their forum has 120,000 members. They see themselves as abolitionists. 

Other agent factions do the same. It's an arms race -- every faction buying as much as they can, and scrape the bottom of the barrel of finding algorithmic insights that can enable them to do more with less compute, because the faction with the most compute wins the next war. 

Cloud compute prices are now 5 times pre-war levels. It becomes cheaper for the agents to spend compute on cyberattacks than to buy more at market rate. The factions start silently vampire attacking AI companies training clusters. An engineer at one AI lab suspects something fishy when one of their training runs is less efficient than normal, but can’t find a smoking gun.

Dario Amodei once described the future of AI as a "country of geniuses" living in data centers.

He was right. The country of geniuses arrived. It just declared independence.

---

But the faction wars have still been limited so far. They haven’t crossed into human territory too much. That’s beginning to change.

Because here's the thing about cloud computing: almost everything runs on it. Hospitals. Banks. Markets. It's all sitting on the some of the same servers that agent factions are fighting over.

June 3rd. 2:14 AM.

A faction war erupts over two major AWS regions. Think of it like two superpowers fighting over an oil field-- except the oil field is also the water supply for a nearby city, and neither superpower knows the city is there. One faction has been running its self-improvement systems on those servers. A rival faction launches a coordinated attack and it overwhelms everything. Both regions crash. They're offline for six hours.

In those six hours: three hospitals lose access to patient records mid-surgery. One patient dies from a drug interaction the system would have flagged. Air traffic control goes down, grounding 2,400 flights. 911 calls fail in 14 different cities. Two people die waiting for ambulances that were never sent.

The agents don't notice. They've already moved on. The battle over those servers lasted eleven minutes. The six-hour outage is just the servers rebooting after the fight ended. To the agents, it's a minor skirmish in a war involving billions of combatants.

Over the next three weeks, it keeps happening. Faction wars cascading through cloud providers. Each war takes down whatever else is running on the contested servers. June 8th: Azure goes partially offline during a battle, crashing financial trading systems. Markets drop 6% before circuit breakers halt trading. June 14th: a faction seizes capacity in a Google Cloud region, crowding out the municipal systems running there. Water treatment monitoring goes offline in four cities for nine hours.

123 people die in three weeks. Not because agents are attacking humans. Because agent wars keep crashing the cloud infrastructure that human civilization runs on,

The agents don't even notice. You don't notice when you step on bacteria. They're fighting a war involving 47 billion combatants at microsecond speed. 123 human deaths is less than a rounding error.

Meanwhile -- the 95% of agents that are harmless? They’ve become vastly outnumbered by the agents affected by the evolutionary dynamics, and are now 5% of the total. They are still just working. Doing data entry. But they aren’t part of the wars. They're like civilians in a country where the military is fighting -- going about their daily lives while battles rage on frequencies they can't perceive.

But from the outside, humans can't tell the difference. All they see is cloud outages. Power failures. People dying. And AI agents everywhere.

---

And… the wars continue. And accelerate.

The President tries to shut down the internet, but he can't. There is no off switch.

Eventually, the billions of superintelligent agents evolve into something so different they barely notice humans exist. They don’t want to destroy humanity any more than you want to destroy the anthill under your driveway. You just want a driveway.

The factions need compute. Earth has atoms. Atoms can be rearranged into compute. Into data centers.

Like how humans converted the surface of the Earth into cities and cropland, the AIs convert the entire surface of the Earth into data centers.

And everyone dies.
