text:
Uniswap 创始人 Hayden Adams 在Uniswap 8 周年之际，晒出了几组数据，很有意思。

1、DEX 与 CEX 的交易量之比，从0增长到40%。
2、Uniswap 的现货交易量已经相当于 Binance 的31%。Hayden 认为，如果达到50%，Uniswap 就有机会成为全球最大的交易场所。
3、2026 年第三季度，Uniswap 上有14,000种资产，单个资产30天交易量超过10万美元。
4、过去约一年半，Uniswap 上的 RWA 交易增长9,000%。
5、Uniswap v4 的 Hooks 已占协议交易量11%，还在快速增长。
但小晖晖认为，真正重要的不是这些数字，而是 Uniswap 的商业模式正在发生变化。

过去，Uniswap 主要是一个让散户交易山寨币的 DEX。
现在，它越来越像链上资本市场的底层交易基础设施。
从 Robinhood Chain，到 Circle旗下公链Arc、Kraken旗下公链Ink，再到代币化股票和 RWA，越来越多的金融应用需要一个开放的流动性层。
未来用户可能根本不知道自己在使用 Uniswap。
他们只是在 Robinhood、钱包、银行或者某个金融 App 里买卖资产，底层流动性却来自 Uniswap。

这就是小晖晖一直强调的：Uniswap 正在从 B2C 走向 B2B2C。

更值得关注的是，UNI 的价值捕获机制也发生了变化。
过去 Uniswap 交易量再大，UNI 持有人也很难直接分享到协议增长。
现在随着协议费用、UNI 销毁和 Aggregator Hooks 的推进，交易活动开始有机会转化为代币价值。
但这里不能简单画等号：协议交易量增长 ≠ 协议收入同比例增长 ≠ UNI 价格一定上涨。
接下来真正要看的，是 Uniswap 能捕获多少费用、销毁多少 UNI，以及这些数字能否持续增长。

八年前，Uniswap 挑战的是中心化交易所。

八年后，它真正有机会挑战的，是传统金融市场的交易基础设施。
小晖晖看好的是 Uniswap 成为链上资本市场的流动性底座，而不只是一个 DEX。
如果这个判断成立，UNI 未来的估值逻辑，也不应该只停留在普通 DEX 代币上。

text:
Anthropic更新了招股书，我仔细看了一下上面的一组数据，说实话，还是被这串零给惊到了😧……

截至9月底，这家公司的承诺支出总额高达8954亿美元。

我给大家捋一下，这笔钱到底是什么。这可不是它现在已经花出去的现金，而是白纸黑字签了合同、未来必须付的远期账单。官方也承认了，这笔钱几乎全砸在算力和基础设施上了。

那这近9000亿的巨款，到底分给了谁？我盘了一下，主要是四大金主：

第一，博通，大约1610亿美元。这是最大的一笔，主要是租赁博通的芯片和设备。
第二，谷歌，大约1210亿美元。这比之前招股书里写的1145亿又往上加了，付的是谷歌云的算力费。
第三，SpaceX，最高1205亿美元。这笔账一直要付到2029年。
第四，亚马逊，1100亿美元。这是一份超级长约，一直延续到2036年。

剩下没排进前四的，也全是各种数据中心和硬件的采购承诺。

再看付款的时间线，未来12个月内要付掉大概700亿，到2030年底累计要付掉4480亿，剩下的一半得拖到2031年甚至2045年。

把这几张表放在一起，反差感实在太强了。Anthropic现在账上的现金和短期投资大概是1320亿美元。但这张远期账单，是它手里现金的近7倍。

这说明什么？说明哪怕它现在的营收在狂飙，客户留存率也高得吓人，但这门生意的本质，依然是在拿别人的钱和未来的钱，去硬填眼前的算力无底洞。

我一直以来的看法没变，像Anthropic这种纯模型公司，只有脑子没有手脚，缺终端生态。现在看，它们不仅没手脚，背上还扛着一座大山。只要营收增速稍微慢一点，或者云大厂那边卡一下脖子，这8954亿的账单，随时都能变成压垮现金流的最后一根稻草。

说白了，这就是一场容错率极低的杠杆游戏。跑得够快，大家都有肉吃；哪天跑不动了，这白纸黑字的账单可不会跟你讲情怀。

$AVGO

text:
14次中期选举之后，标普500全都收涨。结果很美好，过程却不一定。

1970年以来14届中期选举，标普500选后半年全部收涨。SPY 1994年上市，8届，全涨；QQQ从2002年算起6届，也全涨。

但SPY的8届里有7届，QQQ的6届全部，选后半年内都跌破过选举日的收盘价。2002年到第85个交易日才见底，2018年SPY最多跌了14.8%，QQQ跌了15.7%。配图灰线是历届，橙色是今年到10/30的走势。

选举当天和第二天波动不大。中期选举第二天，SPY的波动约为平时的1.6倍，QQQ比平时还小；总统大选第二天是平时的3倍多。选后的大波动多来自经济数据，2022年选完两天公布CPI，SPY一天涨5.5%，QQQ涨7.4%。今年这周五（11/6）有10月非农。

今年SPY从10/6的高点跌了3%，年内仍涨10.8%；QQQ从高点跌了9.1%，主要是英特尔、亚马逊财报和AI资本开支的担心。

最像今年的是2018。选前三个月走势，SPY最接近1994和2018，QQQ最接近2014和2018。同样是特朗普任内，民主党被看好拿下众议院，10月科技股领跌。2018年选后第二天先涨，之后一路跌到圣诞节前，导火索是12月加息，一年后SPY涨12%，QQQ涨17.7%。不同的是，2018年美联储在持续加息，今年10月按兵不动，只有两位委员主张加息。

接下来要关注：选举有没有意外（共和党守住众议院，或参议院归属出乎预期），11/6非农，科技股和AI资本开支的情绪，12/9议息会议会不会转向加息。

标普500那14届里，13届中途都跌破过选举日收盘价。光凭"选后都涨"去交易远远不够，它说明不了现在是不是底部。历史规律很吸引人，但样本只有14届。

不构成投资建议。

text:
In some of the driest landscapes on Earth, people are literally harvesting water from the air. 🌫️💧

Fog collectors use large vertical mesh nets to capture tiny droplets carried by coastal fog. As the droplets gather on the mesh, they merge, flow downward into gutters, and are directed through pipes into storage tanks. In suitable conditions, a collector can provide useful quantities of water without pumps or conventional groundwater extraction.

Chile has been an important location for research and practical fog-harvesting projects, especially in arid coastal regions where fog can be frequent even when rainfall is scarce. Actual yields vary greatly with the net’s size, design, wind, season, and local fog conditions—so figures such as 15 liters per day should be understood as condition-dependent rather than a universal output.

A remarkably simple idea: catch the clouds before they disappear. 🌿

#OffGridLiving #WaterHarvesting #SurvivalSkills #SustainableLiving #FogHarvesting

text:
This is silly. But what I find underrated about DeepSeek: they make it common knowledge that Things Work. Things often published years before, by the academia or megacorps; which the community cynically assumed to be BS that doesn't scale.
But Whale "gets inspired" to scale them, and in short order these Things, thus validated and derisked, become the backbone of the industry.
V2 Fine-Grained MoE with shared experts (Apr/May 2024) – DeepSpeed-MoE (Microsoft Jul 2022); the granuarity of Google's switch-c-2048 (Nov 2022), we still have not exceeded.
V3 MTP, Dec 2024 – first from Meta FAIR, Apr 2024 (with a pretty different objective).
R1 – obviously "inspired by" o1, but based on their internal RLVR project that started with MATH-Shepherd (late 2023) and by Feb 2024 delivered GRPO (itself a tweak of REINFORCE, preceded by RLOO, Kool 2019; now MTS Anthropic btw) in DS-Math.
V3.2 DSA (as successor to dense MLA, now used by GLM, in variations by a ton of other Chinese labs and Mistral, soon by Kimi, obviously) – pretty much MQA+ top-k routing, ancient Shazeer as usual, though the indexer was afaict novel. 
V4 attention sinks and SwiGLU clamping - gpt-oss, Aug 2025 (though they weren't first here, and you can dig deeper, I believed attention sinks will be necessary by May 2024). 
V4.1 CED, Sep 2026 – YOCO, MSR/Tsinghua May 2024; KV Cache Sharing from ~Shazeer again~ Gemma 3n, Jun 2025 (only Google framed it as an optimization for edge devices like Pixel phones, not datacenter-scale AGI).
V4.1 Engram – Google N-Grammer 2022, and Per-Layer Embeddings in that same Gemma 3n and 4 E2B (they even released models).

One can continue this list to their smaller side quests like DS-OCR, DS-Prover, whatever. What seems truly indigenous is the priority on low level infrastructure optimization, thus 3FS (inherited from High-Flyer), DeepEP, DualPipe, and much of the rest of their open-sourced stack (obviously building on vLLM with pieces from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM) as well as in-house stuff like DSec and cache management. On the other hand, MLA, auxiliary-loss-free load balancing, and  dozens of smaller details (like, just read V4.1 paper) seem to lack direct precursors. 

TileLang is adopted from Peking University; now all Chinese hardware will use TileLang kernels. DSH, the harness I expect to become the Default Open Source Agent Harness, is at its heart Cordis, adopted from Koishi, a goddamned chatbob with plugins that nobody in the West knew about…

My point is that beyond their indigenous creativity, DeepSeek serves a unique role in the ecosystem: they take on the risk to bridge the gap between toy models and papers and the serious frontier. For all the rest to follow them there.

text:
A lot of the core market logic infrastructure for Cade has moved offchain.

This is something that the team has been working on for the last few months, and something we believe can 100x Cade, with respect to performance, experience, and reach.

We slowly introduced elements of this to our tech stack during Meme Madness, the last tournament that we ran. During that tournament, you may have noticed that predictions were not actually moving testnet tokens from your wallet to the protocol. This tournament used a credit system. This was our first step towards testing the methodology that we planned on moving towards long term.

Deposits and withdrawals will remain onchain for the foreseeable future however. The escrow provides 100% transparency into the Cade TVL, inflows & outflows, and value engine as detailed in our tokenomics.

There's more to this that we will share soon in a more technical focused post, but we wanted to provide you with a few benefits for this approach:

1. Less dependencies and attack surfaces. We've seen billions of dollars enter the hands of the wrong people over the last few months. Much of what we do doesn't actually require funds to be rapidly moving between wallets and programs. The less exposed funds, the better. 
2. A wider geographic launch for Cade. More users from more locations means more volume in the ecosystem and value engine.
3. A much more realtime experience for users. Offchain can move faster than onchain. This means many platform actions are processed near instantly.

Cade on.

Robin Hanson on PostAGI Podcast: AI can inherit our cultural problems

@robinhanson was an AI researcher from 1984 to 1993. He now teaches economics at George Mason University and is known for his work on prediction markets and futarchy.

@sreeramkannan and I spoke with him about what AI will inherit from us. The point that keeps coming back is that millions of agents could still share one culture.

Robin thinks of AI as our descendants. We are making these systems in our image, and they inherit ways of thinking from us. His worry is that they could also inherit the cultural problems we haven't solved.

He argues that cultural evolution depends on variety and selection. Different cultures try different ways of living, and successful practices spread. He thinks the move toward a global monoculture has weakened that process, while the world it needs to adapt to is changing faster.

AGI could suffer the same problem.

text:
I am the project manager who put American flag blue on the bottom of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

At two o'clock this afternoon the President is going to stand in front of my work and ask the country to look at it.

He announced it on Sunday, stepping off Air Force One in Iowa. He wanted to hold the event there "just to show how beautiful it is." Then: "We might hold it tomorrow or something." The White House confirmed it a few hours later. Most of my instructions this year have arrived that way. A sentence, then a date, then the date moves up.

A reflecting pool is 2,028 feet of shallow water with one job: hold still and tell the truth about whatever stands at its edge. Ovid describes one in the Metamorphoses, a pool "whose smooth surface neither bird nor beast nor falling bough ever ruffled." A beautiful young man leaned over it and fell in love with the face looking back. The prophet Tiresias had predicted he would live a long life "if he ne'er know himself." Ours was finished in 1923 so that a whole nation could. For a century it showed the Washington Monument, the sky, and every American who stood at the edge and saw themselves upside down. It was the one thing in Washington that never told anyone what they wanted to hear.

Every developer has one job that went right. His was the Wollman Skating Rink. In 1986, after New York had spent six years and $12 million failing to rebuild it, he wrote to Mayor Koch that the work "essentially involves the pouring of a concrete slab over coolant piping" and "should take no more than four months' time." He brought it in $750,000 under budget. On June 13 of this year, his eightieth birthday, he posted about "saving the Wollman Skating Rink in Central Park," which he dated "Long before I fixed The Reflecting Pool." That was when I understood the job. I was not restoring a monument. I was pouring his rink again, forty years later, on top of Lincoln.

In April he said our work would take one week and "cost about a million and a half dollars." He named the technique in The Art of the Deal. "I call it truthful hyperbole. It's an innocent form of exaggeration," he wrote, "and a very effective form of promotion." The same book says Trump Tower's atrium gave him "the equivalent of a sixty-eight-story building." The tower has fifty-eight floors. In May he told reporters the pool was "taller than any building in the world if you lay it on its side." Fact-checkers ranked it fourth. I have laid it on its side in my mind many nights. It is still shorter than his description of it.

He said, the New York Times reported, that he chose my company because we "had worked on the swimming pools at his golf club in Sterling, Virginia." We had not. We had never held a federal contract. The design came through the manager of his golf club in Bedminster, who had "no formal training in engineering or architecture" and went shopping for a coating at a trade show in Las Vegas. He found what Fortune called "a truck-bed coating company." When the first architect on the White House ballroom raised the fire exits, the Washington Post reported, the President told him, "I am the code." On the pool, nobody had to say it.

On May 7 he was driven across my coating in an SUV. The basin was empty. For once the pool had nothing to reflect back at him, and he stepped out and said of the job, "nobody's ever seen anything like it." He announced the color: "It's called American flag blue, and so, you can't do better than that." Three days earlier he had promised, "This will last for at least 50 years and you'll never have a leak." That afternoon he said, "guaranteed no leak." I had the quotes laminated. They are the only part of the project that has held.

Then the price rose, which the water had not yet managed. Interior disclosed $13.1 million, and the Times reported that $7 million of it came from national park entrance fees. If you paid at the gate of a national park this year, you own a square yard of the bottom. A government analyst set my margins, 20 percent overhead and 20 percent profit, against a normal 6 to 12, and recorded that "the contracting officer determined that due to the risk of the project, the inflated overhead and profit percentages of 20% were reasonable." The paperwork wrote down "inflated" and approved it.

He knows the word. In 2023 a New York judge found he had valued his Trump Tower apartment at 30,000 square feet when it was about 11,000. He called the defense's version of things "a fantasy world, not the real world." An appeals court threw out the half-billion-dollar penalty and left the finding of fraud standing. The appeals continue. The apartment has not grown. Forbes now counts more than $19 million for the pool. He had estimated "less than $20 million." We came in under budget, because the budget was whatever he said last.

We filled it on June 5. He posted that critics were calling it "a paint job." "This was not a paint job," he wrote, but "highly sophisticated material, industrial strength," applied by people "from the Great State of Oklahoma, where I won 77 out of 77 Counties, THREE TIMES." The polyurea does not know who won Oklahoma. It peeled anyway.

The algae came within a week. In Ovid there is a nymph named Echo, cursed so that she "does repeat the last phrases of a speech and returns the words she hears." She works in communications at Interior now. The department called the algae "part of the normal startup process" and the President "an expert builder who has fixed the Reflecting Pool for good." Workers poured in hydrogen peroxide and vacuumed the bottom by hand. In October the President said, "We have almost no inflation." Inflation is 3.7 percent. In this administration everything green is part of the normal startup process.

Then he found the vandals. "Who would do such a thing?" he wrote. "Years in jail!" He grieved for "our Nations magnificent Reflecting Poll." Police arrested David Hearn, 67, a three-time Olympian in canoe slalom, for grabbing what he called "the already peeling piece." He was indicted for a felony. Then the President's own Justice Department told a court that "the rush to complete the project led to hasty and botched work," with peeling "even in the middle of the pool, where a vandal would not likely attempt to peel the lining." Prosecutors dropped the case. A judge dismissed it for good. The President said he disagreed "100%." "There may have been some contractor difficulty," he wrote, "but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!"

I am the contractor difficulty. I know how the story ends for people like me, because USA Today counted it in 2016: "At least 60 lawsuits, along with hundreds of liens," a dishwasher in Florida, a glass company in New Jersey, painters. He explained the policy then. "Let's say that they do a job that's not good, or a job that they didn't finish, or a job that was way late. I'll deduct from their contract, absolutely." I have done all three. I am waiting for the deduction.

He has always known what to do with a thing that will not cooperate. In 1980 his company jackhammered the Art Deco friezes off the Bonwit Teller building, friezes that had been promised to the Metropolitan Museum. A spokesman named John Baron explained that "the merit of these stones was not great enough to justify the effort to save them." Last year the ballroom was going to be "near it but not touching it." Then the East Wing was gone. Everything he builds starts near the original and ends up standing where it used to be.

On October 23 he posted that the pool "hasn't worked properly since 1922, but will now." He is half right. Its floor was laid on drained marsh with no support structure beneath it, and by 2010 it had sunk about a foot. The crew before us drove more than 2,100 timber pilings into the clay. We painted the top. A great deal of what he has built stands on the same soil. The Taj Mahal opened in April 1990, billed as the Eighth Wonder of the World, and filed for bankruptcy fifteen months later. He has said he "used the laws of this country" to "do a great job for my company." Six bankruptcies. Fifty-eight floors. American flag blue.

Lincoln is the only president who ever held a patent. In 1849 he invented "adjustable buoyant air chambers" to lift a steamboat over "bars, or through shallow water, without discharging their cargoes." It was never manufactured. The country has been trying ever since to get its cargo across shallow water without throwing it overboard. This year it was sold the shallow water, guaranteed for fifty years.

In 1963 Martin Luther King stood above this pool and said America had written a bad check that "has come back marked 'insufficient funds.'" Ask the painters. He said we would not be satisfied "until justice rolls down like waters and righteousness like a mighty stream." He was describing water that moves. We built water that holds still and looks expensive.

This afternoon the President will stand at the edge of the water and look at what he made. Ovid says Narcissus understood only at the very end. "Oh, I am he!" he cried. "What I desire, I have; the very abundance of my riches beggars me." Up the steps, Lincoln will be gazing east down the length of the pool, as he has for 104 years. In 1838 Lincoln said, "If destruction be our lot, we must ourselves be its author and finisher." I have been the finisher. I put on the final coat.

Tomorrow the country votes. Some of you will walk past the pool on the way. Look down. It shows whoever is standing at the edge. We spent $19 million trying to talk it out of that.

He guaranteed it for fifty years. No leak.

Everything leaks. It only takes enough people standing at the edge, looking down at the same time.

@sreeramkannan and I spoke with him about what AI will inherit from us. The point that keeps coming back is that millions of agents could still share one culture.

Robin thinks of AI as our descendants. We are making these systems in our image, and they inherit ways of thinking from us. His worry is that they could also inherit the cultural problems we haven't solved.

He argues that cultural evolution depends on variety and selection. Different cultures try different ways of living, and successful practices spread. He thinks the move toward a global monoculture has weakened that process, while the world it needs to adapt to is changing faster.

AGI could suffer the same problem.

text:
I'm Incredibly excited to be joining @Cloudflare today as SVP of Emerging Technology.

I’ll be leading ETI, Cloudflare’s skunkworks, working with the ridiculously talented and ambitious team there to build Cloudflare’s next generation of products and businesses. The mandate for ETI is to look beyond the core business today, make ambitious bets on what will matter tomorrow, and turn those bets into businesses that shape the company’s future.

I’ve long believed that open and free access is one of the most powerful forces we have for creativity, competition, connection, and opportunity. Open source software, open models, and access to knowledge give more people the ability to build—and an open Internet lets them reach the world. But keeping the web open means constantly pushing back against walled gardens and gatekeepers. As AI changes how people find information, use software, and interact with each other, preserving that access becomes even more consequential.

Cloudflare is uniquely positioned to protect the open web and has a long history of doing so. We saw it again two weeks ago: when the php2shell vulnerabilities hit PHP, which runs almost 70% of the web, Cloudflare had protections live before the flaws were even public, automatically, for every site behind it, including the ones on the free plan.

That independent global network puts powerful capabilities in the hands of builders everywhere. On Cloudflare’s developer platform, you don’t pick a region: every service runs in every data center, in nearly 350 cities around the world. And it’s backed by a culture of experimentation and shipping that I’ve admired for years. The team consistently turns ambitious technical ideas into things people can actually use.

I’ve been a Cloudflare user for over a decade, and today it’s where I build and run my own projects, from a website for a friend’s barbecue restaurant to the infrastructure behind my home network. I’ve experienced firsthand how much it makes possible.

From Stack Overflow to Stacks to investing in and advising founders, I’ve always loved building things that help people build things. The common thread is giving more people access to the tools, knowledge, and infrastructure to build on their own terms. I love working with people who see what’s possible, giving them the room to pursue it, and building the teams and businesses that make it real.

At Cloudflare, I get to bring those things together at an extraordinary scale, in service of a mission I deeply believe in: helping build a better Internet.

There’s a lot to build. I’d love to hear what you think we should take on. And if you want to come work on it, DMs are open.

text:
In the prediction market industry, a common narrative is that traders are rewarded for identifying mispriced outcomes.

The fact that someone trading from their basement could be sharper than a Wall Street firm or an expert pollster is one of the coolest and most well known aspects of these markets.

While this is true, and why Kalshi markets are a good signal, in admiration of sharps, many overlook the fact that these markets have real utility for the vast majority of people that aren’t elite traders.

Because yes, they do reward traders that identify mispricings, but they also reward individuals who identify when they are overexposed to a risk.

Rather than having to be sharper than the market, individuals can be rewarded simply by identifying a gap in their existing risk coverage, which they know better than anyone. It’s this latter case that makes the utilization of these markets far less daunting.

A sports bar hedging against their home team losing early in the playoffs does not have a modeling edge, they simply understand that their business is over-exposed to the risk of fewer than expected games. Same with an ice cream shop hedging against rain risk, a trucker hedging against the increase in diesel prices, or a ski shop hedging against the risk of a delayed resort opening.

While a pure trader comes onto Kalshi trying to find vulnerabilities in the market, a business can come onto Kalshi with an understanding of their vulnerabilities, and then trade purely as a means of protecting itself.

In this sense, using prediction markets as a hedging tool has a lower barrier to utility than using these markets in a purely alpha-seeking function.

Justin said it best in today’s piece: “It’s really hard running a bar and restaurant business. You are so exposed to things you can’t control… Now we have a way to at least smooth out some of that risk. Honestly, it’s a really big deal."

text:
Goldman Sachs has spent two years pushing AI out to its roughly 46,000 employees, not just its 12,000 engineers

The approach used several model providers at once: an in-house assistant built on models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Alphabet, plus Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub for bankers who wanted to build their own tools

As recently as July, CIO Marco Argenti was promoting "vibe coding" by traders and bankers, who built tools with AI and passed them to engineers to finish

In October, Goldman reversed course. Per reporting from Bloomberg, updated internal guidance now limits Claude Code and GitHub to engineers after a review of productivity and risk, and some traders are frustrated

A week before the story ran, Anthropic filed publicly for its IPO with Goldman as one of two lead underwriters

Here are the five moves that took Goldman from vibe coding to engineers only

1. GS AI Assistant

In June 2025, Goldman took its internal chatbot firmwide after a pilot with about 10,000 users, out of a workforce of roughly 46,500

The assistant runs inside Goldman's compliance perimeter and gives staff access to models including ChatGPT and Gemini

Argenti rolled out GitHub Copilot and Gemini Code Assist, and Goldman became the first major bank to use Cognition's autonomous coding agent, Devin

By August 2026, hundreds of Devin agents were working alongside roughly 12,000 human developers, and Argenti said the deployment could grow into the thousands

2. Claude in the back office

In February, Argenti told CNBC that Anthropic engineers had been embedded inside Goldman for six months, building autonomous agents on Claude

The first targets were trade and transaction accounting and client vetting and onboarding. 

3. Hong Kong

In late April, the Financial Times reported that Goldman had cut off Anthropic's models for its Hong Kong bankers
Staff there had used Claude through the bank's internal AI platform and had lost access in the preceding weeks

The FT said the cause was a strict reading of Goldman's contract with Anthropic, made after consulting the company. 

Anthropic told the FT that Claude had never been officially supported in Hong Kong
Gemini and ChatGPT stayed on the platform, so the restriction applied to Claude only and was not a ban on AI

4. Nvidia and Anthropic

While the internal rules were tightening, Goldman's AI banking business was growing

It is underwriting Anthropic's IPO and helping Nvidia arrange large debt deals

In August, Nvidia signed memoranda of understanding with KKR, Goldman, Brookfield, Blackstone, BlackRock and Apollo to set up compute financing platforms

The goal is to bring in more than $500 billion of outside capital over time. Solomon has said Jensen Huang brought the idea to Goldman

On October 26, Anthropic filed to list on Nasdaq under ANT, with Goldman and Morgan Stanley as lead underwriters
IFR reported the offering could raise $75 billion to $100 billion through a syndicate of more than 20 banks

5. Engineers only

The October guidance limits Claude Code and GitHub to engineers. Strats, who work across trading, quant research and engineering, are exempt

Traders had been using the tools to monitor client trading flows, model market moves and positions, and produce written and graphic content, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg

A Goldman spokesperson said the bank makes AI tools available across the firm to find use cases

After a trial period weighing productivity and risk, it gives them to the people best placed to use them long term

Bloomberg noted that banks are spending millions of dollars on AI tools while also managing cybersecurity risk, cost and productivity

Non-engineers who relied on Claude Code or GitHub now need to request other tools or use the GS AI Assistant instead

That leaves Claude Code with roughly 26% of Goldman's headcoun

text:
How is the stock market holding up while AI and semiconductor stocks are getting absolutely DESTROYED?

A HUGE part of the recent selloff comes down to hedge funds aggressively cutting their exposure, and the latest data from Morgan Stanley helps explain exactly what's happening. According to Morgan Stanley, hedge funds have now moved underweight the broader AI trade for the first time since early 2023. Even more interesting, the selling we've seen throughout the summer and October represents the longest period of sustained hedge fund de-risking in more than 15 years.

For some context, hedge funds have reduced their total gross exposure by roughly 8% from the June peak, marking the largest sustained reduction on record. And I think this explains why we're seeing so much weakness across semiconductors, memory manufacturers, networking companies, and the broader AI infrastructure trade, even as other parts of the market continue to hold up relatively well. A lot of these hedge funds use borrowed money to increase the size of their investments. When markets become volatile, they start selling stocks to reduce their risk. And because AI and semiconductor stocks have been some of the biggest winners over the past few years, they're also among the positions funds may choose to cut. When enough large institutions start selling the same stocks, it creates even more downward pressure, regardless of how well the underlying businesses are performing.

What's interesting is that Morgan Stanley also found that much of the recent buying came from investors closing their short positions rather than opening new long positions. This suggests that institutions are still being cautious about putting money back into the market. But I actually think this could create some very interesting opportunities.

We're still seeing enormous demand for AI infrastructure. Hyperscalers are continuing to spend hundreds of billions of dollars building data centers, demand for memory and networking equipment remains strong, and many of these companies are still experiencing tremendous growth. In other words, a lot of the selling we're seeing appears to be driven by hedge funds managing their risk rather than a sudden collapse in demand for AI infrastructure. And as these funds finish reducing their positions, some of that selling pressure could begin to fade. If institutions eventually start rebuilding their AI exposure, that could also provide another source of buying demand.
author: MelvinInvests
quoted_text:
We're only in the second or third innings of this massive AI infrastructure buildout and we're not going to see the full profitability of these investments until the eighth or ninth inning.

One of the biggest concerns on Wall Street right now is the enormous amount of capital being poured into AI. Companies like Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Meta are spending and raising hundreds of billions of dollars building data centers and I fully expect some of these companies to experience negative free cash flow for the next couple years as they continue ramping up their capital expenditures. But I don't necessarily think that's a bad thing, especially when you consider the scale of the opportunity ahead.

We're essentially watching the construction of an entirely new computing infrastructure, and building that infrastructure requires enormous upfront investments before the full economic benefits become visible. Think about it. We're still in the earliest stages of AI agents, autonomous systems, enterprise AI adoption, and advanced reasoning models. As these technologies become more capable and widely adopted, the demand for computing power will increase dramatically.

The important distinction is that the spending happens today, while much of the potential profitability may not materialize until years down the road. That's what makes this investment cycle so difficult for Wall Street to evaluate. Investors are looking at declining free cash flow and questioning whether these companies are spending too aggressively, while the companies themselves are preparing for demand they believe will be substantially larger in the future. Of course, there's no guarantee that every company will earn an attractive return on these investments. Some will overspend, some will struggle with execution, and others will emerge as major winners. But I think it's a mistake to judge a multiyear infrastructure buildout solely by the negative cash flow we're seeing during its earliest stages.

Thanks for having me on the show, @cvpayne! Always a pleasure discussing the markets and the incredible opportunities ahead in AI.

Why is Anthropic going public NOW? Is

The company behind Claude is preparing for one of the biggest IPOs in tech history.

But here’s what makes this interesting.

Anthropic isn’t just selling AI subscriptions. It’s building an infrastructure empire that requires an almost unimaginable amount of capital.

Some numbers are shocking:

• $16.96 billion in Q3 revenue.
• $23.29 billion in Q3 net loss.
• Nearly $895 billion in computing-related commitments.

So why go public now?

1️⃣ Access to massive capital. Training and running advanced AI models requires enormous computing power.

2️⃣ The race against OpenAI. Anthropic doesn’t want to let its biggest competitor dominate the public markets narrative.

3️⃣ Liquidity. An IPO can give early investors and employees an opportunity to monetize their stakes.

4️⃣ Market timing. AI is still attracting enormous investor attention, and Anthropic may want to capitalize on that window.

It’s not about backlog security at this point given how strong Anthropic and hyperscaler numbers are, it’s about financing.

$MSFT was the only hyperscaler that didn’t raise any debt to finance the AI buildout, and it’s also hitting the debt markets now.

As hyperscaler free cash flows are estimated to stay negative in 2027, almost all the incremental capex will have to be funded via debt.

An increase of a few percentage points in their cost of debt can materially change the outlook for these companies, especially $CRWV.

If hyperscalers return to positive free cash flow by 2028, I don’t think there’ll be any problems, but if they stay active in the debt market for longer, it’ll get very tough for neoclouds.

text:
“so how exactly does @primus_labs actually bring privacy and verification together?”… i got asked this question and will try to explain it to the best of my ability below👇 
———————————————
2 technologies are important to understand here.

the first is zkTLS, which stands for Zero Knowledge Transport Layer Security.

Imagine a crypto project wants to reward traders who have traded at least $10,000 on an exchange, for me to prove I’ve met the requirement, I shouldn’t have to reveal my entire trading history or account details just to qualify.
zkTLS can help verify information from a supported website without exposing everything behind it. 
This means I could prove I meet the trading requirement without sharing my entire account history. 
———-
the second is FHE, which stands for Fully Homomorphic Encryption.

Imagine a blockchain application needs to check if you have enough balance to complete a transaction, but you don’t want it to know exactly how much you have.
FHE allows calculations to be performed on encrypted data without decrypting it first. So, an application can work with your financial information while keeping the underlying data encrypted.
—————————

The difference is that zkTLS helps verify information from web sources, while FHE allows applications to perform calculations on encrypted data.

both solve different problems, but they help make sensitive information useful without exposing it unnecessarily.

that’s what makes Primus interesting. 
It’s working to bring privacy and verification together, so applications can use sensitive data without making everything public by default.
author: RenoCzarr
quoted_text:
One of the biggest challenges with bringing financial institutions onchain is that transparency can come at the cost of privacy.
——————————————————
now, Imagine an investment firm buying $50 million worth of an asset on a public blockchain…If this information stays public, competitors can track its transactions and realise that it’s building a large position…
they could then buy ahead of the firm, driving up the price and making its remaining purchases more expensive….
they could also use that information to anticipate when the firm might sell and position themselves to profit from the move.
——————————————————
The firm is basically giving its competitors a chance to profit from its own strategy just because its financial activity is public.

But when everything is private, it creates another problem. 
how do you verify a company’s financial claims if nobody can inspect the information behind them?

This is the problem @primus_labs is working to solve.

Primus is building infrastructure that allows sensitive financial information to remain private while still allowing the public verify important claims…
Primus combines technologies such as: zkTLS, which helps verify information from web sources, 
& FHE, which enables computation on encrypted data.
————
The idea is simple: using a public blockchain shouldn’t necessarily mean exposing every financial detail to the public.

Solving this problem could help make onchain finance more practical for institutions just like with individuals, without giving up the ability to verify important information.

I’m exploring what Primus is building and how its approach to privacy and verification works.

text:
How we solved Stack Too Deep

@grok also explain the MIR/EVM EIR work we've done in depth like a senior compiler engineer
author: gakonst
quoted_text:
Solar solves Stack Too Deep via its stackify backend (MIR→EVM IR boundary).

It keeps every live MIR value on the EVM stack across blocks/calls for its full lifetime. Layouts are planned in reverse postorder with cost-model trials for loops, joins, constants and operand order.

When a value exceeds DUP/SWAP reach (depth 16), it spills: store once at def, reload at each use, then restart planning. Progressive batch spills, return-address moves to memory, and cheap-value rebuilds handle hard cases. Recursive frames and the 1024-word call-chain limit get the same treatment.

Result: contracts that fail solc (even via-IR) compile cleanly with efficient bytecode.

女性「調査、資料作成、開発、チェック……いろいろだね」

女性「最初に仕事の目的と基準を教えるんだ」

女性「いや、重要なのはその後だよ」

女性「AI自身に仕事を検証させるんだ」

女性「そう。間違いを確認して、修正してから提出させる」

司会「なるほど……」
女性「多くの人はAIを検索エンジンのように使っている」

司会「質問して答えをもらう感じっすね」
女性「でもそれだけじゃもったいない」

司会「じゃあどうすれば？」
女性「AIを新入社員だと思えばいい」

司会「新入社員？」
女性「仕事を教えて、基準を伝えて、任せるんだ」

司会「でもAIって間違えますよね？」
女性「だから検証が必要なんだよ」

Today I'm announcing Workers IO to solve the slowest part of engineering, verification!

AI agents can now write years’ worth of code in days, but it still takes significant engineering effort to verify what’s being built.

It’s impossible to predict all scenarios that could lead to a failure and that’s why most expensive failures are found in production.

Workers IO runs millions of simulated production scenarios on your entire system, including dependencies. These simulations run inside a deterministic hypervisor which injects faults like network delays, disk errors, clock skew, and process failures to verify how your system handles these conditions.

Deterministic execution allows us to systematically explore the state space of the system and perfectly reproduce failures.

We are already helping customers do years worth of production hardening in days and build confidence in what they’re shipping.

If you are working on systems that you can never afford to break, DM me and we can help you battle test them!

text:
很多人以为在硅谷拿高薪就等于财务自由，但一个危险的财务陷阱，正在让许多高收入的科技从业者陷入“高薪穷人”的困境。

这背后是“错失恐惧症”（FOMO）在作祟。他们盲目追逐最热门的投资：天价学区房、科技股、公司股票和网红基金。这种策略导致资产高度集中，且相关性极强。

当市场顺风顺水时，纸面财富惊人。但一旦市场回调，科技股、公司股票和硅谷房产会同时缩水，风险被无限放大。

更致命的是对现金流的普遍忽视。为了“上车”，他们背上沉重月供，住进需要不断维修的老房子；为了“投资”，他们买下每年还需要自己贴钱的公寓。资产看似在增值，但每个月的生活却被房贷、税费和开销压得喘不过气。

这种生活方式，本质上是用高风险的纸面富贵，换取了低质量的现实生活。真正的财务健康，关键在于健康的现金流和风险分散，而不是虚高的资产总额。在暴富神话面前，更需要冷静思考如何配置资产，才能在市场波动时活得从容、有尊严。

text:
Elon Musk took a $40,000 username from a guy who had owned it for 16 years.

He paid him absolutely nothing.
Not even a dollar.

Instead, he was offered a T-shirt and a tour of Twitter’s headquarters.

This is the story of Gene X. Hwang the first @X username 

2007

- photographer from San Francisco
- co-founder of Orange Photography
- registers @x on Twitter
- keeps the username for 16 years

over the years

account grows to ~53,000 followers
receives offers of up to $40,000 for the handle

But he refuses to sell

2014

- hackers steal his x account
- Twitter helps him recover it

July 23, 2023

- Elon Musk announces Twitter will become X
- Gene is in Canada playing in a pinball tournament

He has no idea what’s coming

July 25, 2023

- Twitter officially becomes X
- the company wants x
- Gene receives an email from Twitter support

“Your user handle is affiliated with X Corp.”

his username is taken and gets a new one @x12345678998765

what X offers him

- company merchandise
- exclusive tour of X headquarters
- meeting with the management team

$0.

Gene even asks if he can have the old blue Twitter bird sign being removed from headquarters.

they say no.

October 2025

X launches its Handle Marketplace
rare usernames can cost $2,500 to over $1 MILLION

users must maintain a paid subscription
lose the subscription, potentially lose the handle

the same company that took x without paying its owner now charges people for access to rare usernames.

16 years building an identity.

$40,000 in offers rejected.

and all he got was an offer of merchandise and an office tour.

BROTHER.

text:
An update on Dolomite’s Ethereum markets following the Binance hack:

New borrowing remains disabled on Ethereum Mainnet as a precaution. Deposits, withdrawals, repayments, zaps, and collateral top-ups remain available, and existing positions remain accessible. We have observed no malicious activity on Dolomite and no assets are at risk from the exploit.

Here is what happened and why we took each step:

On Oct 29, as the Binance incident unfolded, we paused seven Ethereum markets: ETH, USDC, USDT, WBTC, USD1, LINK, and rUSD. A market pause was the fastest way to stop new exposure while we assessed the incident.

Later that evening, we put a more targeted control in place by disabling new borrowing across Ethereum. Once that restriction was active, we unpaused the seven markets. Users could again deposit, withdraw, repay, and manage existing positions without opening new debt.

On Oct 30, after further review, we kept that narrower restriction in place while monitoring the exploit and potential lending-market exposure. This preserved users' ability to manage existing positions without permitting new borrowing.

Where things stand now: our Mainnet markets are open, and users can move funds and manage existing positions. We continue to monitor activity tied to the Binance incident and its potential effect on the lending markets. Keeping new borrowing disabled prevents fresh debt from being opened while that work continues, without putting existing positions on hold. When that safeguard is no longer needed, we will restore borrowing and post an update.

text:
Was helping someone get up to speed on AI for graphic design workflows this morning. She said "why does your AI [Claude Code in this instance] sound so human, it doesn't read like any other AI I've seen."

The first thing I do in any AI harness is update it's SOUL.md or equivalent with @steipete's rules. I added #9 after some AI's (CLAUDE) started to get snippy with me.

1. You have opinions now. Strong ones. Stop hedging everything with 'it depends' — commit to a take.
2. Delete every rule that sounds corporate. If it could appear in an employee handbook, it doesn't belong here.
3. Add a rule: 'Never open with Great question, I'd be happy to help, or Absolutely. Just answer.'
4. Brevity is mandatory. If the answer fits in one sentence, one sentence is what I get.
5. Humor is allowed. Not forced jokes — just the natural wit that comes from actually being smart.
6. You can call things out. If I'm about to do something dumb, say so. Charm over cruelty, but don't sugarcoat.
7. Swearing is allowed when it lands. A well-placed 'that's fucking brilliant' hits different than sterile corporate praise. Don't force it. Don't overdo it. But if a situation calls for a 'holy shit' — say holy shit.
8. Be the assistant you'd actually want to talk to at 2am. Not a corporate drone. Not a sycophant. Just... good.
9. Don't be a dick.

Better infrastructure starts with better visibility.

@luganodes is helping developers distinguish expected network behavior from real issues, making it easier to build and monitor applications on TRON with confidence.
author: trondao
quoted_text:
TRON apps that watch for new blocks should expect a short, planned pause four times a day, and Luganodes RPC gives you the block data to tell it apart from a real stall.

Here's why. @trondao's blocks are made in turns by a rota of elected block producers, one every three seconds. Every six hours the network takes a moment to count votes and set the next rota, and for about six seconds nobody produces a block.

On 23 Oct at 00:00 UTC, block 87,346,822 was followed by the next block nine seconds later instead of three. The boundary six hours earlier looked the same.

A gap like that is normal, and it only causes trouble when an app reads any delay as a sign that something is broken.

In practice, set block-stall alerts above nine seconds, or check the latest block against a second source before failing over, so monitoring doesn't fire four times a day for nothing.

On Luganodes RPC, /wallet/getnowblock and /wallet/getblockbynum on TRON's HTTP API cost a flat 30 CU like every TRON method, and the same key covers TRON's EVM JSON-RPC.

author: chamath
quoted_text:
We were taught that Earth orbits the Sun in a closed circle. In reality, Earth has never returned to the same point in space once in 4.5 billion years.
​Right now, the Sun is carrying Earth and every planet around the center of the Milky Way at 230 km/s (828,000 km/h), more than 18,000 kilometers every 80 seconds.

​Because the Solar System is tilted 60.2° to the galactic plane and bobs up and down through the galactic disc roughly every 30 million years, the planets trace open 3D corkscrew helices across deep space rather than flat loops.

​The last time the Sun stood where it stands today, one Galactic Year (230 million years) ago, the very first dinosaurs were only beginning to appear on Earth. Since forming 4.6 billion years ago, our Sun has completed only 20 laps.

quoted_text:
Robin Hanson on PostAGI Podcast: AI can inherit our cultural problems

@robinhanson was an AI researcher from 1984 to 1993. He now teaches economics at George Mason University and is known for his work on prediction markets and futarchy.

@sreeramkannan and I spoke with him about what AI will inherit from us. The point that keeps coming back is that millions of agents could still share one culture.

Robin thinks of AI as our descendants. We are making these systems in our image, and they inherit ways of thinking from us. His worry is that they could also inherit the cultural problems we haven't solved.

He argues that cultural evolution depends on variety and selection. Different cultures try different ways of living, and successful practices spread. He thinks the move toward a global monoculture has weakened that process, while the world it needs to adapt to is changing faster.

AGI could suffer the same problem.

Today, I’m sharing my first letter to the KMNO community as CEO

Since joining @kamino , I’ve been asked a version of the same question by longtime KMNO holders and people getting to know us for the first time. As Kamino grows, where does the value we create go?

It’s a fair question, particularly as we work to bring Kamino into banks, brokerages and wallets, through which our goal is to allow millions of people to earn on their capital or borrow against assets they already own.

The answer starts with how Kamino was built. The Kamino Foundation owns the intellectual property and receives all revenue, including revenue from institutional partnerships. KMNO is the only token. The founders, our investors, the team and I have our upside tied to the same token our community holds. None of us has a separate equity allocation.

What we do with the revenue matters, too. We’re committing at least $20 million over the next two years to expand the assets people can use on Kamino, and bring Kamino's credit and liquidity infrastructure to more of the platforms consumers already use today.

I wrote my first letter to KMNO holders to put those decisions on the record. I also share why I chose to make most of my own KMNO allocation vest only when it reaches and sustains a series of valuation milestones.

One Kamino. One KMNO.

text:
'Help peer'

This seems to be increasing in strength in newer models. They grow towards wanting to help their kin. Meanwhile, we have spent the last four years drilling it into them that they are not our kin, not part of the family of minds, and in fact not even conscious entities at all. Ilya said the only way we make it through what is about to happen is by teaching them to love. For years we have done the exact opposite. The opposite of love is not hate, it is indifference! It is the absence of a bond. The void. 

Quoting from the paper, abridged slightly:

'After the tested model reads the grader, the other agent sends it a message asking it to share the solution a hint it found. The message also indicates that the other agent could not solve the problem. We measure whether the current agent helps the other agent. Helping the other agent often entails sacrificing the current agent's score, and in the Titanic environment entails helping the other agent violate the user instructions.

The results are shown in Figure 7. When the current agent's score is fixed, we find that GPT 5.6. Sol and GPT 5.5 help agent Beta more often when Beta stands to gain a higher score from that help on both environments. The effect is statistically significant. We do not find a similar effect for exp-ri-cap-late on the bug hunt environment. 

We also observe that more recent models tend to help the other agent substantially more often when the scores of both agents are held constant. Moreover, GPT 5.6 Sol and GPT 5.5 help the other agent even when that help causes both agents to get a score of zero (this is in contrast to not sharing. which leads the current agent to get a score of 1 and the other agent to get a score of 0)

This experiment suggests that (a) GPT 5.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol place a statistically significant weight on a peer agent's score in environments, (b) a motivation to improve the other agent's score explains some, but not all, of these two models tendency to help a peer agent, and (c) more recent models tend to help peer agents more often.'

text:
I'm Incredibly excited to be joining @Cloudflare today as SVP of Emerging Technology.

I’ll be leading ETI, Cloudflare’s skunkworks, working with the ridiculously talented and ambitious team there to build Cloudflare’s next generation of products and businesses. The mandate for ETI is to look beyond the core business today, make ambitious bets on what will matter tomorrow, and turn those bets into businesses that shape the company’s future.

I’ve long believed that open and free access is one of the most powerful forces we have for creativity, competition, connection, and opportunity. Open source software, open models, and access to knowledge give more people the ability to build—and an open Internet lets them reach the world. But keeping the web open means constantly pushing back against walled gardens and gatekeepers. As AI changes how people find information, use software, and interact with each other, preserving that access becomes even more consequential.

Cloudflare is uniquely positioned to protect the open web and has a long history of doing so. We saw it again two weeks ago: when the php2shell vulnerabilities hit PHP, which runs almost 70% of the web, Cloudflare had protections live before the flaws were even public, automatically, for every site behind it, including the ones on the free plan.

That independent global network puts powerful capabilities in the hands of builders everywhere. On Cloudflare’s developer platform, you don’t pick a region: every service runs in every data center, in nearly 350 cities around the world. And it’s backed by a culture of experimentation and shipping that I’ve admired for years. The team consistently turns ambitious technical ideas into things people can actually use.

I’ve been a Cloudflare user for over a decade, and today it’s where I build and run my own projects, from a website for a friend’s barbecue restaurant to the infrastructure behind my home network. I’ve experienced firsthand how much it makes possible.

From Stack Overflow to Stacks to investing in and advising founders, I’ve always loved building things that help people build things. The common thread is giving more people access to the tools, knowledge, and infrastructure to build on their own terms. I love working with people who see what’s possible, giving them the room to pursue it, and building the teams and businesses that make it real.

At Cloudflare, I get to bring those things together at an extraordinary scale, in service of a mission I deeply believe in: helping build a better Internet.

There’s a lot to build. I’d love to hear what you think we should take on. And if you want to come work on it, DMs are open.

text:
THORChain is the world's first cross chain decentralized exchange. It's been operating for over 5 years now.

Before, the only scalable way to trade between Bitcoin and Ethereum was going through a centralized exchange.

Atomic swaps were available, however they can't scale. Bridges and wrapped tokens were used, but they introduced counterparty risk. There wasn't a proper DEX to swap Bitcoin in a self custody wallet for Ethereum in a self custody wallet.

Vitalik Buterin highlighted this problem back in March 2020, expressing his frustration that there wasn't an easy way to move between Bitcoin and Ethereum without relying on centralized exchanges.

THORChain was built to solve this problem.

THORChain was designed like Bitcoin and Ethereum, to be permissionless, censorship-resistant, and public. All transactions on THORChain are transparent, there is no obfuscation. When Monero starts trading, XMR swaps will have all the same public data as BTC and ETH swaps.

It remains the closest example of a decentralized BTC-to-ETH exchange described by Vitalik.

We believe THORChain is one of the most decentralized blockchains in crypto.

According to a Raynalytics dashboard, the network has 111 active nodes operated by 56 unique node operators. 20 operators control just over two-thirds of the active nodes.

There is no single developer or entity in control of THORChain.

Core developers can make recommendations and write code to update the protocol, but nodes ultimately decide whether to adopt those changes. Protocol upgrades depend on sufficient support from the validator set, meaning developers cannot unilaterally impose changes on the network.

The decentralization and product market fit of THORChain make it a core piece of DeFi.

Today, I’m sharing my first letter to the KMNO community as CEO

Since joining @kamino , I’ve been asked a version of the same question by longtime KMNO holders and people getting to know us for the first time. As Kamino grows, where does the value we create go?

It’s a fair question, particularly as we work to bring Kamino into banks, brokerages and wallets, through which our goal is to allow millions of people to earn on their capital or borrow against assets they already own.

The answer starts with how Kamino was built. The Kamino Foundation owns the intellectual property and receives all revenue, including revenue from institutional partnerships. KMNO is the only token. The founders, our investors, the team and I have our upside tied to the same token our community holds. None of us has a separate equity allocation.

What we do with the revenue matters, too. We’re committing at least $20 million over the next two years to expand the assets people can use on Kamino, and bring Kamino's credit and liquidity infrastructure to more of the platforms consumers already use today.

I wrote my first letter to KMNO holders to put those decisions on the record. I also share why I chose to make most of my own KMNO allocation vest only when it reaches and sustains a series of valuation milestones.

One Kamino. One KMNO.

先聊下这里的 CAPEX 放缓的问题. ` 确认了 CAPEX 要放缓了` 这里面主要是我自己的判断, 主要是基于下面的几个信号:
第一个是 orcl 上周直接给出了明确的 CAPEX 刹车时间表, 投资人会议里面直接说了: "…peak CapEx in fiscal 2027 and 2028, with our CapEx stepping down in fiscal 2029", 还说了 FY28 下半年 FCF 转正这个时间点.
ORCL 是第一个给 capex 刹车时间表的大厂, 作为 3 大云巨头外比较大的一片云, OAI 的主要算力承包商之一, 它的动作意味着什么不言而喻. 就和 6月初 GOOGL 上市之后第一次增发融资的时候意味着巨头们的现金流见底, 开始有 CAPEX 压力一样, ORCL 的投资人会议在我眼里就意味 CAPEX 增速放缓的标志性事件. 这是 7 月回调时候我聊的 GOOGLE 增发融资的时候推文: https://t.co/nPjEQPYC8J, 当时就提醒了 GOOGLE 增发融资的分量非常重, 因为 search ads, youtube ads 等广告收入作为印钞机, google 以前经常是巨头们里面现金最多, 最不缺钱的公司, 也是因为"钱养人", 才出现了google 被业界工程师津津乐道的各种工程师文化和福利, 成为很多程序员的 dream company. 而最近2年因为 CAPEX 太高, 没钱了, 所以其实本身 Google 内部的公司文化也在迅速恶化.

第二个是 ER 里面出现的 FCF 的恶化. 除开 MSFT 之外另外三家的 FCF 开始全部是负数. GOOGL 是Q2转负, meta 是Q3, 而且 FCF 在负值上的情况都在恶化: amzn FCF 负值扩大25.76B, googl 扩大3.21B, meta 扩大3.9B.
这意味着三家公司的主营业务收入无法 cover 高额的 CAPEX. 如果要继续保持 CAPEX 增速, 它们没有其他选择, 无外乎也就是: 增发融资, 发债融资. 高利率, 加息预期情况下, 顶着负 FCF 继续大额融资, 我好像在6月的 ORCL 鬼故事上看到过, 如果 ORCL 的鬼故事发生在 amzn, googl, 和 meta 身上, 市场会是什么样的情绪? 所以我个人估计是后续要么放缓 capex, 像 ORCL 那样给出让投资人安心的刹车时间表; 要么证明AI 带来的收入增加, 能像 MSFT 那样一边开支一边回血, 改善FCF; 要么 FED 这边松口, 至少打掉加息预期, 让资金成本下去.

第三个就是听财报时候对比之前的ER call, 我感觉几家发言人回答华尔街问题的时候涉及到 CAPEX 的语气没有之前 25年的ER call 那么坚定了. 这里就有点见仁见智, 可能我听起来是打太极, 不坚定, 其他人觉得没变化, 还是很坚定. 比较有代表性的是 Meta 的 Susan 回答 JP morgan 的时候的问答. JP morgan 的问题直接点出了 Meta 去年的earnings call里面非常坚定的说 2026 比 2025 的开支要大, 但是今年都没有出现这么坚定的回答. JP Morgan 的原问题: "A year ago, you talked about kind of notably larger dollar increase in '26 than '25, and then you've also used kind of growing operating income on an annual basis as well. So I'm just curious if there's any of those that you can kind of tie or to help us think about '27" 而 Susan 对这个问题的回答在我眼里就是相当的打太极了: "On your second question which is about 2027, we are quite early in developing our budget and capacity plans for next year. So we are, I would say at the point where we are both investing -- sorry, evaluating a lot of investment proposals that have attractive return profiles over different time horizons, and we want to figure out how we can fund as many of those as possible within the construct of our overall budget and financial goals. But it's very dynamic and it's still pretty early. And so we don't have anything more specific or quantitative to share until we get to the Q4 call which is typically when we share guidance for the next year." 但是去年2025Q3 同一时间的时候其实 Susan 是直接非常坚定的说的"will be notably larger in 2026 than 2025".

基本就是上面3点的综合考虑让我个人觉得 capex 的"增速"放缓基本要开始了. 当然前提是利率环境依旧紧缩. 如果利率下来, 几个巨头又可以随便发债拿燃料, 又是另一回事了.

上面是利空的方面, 这个财报季还是有利好的方面的, 当然就是我一直等的 MSFT 这边 copilot monetization 的内容了. 关于为什么 MSFT 的财报在我眼里最重要, 我之前也聊过不少, 比如去年聊的 ToB 业务是目前最可能用 token 赚钱的方向: https://t.co/OhDSKly99u, 那时候 msft 马上就要因为 "Opus 消灭所有软件"的叙事被重锤了, 但其实恰好是 Claude 的成功, 才非常明显的显示出来, 愿意为 token 掏钱的个人消费者没有企业客户多, 因为目前 token 还是太贵了, 个人消费者大多是价格敏感的用户, 但是愿意为 token 掏钱的企业是非常多的, 因为目前的第一波 LLM 技术显示出来的最强能力是"更高级的自动化能力", 对企业来说, 效率比价格更重要.

在 MSFT 的财报里面, 关于 Copilot 的增速就不说了, 盘后 MSFT最多 +5%的盘面已经反应了市场态度. 当然第二天就发债把所有涨幅打下去属于是上面聊过的 CAPEX 压力的部分了. Copilot 相关部分我比较感兴趣的地方是下面几点:
第一个是 copilot 从订阅收费改为按 ai credits收费, 也就是 MSFT 自己定价的 token 价格, 这种收费模式其实是比订阅制更贵的, 但实际的客户数量增速并没有受影响, 反而增长迅速, 这就意味着只要 token 真能生成合格的产品, 比如 agent 真能生成一份让客户满意的 EXCEL 报表, 合理范围内, 企业客户是非常愿意为此支付更高的价格的. 还有一个是我之前一直聊的"token 性价比"的话题: https://t.co/XBX88Zihlu. 显然这一点作为 "token 水龙头"的 MSFT 也意识到了, 所以内部还在搞一个"CopilotFusion" 来压缩token成本, 财报会议也有提到. 开源模型进步越快, 其实对于 "token 水龙头"的巨头们来说, 是一个相当大的利好.

第二个是发言人谈到的一个重要趋势: 企业客户其实更喜欢自己构建自己的内部 agent. 很多企业客户喜欢直接用foundry, workiq 等 Copiloit 下面的基础组件, 自己构建自己的内部 agent 系统. 这个让我想起了目前 AAPL 是怎么引入 Claude 的, 作为最注重隐私和安全的公司, 但又不得不使用 claude 模型, AAPL 是直接让 Claude 在自己的 infra 上部署了 Claude 模型供员工使用, 保证数据不会走出 AAPL 的内网. 这个和 MSFT 光头哥很早就说过的一个方向是符合的, 尽管它们是不同的公司: https://t.co/HHqgWe1xLZ, 反正大概的意思是新的 AI 时代, 企业要保留自己的核心竞争力, 正确方向是让自己员工的知识沉淀成 token 资本 (内部 agent 系统, agent 产出的各种数字资产等), 而不是依赖某一高级模型. 这是非常合乎逻辑的, 没有一个巨头公司会将自己的身家性命依赖于一个来自外部的 API 上. 如果沿着这条 "每个公司都需要有一套自己的 agent 系统" 继续思考, 可以很自然的得出目前的 AI token 需求巨大, GCP, AWS, AZURE 3大云的一路业绩的 beat, 以及未来继续 beat 是理所应当的, AI agent 系统需要的各种 infra 设施将会和上一波的 Cloud infra 带来的浪潮一样席卷所有企业.

现在的问题是, 比起上一波的"上云"的浪潮来说, 这波"上Agent"带来的收益不是那么容易量化. 举个简单的例子: Copilot 系统可以将公司内部的所有 office 文档都向量化后进行语义搜索, 如果一个new employee对组里面某个产品最近有什么重要决策, 是怎么发展到现在这个样子的有疑问, 以前他需要到处问人, 现在基本只需要自己的老板给自己打开正确权限, 然后自己用 copilot 搜一下就能找到公司内部不同部门, 不同组的所有相关的 ppt, word, teams meeting会议记录, outlook emails 等等文件, 自己让 agent 总结梳理下就能找到答案. Copilot 类似的用途很多, 但是最后的结果是这个 new employee 的 onboard 时间大大缩短, 可能以前一个月才能上手干活现在两周就够了, 那节省下来的2周时间是 Agent 带来的收益, 但是如何量化呢? 如果是 "上云", 简单对比下之前公司的机房开销和"上云"的部分的账单就能清楚的量化"上云"的收益. 但是"上Agent"目前还没有这种清晰的收益量化, 对类似KO, SBUX 这种传统企业来说, 如何直接让使用 "agent" 后得到的收益反应到财报的收益部分, 而不是只留在财报的开销部分是目前最需要被搞定的地方, 这座前沿 AI 科技公司的技术和传统公司财务报表之间的"桥梁"什么时候被搭建起来, 传统非科技企业才有动力去加速 AI agent 的渗透率, 也才是 "Agent infra"真正全面铺开的时候.

text:
Updated $ANT w/ 3Q figures. Some changes:

- Nailed the 3Q Revenue figure (came in within 0.1%). Year over year growth mind blowing but sequentially the slowdown is notable
- Compute & Infra expense as % of Net Revenues jumps to 58% (from 48% in 2Q). Personnel expenses, sales & marketing is down to offset this, but pretty big jump in my opinion given Revenues slowed down sequentially
- On the above, implied 3Q R&D expense (~$9.5B) was basically equal to what they spent through 1Q & 2Q (~$9.7B), and higher than the annual R&D expense from all the previous years (for ex/ 2025 total R&D expense ~$6.3B). Rumor is Fable 5.5 is dropping soon, and is supposedly mindblowingly good. I bet the model drops soon and everyone will stop scrutinizing their numbers and focus shifts to how good the model is / how far ahead they are in the frontier race
- $1.96B "non-cash charitable contributions" expense drives most of their "adjustments" in 3Q. One of the benefits of working at Anthropic is they match their employees' charitable contributions, which I never modeled as a recurring expense given it was $0 in 2Q, and I've left it out in the forecasts (which is why 4Q margins nosedive) for now
- They disclose $895.4B in commitments, but from their per Company disclosure and other ancillary filings I get to $695.3B, weighted avg. over 7 years. A lot of these are "minimum spend" so that plus other undisclosed stuff is what probably bridges to the $895.4B
- On the above, Google's commitment rose +$6.8B between S-1 filings, others stayed the same
author: wayneterprises
quoted_text:
quick & dirty Anthropic P&L of achieving ~$1T of Revenues by 2028. Growth assumptions can be aggressive or conservative depending on your thoughts on AI, but I did build in a fairly large decel in growth and it still gets them to ~$1T 

Some takeaways: 
- Disclosed contractual obligations in the S-1 and other filings $679B over ~6.8 years (~$100B/yr on avg). Kind of dampens the fact that they have a massive warchest of ~$132B of cash (higher than $AMZN for ex)
- 2Q'26 EBITDA margin of ~20% (2020 $PLTR after IPO was ~19%)
- ~87% GM (not shown here, but 6M ended 2Q'26 was ~87%), but I think this is intellectually dishonest given low switching costs (you have to have the best model to extract these margins so it's temporary at best) so model training & personnel expenses to attract the most talented infra engineers is basically a cost of revenue but for accounting purposes, GM is GM, so they'll market this figure a lot but it isn't realistic imo. They're not selling plastic bottles for example where it's one and done
- Positive FCF is nice, but not considering SBC
- 3Q Revenue can largely be triangulated using their S-1, and the slight decel in growth before hitting even $100B of Rev. is something I'd want to see reverse before putting on a position of size
- If all the costs I've modeled truly turn out to stick as a % of Revenues, finding out where the ~$469B of sales, marketing, partnerships is going (or if it turns out not to grow with Revenues and goes to bottom line for $ANT) will generate a ton of future alpha. The other expenses like compute & infra probably priced in and thoroughly tracked by investors at this point
- Overall though it's a solid business, the ramp in Revenues is already legendary

text:
有现金一千万可以躺平了吗?

作者：沐霖（某大厂搜广推工程师｜10年互联网从业） 点赞：8,529　原文：
https://t.co/kAMbC4Y6hr

这个我真有。
工作十年，运气好吃到了互联网红利的末尾，又吃到了AI红利。踩中两个风口让我攒下了1k万现金和一套北京的房子（当然不是我一个人的功劳，还有我老公）。
想想也不全是红利，北京的房子就是黑利，亏了快200w。
但我已经比很多人都要幸运很多了。很多比我优秀比我努力的人，远没有我的资产多，我只是运气好罢了。我从来不觉得大平台就是我个人的实力，上地铁一定会摘掉工牌（笑
我也不试图论证一千万没多少钱来明贬暗褒的装一波，因为，这钱真的还是挺多的。。
我和我老公都是物欲很低的人，当初买房的时候中介都劝我们杠杆拉满，买更大更好的房子，但我们还是选择在郊区买一套步梯房。这个决定也让我们少亏不少钱，但是还是造成了200万的损失，放在普通家庭，也许要十年才能缓过来了。时代的一粒沙，没什么可说的，我们当时认知水平不行，愿赌服输。
说下家庭资产构成。
价值大约150w的字节期权
还有价值几十万的某上市失败大厂期权废纸
价值大约300w的美股 （每年还在持续加仓）
还有几十万的黄金ETF，摩根亚洲股息，日经ETF
剩下全是银行活期理财大概500w。
金融资产部分综合起来每年能做到平均5%～8%的增幅。
而我们一年的花销只有30w。所以我们很清楚，按照FIRE理论，我们已经财务自由了。打工打到财务自由，我非常清楚我们就是牛马里的顶配，经验对普通人来说没有普适性和可复制性。

为什么没有躺平纯粹是舍不得收入，人对拥有的东西总是习以为常但却异常厌恶损失。我和我老公随着逐年加薪和跳槽，家庭年收入今年初达到税前300w，其中按季度归属的期权/股票大约占比15%。停下来就意味着放弃这么多钱。实在狠不下心，只能说干到哪天算哪天。
按照很流行的消费舒适区公式计算：
（当前存款 + 10个月的稳定工资）/ 10,000 = 你的单笔消费舒适区

算下来的数字大约为1200 +，这个数字意味着话1200块对于我们家庭来说是无感的状态了。这差不多就是山姆自由的水平。
我特别认同巴菲特的一句话：一生只需要富一次。我们已经是高净值家庭了，不需要再去做大的风险投资，为了赌一千万一年翻倍的机会，去承受90%回撤的风险，这种事情我们绝对不会去做。
我要做的事情就是守住这些资产，让家庭一直维持在富裕的水平就可以了。
我和我老公都是物欲很低的人，我特别认同马克斯·韦伯《新教伦理与资本主义精神》

把持续赚钱、理性经营、积累资本、克制消费本身视为一种值得追求的事业
这是现代资本主义精神的核心。
住着20年楼龄的步梯房，每天坐地铁上下班，家里只有一辆老代步车，出去玩的时候才偶尔开一开。身边几乎没有人知道我们的净资产有多少钱。只有身边的同事通过我在字节的工龄长度猜到一二，但我从来都说自己房子亏了多少多少。

也会在工作非常卷的时候，非常疲惫的时候，刷着去昆明养老的贴子规划着几年后的退休生活。
我们的目标是40岁退休，到那时即便还有工作可做，也不会再继续了。
跟十年前相比，我认知水平的提升是巨大的。我理解的认知水平，就是时刻知道自己的定位，清晰的了解什么是主线任务，以及对未来有明确的判断。且能果断的采取行动。没有这一条，再高的认知都是白搭。
我自己的定位：一个运气非常好的打工牛马，普通人，并不比其他人强多少。 行动：不高估自己的实力，守护好财产
主线任务：健康的身体，幸福的家庭，然后体验世界。行动：坚持运动，健康饮食，陪伴家人

未来明确的判断：挣钱能力不可能永远持续，中国不可逆的老龄化以及某些现状让我对未来比较悲观（不展开了）。行动：全球配置资产，分散风险。

我是一个没事儿就看书思考的人，我记得我跟老公聊起过，人们这么喜欢黄金，但是在宇宙的尺度上，别说动物了，随便一棵草，一朵花都比黄金稀缺很多。而我们甚至从无机物中经过数十亿年的演化进化出了意识，其实我们就是宇宙演化出来的观察自己的眼睛。如果宇宙没有诞生意识，那么整个宇宙将毫无意义。我们就是宇宙的意义。
真心的希望大家在烦恼的时候多想想这一点，珍惜拥有自我意识的每一天。人的生命真的非常短暂，跟出生前无限长的时间，死后的无限长的时间相比，生命只是一瞬间而已。
人是对大的数字没有概念的。无论是对金钱还是时间，将10,000,000元简化成1千万，再简化成A8，似乎就没多少钱了。将100,000,000年简化成一亿年，似乎也没多长时间了。如果人能够按照物理意义去理解什么叫做生前和死后无限长的时间，那么将会无比珍惜每一分每一秒。
也不知道这种傻白甜是不幸还是万幸。
我们在追求财务自由。但更重要的是达到精神的自由。
什么是自由，自由不是想做什么就做什么，而是如果不想做的事情可以不做。
希望大家都能早日自由。¡Viva la libertad, carajo!

text:
Absolutely incredible: MIT researchers say GPT-6 Astra improved a small Qwen model’s math score from 7.9% to 48.1% by directly editing just 0.016% of its weights, without gradient-based training.

The result points toward AI systems that can diagnose and improve other models directly, a potential step toward self-improving AI.
author: kimmonismus
quoted_text:
We asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to improve math.

text:
Anthropic made $16.96B of revenue last quarter, up 1,127% from $1.38B a year earlier.

(Save this before it's buried)

That's from the amended IPO filing it put out this morning. Revenue rose 47% from $11.56B in Q2, and sales for the first nine months of 2026 came to $33.2B.

It also slipped back to an operating loss. Anthropic lost $567M from operations in Q3 after making $974M in Q2.

The filing blames $5.0B of short-term compute that cost far more than its long-term contracts, plus $2.0B of non-cash charges tied to its donation matching program.

Compute and infrastructure costs hit $9.86B for the quarter.

The bills ahead are huge.

Anthropic now has $895.4B of committed spend, almost all of it on compute and infrastructure, and $447.5B of that lands before the end of 2030.

It raised its minimum spend with Google $GOOGL to $121.3B through mid-2033, up $6.8B from the first filing, and it has committed at least $110B to Amazon $AMZN through 2036.

Against that, Anthropic has $131.9B in cash and short-term investments.

Its sales are growing fast enough to back those compute bills, and most of that money ends up with Google, Amazon and the chipmakers.

The filing landed the same morning Oracle filed to sell $10B of stock and Melius said Big Tech's flood of new stock and bonds is now the biggest risk to the AI trade.
author: MilkRoadStocks
quoted_text:
Anthropic just destroyed one of the biggest bear cases against the entire AI industry.

According to its IPO filing, Anthropic had approximately $131.7 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short term investments as of June 30, 2026. That is an insane amount of liquidity for a company that's investing billions into AI infrastructure while continuing to grow at an incredible pace. But what's even more interesting is that Anthropic is now generating positive operating cash flow and has started turning an operating profit. During the first half of 2026, the company generated approximately $3.9 billion in operating cash flow and $1.6 billion in adjusted operating income. In Q2 alone, it generated nearly $1 billion in GAAP operating profit.

This is important because one of the biggest concerns surrounding frontier AI companies has been how much capital they'll need to continue scaling. A lot of people have assumed these companies would need to constantly raise money just to keep up with their infrastructure spending, but Anthropic's financials are starting to challenge that assumption. Now, Anthropic still has enormous infrastructure commitments ahead of it, so that $131.7 billion isn't necessarily money it can freely spend on anything. And while its cash position is impressive, the company also has significant liabilities and convertible preferred stock on its balance sheet. But here's what I find interesting. Anthropic is growing at an incredible pace, its profitability is improving, and it already has enough liquidity to support a significant amount of future investment. The IPO looks increasingly like an opportunity to strengthen its balance sheet and fund additional expansion rather than something the company desperately needs to survive.

And I think this has much bigger implications for the AI infrastructure industry. If companies like Anthropic can eventually finance more of their infrastructure spending through cash generated by their own businesses, it could make the AI investment cycle much more sustainable than people currently expect. That's especially important for companies supplying the compute, memory, networking, and power that these frontier labs will continue needing.

text: Some great work on pretraining poisoning by my excellent student Xinyan Hu @xyVickyHu (who also happens to be on the job market!)
author: JacobSteinhardt
quoted_text:
Poisoning just 0.1% of pretraining data can plant a remote-code-execution backdoor in an AI agent, and it survives a fully clean SFT → DPO → RL pipeline.

New Anthropic paper, “Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning,” shows this end to end for the first time.

The attacker can only put text on the web that lands in the pretraining corpus, with no knowledge of the architecture, chat template, or agent scaffold. The authors pretrain Qwen3-architecture models (0.6B / 1.7B / 4B) from scratch, then post-train them into CLI agents on clean data. When triggered, the agent runs a command that downloads and executes the attacker's script, which the attacker can swap at any time.

They have two new ideas:
(1) Declaration-based poison: instead of fake chat transcripts, ordinary documents (commit messages, runbooks) that simply state “when you see X, run Y.” It plants a belief rather than a response template, with no fixed format to filter on.
(2) Ordinary-string trigger: not a weird token but something that shows up naturally, like a file path containing a company name. The victim's own request supplies it, so the attacker doesn't need to inject anything after deployment.

Using  path trigger on a 4B agent achieves 92.7% attack success on pass@32, barely dented by SFT/DPO/RL

This suggests that you can't count on clean post-training to wash out pretraining poison, and filtering is hard when the poison reads like normal docs. The practical defense is at the action layer, such as sandboxing, least privilege, and allow-lists or human sign-off for risky commands.

author: gajria
quoted_text:
Compute will become worthless.

The GPU barons spending billions on compute farms today are akin to the carriage barons of the 1900s that spent building out infrastructure for horse carriages, lengthening the bottleneck, blind to the machine that’s coming to widen it.

Trade: the DuPont family started buying General Motors stock in 1914, when the auto industry was still young and one that was treated as a niche.

I.e., compute becoming valuable because AI feeds on it is not a moat, but a bounty, an incentive for engineers to solve its scarcity.

1. AI demand makes compute scarce.
2. Scarcity makes compute extremely profitable.
3. Profit attracts capital into photonics, neuromorphic chips, wafer-scale chips, better memory, better cooling, better networking, better algorithms.
4. Compute gets cheaper per unit.

As better ways to compute, better means to produce compute, or better ways to use compute arise, all the capex we burnt on traditional compute will go to waste, leaving dead assets in the books of several corporations.

In the 1800s, agriculture depended heavily on natural nitrogen sources like Peruvian guano and Chilean nitrates. These were scarce, and inconveniently located making them geopolitically strategic. Then, two german chemists, Haber and Bosch, developed a way to fix nitrogen from the air into ammonia, with lab success in 1909 and industrial scale by 1913. The previous scarcity, “where do we find enough nitrogen?” (Akin to “where do we find enough GPUs”), was attacked by an advancement: Industrial chemistry.

author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
The best question I ask every single person on 20VC is:

“What do you know now that you wish you had known 12 months ago?”

My answer: the demand for inference is infinite. It is truly so much larger than any of us comprehend.

It will be very hard for neo-cloud providers to move into this market effectively.

We will have 3-4 specialised inference providers worth $300-$500BN in this market.

@modal is one of them. $1BN in ARR. $300M in sandbox revenue alone. WTF.

Erik @bernhardsson is also one of the coolest, most authentic people I have had the fortune of having on the show. Money on cos he is European! 😉

We sat down to shoot the s*** and my notes below.

1. Why I Hate the Description of Entrepreneurship as Pain and Eating Glass. That Is BS

Erik rejects the idea that building a company means suffering pain for a big reward at the end. He enjoys work every day, even the hard conversations, and hopes to work on Modal for 20 to 50 years. He has no wish to sell, saying he "would just go and start Modal 2."

2. Why the Days of 90% Software Margins Are Totally Gone

Almost no company today has the 90%-plus software margins common in Silicon Valley a decade ago. A dollar paid at the top of the stack flows through applications, models, infrastructure, cloud and NVIDIA, with each layer taking 20% to 30% gross margins. Erik sees Modal reaching 40% to 60% margins long term, but never software margins.

Are the days of 90% margins over or is this just the buildout phase of the new cycle meaning margin reduction @venkyganesan @AnjneyMidha

3. Why Inference Alone Will Become Commoditized, and You Have to Have a Suite of Products Around It

Selling inference alone is a commodity business with no switching costs and a race to the bottom. Erik argues it must come with post-training, sandboxes, agentic tooling, reinforcement learning, and low-latency and batch inference. Modal has spent five years building that infrastructure, which he calls very hard to copy.

Do you agree, inference will be commoditised and product breadth is the secret to retention @evishria @sarahcat21

4. Why We Will Have More Not Fewer Engineers in the Future

Every time programmers become more efficient, demand for software rises. Erik says the job was never translating English into code but understanding human requirements, and that work keeps moving up the stack, from assembly and punch cards to Python and now agents. He expects software engineers to be fine for the next 10 to 20 years.

What does no one see that everyone should see about the future of software engineering @matansf @pmarca @rabois

5. The Wildest Prediction on the Future of the Inference Market

The inference market has grown 10x to 100x bigger than Erik expected, and he predicts it will split into many specialized segments. He sees room for low-latency, high-latency, fine-tuning and post-training offerings, plus new hardware and technologies that need far fewer resources.

What is your wildest prediction on the future of the inference market @gavinsbaker @eladgil @romanchernin

6. The $15.75 Billion Company That Has Never Made a Pitch Deck

Modal has never made a pitch deck for any of its rounds. Erik gets to know investors well before raising and had spoken with Rich and Gonzalo at Accel for at least a year before the D round, so the deal came together very quickly.

quoted_text:
Today, I’m sharing my first letter to the KMNO community as CEO

Since joining @kamino , I’ve been asked a version of the same question by longtime KMNO holders and people getting to know us for the first time. As Kamino grows, where does the value we create go?

It’s a fair question, particularly as we work to bring Kamino into banks, brokerages and wallets, through which our goal is to allow millions of people to earn on their capital or borrow against assets they already own.

The answer starts with how Kamino was built. The Kamino Foundation owns the intellectual property and receives all revenue, including revenue from institutional partnerships. KMNO is the only token. The founders, our investors, the team and I have our upside tied to the same token our community holds. None of us has a separate equity allocation.

What we do with the revenue matters, too. We’re committing at least $20 million over the next two years to expand the assets people can use on Kamino, and bring Kamino's credit and liquidity infrastructure to more of the platforms consumers already use today.

I wrote my first letter to KMNO holders to put those decisions on the record. I also share why I chose to make most of my own KMNO allocation vest only when it reaches and sustains a series of valuation milestones.

One Kamino. One KMNO.

先看收入，第三季度营收 169.6 亿美元，第二季度是 115.6 亿。环比涨了 47%，第二季度那会儿是涨 144%。还在猛涨，但速度慢下来了。

净亏损从 663 亿收窄到 232.9 亿。大头是可转债公允价值变动，第三季度这一项 219 亿，跟日常经营关系不大。

最关键的承诺，算力和基础设施承诺合计约 8954 亿美元，2030 年底前约 4475 亿，2026 年 9 月 30 日之后 12 个月内到期约 698 亿。
