text:
Talked with researchers at Chinese AI labs. I came back thinking the gap between US and Chinese labs is getting wider.

1/openai and anthropic are already in RSI territory. You can feel the speed-up from the outside.

Chinese models aren't strong enough to get there yet. Most of the "RSI" I heard about is automating steps researchers used to do by hand.

2/Everyone there is now obsessed with data, mostly because distillation got a lot harder. So labs are going all in on synthetic and expert data. 

3/After GPT-6 Astra, everyone is looking at robotics. Robot companies are already plugging Astra into their hardware. Almost nobody is seriously doing AI for science though.

4/One more thing from this weekend. DeepSeek open-sourced a research prototype of a coding agent.The line in their README I keep thinking about: "take as little human attention as possible."

The model gap isn't closing soon, so they're thinking hard about how little you should have to babysit the agent.

text:
今天美股这出高开低走，各位手里有仓位的应该都感受到了。开盘看着挺像回事，油价一跌，指数高开，情绪回暖。结果盘中一路回落，纳指一度把涨幅全吐了回去。

这走势背后没什么阴谋，就是典型的“事件驱动型博弈”。市场在几件大事落地前，先抢跑，再撤退。

第一层，开盘的高是油价给的。

周一布伦特原油盘中重挫，核心原因是市场在定价中东局势缓和的可能性。能源价格一跌，通胀预期跟着松动，对科技股是直接的利好，所以开盘资金敢往里冲。

但高开之后，资金立刻被几件事摁住了。

第一件事，今晚的苹果财报。

苹果是今晚盘后交卷，市场对这份财报的预期本身就带着分歧。内存成本对毛利率的挤压、折叠屏的良率和供应、以及新CEO第一次面对分析师的表态，全是未知数。在财报落地之前，资金没有理由在盘中把科技股往上顶。苹果自己盘中就跌了超过2%，龙头先软，指数很难硬。

第二件事，明天就是中期选举。

选举结果对财政、关税、产业监管的走向都有直接影响，在结果出来之前，大资金天然倾向于不押注方向。今天的盘中回落，很大程度上是这种“等待”心态的具象化。

第三件事，AI板块内部还在剧烈分化。

Marvell收购Lumentum的交易官宣后，两家股价盘中继续承压，Marvell跌超8%，Lumentum跌超14%，换股带来的稀释压力和整合不确定性，让光通信这条线今天完全没跟上大盘的节奏。甲骨文因为宣布发债和增发，股价也跌了6%左右。亚马逊和英伟达在涨，但Marvell、甲骨文、苹果在跌，指数就被拽住了。

所以今天有没有情况？

有，但不是一个单一的雷。是资金在几个明确的短期不确定性面前，选择先把开盘的情绪溢价落袋，等苹果财报和中期选举给出答案再说。这不是系统性风险的信号，是典型的事件密集期的盘中摇摆。

真正决定方向的，是今晚苹果的指引和明天的选举结果。在那之前，盘中的高开低走，看看就好，关于苹果和PLTR的财报明天收集好资料再给大家分享，睡了睡了……

author: Kshsb783142
quoted_text:
突发消息啊各位，前两天刚聊完Marvell想收购Lumentum这事儿，刚刚靴子直接落地了。

Marvell官宣，将以全股票交易方式收购Lumentum，交易隐含企业价值约1150亿美元，对应Lumentum每股约1132美元，比消息泄露前的收盘价溢价大概24%。

Lumentum的股东每持有一股，能换4.5股Marvell的股票，交易完成后，原Marvell股东占新公司67%，Lumentum股东拿33%。交易预计要到2028年上半年才能彻底完成，中间还得过双方股东和各国监管这两道大关。

先看这笔交易的本质，它跟咱们之前想的可能有点不一样。

之前觉得是Marvell硬吞Lumentum，但现在看，它更像是在为自己的未来买一张不可或缺的门票。Marvell的强项在电互联和定制芯片，但AI数据中心正从电往光迁移，光互联成了新瓶颈。Lumentum手里握着高性能激光器、光模块和化合物半导体制造，这些是光通信最底层的东西。Marvell买下它，等于把电和光的技术链条打通，搞全栈整合，直接去跟博通抢AI互联的生意。

管理层画的饼也不小：合并后目标市场规模能冲到5500亿美元，每年能省出超过10亿美元的成本，而且交割第一年就能增厚Marvell的每股收益。英伟达今年早些时候还分别给Marvell和Lumentum各投了20亿美元，等于提前给这笔交易盖了个章。

回到最现实的交易结构。这笔千亿美元的交易，Marvell一分钱现金没掏，全靠全股票交易。为了买下Lumentum，Marvell必须疯狂增发新股，这意味着原来持有Marvell的股东，手里的股份被严重稀释了。之前消息刚传出来的时候，Marvell的盘前股价一度重挫超10%，今天盘前，市场的关注点依然会集中在股权稀释和债务压力上。

Marvell买Lumentum，战略上绝对正确，甚至是必须走的一步。但在财务上，这是一场豪赌，赌的是未来十年光互联的需求能把这些稀释的债务全赚回来。交易2028年才完成，中间这两年，AI资本开支会不会放缓，光通信的竞争格局又会变成什么样，全是变量。

这步棋走得对不对，现在没法下定论，只能交给时间去验证了。

text:
I know that ground stations are a bit obsolete in terms of data, so let me give you some numbers for you to know  why @NorthwoodSpace is a no brainer at the moment: 

Data from space today

1- Observation: ~3,000 data sats × ~0.2 TB/day ≈ 0.6 PB/day

2-Broadband: Starlink alone has 300+ Tbps of capacity in orbit, all landing on its own ~150 gateways

3- AI: close to zero, since the first orbital GPUs are still demos

What we can take today

- Open ground: ~1,000 high-rate dishes × ~1 Gbps = ~1 Tbps at peak (~10 PB/day if always busy)

- On average that looks like plenty. In practice it isn’t: one dish serves one satellite for a ~10 min pass, so data waits 45 to 90 min to come down

What the future will look like for data in space by 2030

- Observation: 10k to 20k data sats × ~3 TB/day = 30 to 60 PB/day
- Peak downlink: 40% over land × 5 Gbps links = 20 to 40 Tbps
- AI compute: 1 GW in orbit ≈ 1M GPUs at 2k tokens/s each
2B tokens/s ≈ 0.7 Tbps for text with prompts, ~7 Tbps with images and video

Each GW needs 1 to 10 Tbps (10 to 100 PB/day)

- 5G and broadband: each Starship V3 launch adds 60 Tbps
- ~50 launches by 2030 adds ~3 Pbps, before D2D, Kuiper and China

How much the ground has to grow

1- Open ground: ~1 Tbps → 20 to 40 Tbps observation, ×3 for latency, plus 1 to 10 Tbps AI ≈ 100x by 2030

2- Gateways: ~0.3 Pbps → 3+ Pbps ≈ 10x
Late 2030s, with 500k sats and ~100 GW of orbital 

3- compute: ~1,000x

But what about the Starlink mesh effect, will this affect needing more ground stations?

fair question, V3 lasers route bits across orbit to the best gateway, so traffic over the ocean hops to land

That means fewer sites, but each one much more congested

3 Pbps in orbit still needs 3 Pbps of landing, just need it in different times > delays > worse UX for users

Thesis for ground stations right now is simple: 

- Every user, cloud and model lives on Earth, so the last hop is always down
- Lasers can’t punch through clouds, so you need RF or many optical sites for weather diversity
- Countries want their bits landed in-country
- Governments won’t route command links through a competitor’s mesh
- Spectrum per site is finite, so more bits means more apertures

Ground is the next cloud: multi-beam, sited at power and fiber, live in months

When a partner called Cheetah squeezed AppLovin too hard, he started a game studio to compete with them and named it Lion Studios, “because lion is the only animal that can kill a cheetah.” It went from zero to over $250 million in revenue in two years.

Humans are ~1,000,000x more sample efficient than LLMs, and there are no good explanations.

We’ve found that a big part of the answer is that LLMs are *massively* underparameterized by many orders of magnitude. The brain has 100T synapses learning from ~200M tokens of language. Chinchilla prescribes a 1T-parameter model on 20T tokens. That’s 7 OOMs apart in parameters per token.

text:
More context : 

A single Waymo car uses 4 H100 GPUs just to drive itself. That is about $200k worth of compute inside one car.

Right now, the Nvidia Orin self-driving modules used in Mercedes pack, and Tesla FSD use 64GB of LPDDR5X RAM.

Most people think better tech means we will need less memory over time. The exact opposite is happening. 

Tesla's upcoming AI5 chip will jump to 96GB, and the AI6 chip is going straight to 144GB.

Even your smart fridge and smart TV need RAM now. 
Soon, literally every physical object around us will have memory built into it. 
And as robotics takes off, those memory numbers are going to get much bigger.

There is no way around the hardware bottleneck:
If AI robots run on the cloud, you need massive data centers full of memory.
If AI robots run on-device, you have to pack huge amounts of RAM directly into the machine.

Either way, the world is going to need an insane amount of memory. 

This is not a problem we can fix easily.
author: jun_song
quoted_text:
Hate to break it to you, but the global hardware shortage has not even started yet.

Right now, only 1% of humanity is burning any real amount of AI tokens. The rest are just using free accounts once in a while to ask dumb questions like "Who would win in a fight between a baby seal and 300 hamsters?"

And like Elon said, most RAM will not even go into data centers. It will go into Physical AI, which is robotics.

That is because robotics is the only thing that can actually boost human productivity in a real way.

People on X freak out every time AI solves a hard math problem, while people in the real world just go on with their lives like nothing happened. Meanwhile, robotics is already taking over factories and changing the physical world.

Imagine when these robots start replacing our daily chores. How much more RAM and compute will we need then?

Like I have said many times, building a new fab to make RAM takes at least 5 years, and supply is already fully booked out until 2029.

Even if the so-called AI bubble pops, this massive RAM shortage is not going away.

Starting next year, even the new iPhone might be too expensive for most people to afford.

quoted_text:
Thank you @JonathanVanian and @CNBC for including Dazzle in your piece on the importance of humans in the loop for AI personal assistants!

Because Dazzle’s context is built from photos, we lean heavily into taste and visual nuance.  Multimodal AI is incredible at this, but commerce (especially around soft goods) frequently benefits from human discernment to bridge the gap between intent and catalog data.

One of Dazzle's investors, @lessin, previously ran Fin.  He often points out how quickly customer trust evaporates if someone orders red shoes and green ones show up.

Two recent examples from my personal shopping that highlight why agentic commerce sometimes benefits from human insight/intervention:

• A silver geodesic dome tent: The finish options were "Clear," "Mirrored Clear," and "Mirrored Smoke."  The model selected Clear, but cross-referencing my style photos I actually wanted Mirrored Clear.  Our concierge team caught this before placing the order.

• My daughter's group Halloween costume: The chosen black t-shirt was part of a two-pack that was sold out in my daughter's size until mid-November.  The agent correctly flagged the "out of stock" and offered alternatives, but our human concierge realized the same shirt was bundled in a different two-pack as well and got it here on time.

Autonomous agents are advancing rapidly, but when personal taste and high expectations intersect, having human diligence in the loop ensures our users get the precision and care they deserve.  

Also, Dazzle's human concierges rock!  Thanks, team!  @itsdazzleai

text:
Meet qwenGPU: Qwen3.5-2B with a SIMT GPU inside its weights, 45 compiled layers in front of Qwen’s own, using its Gated DeltaNet layers as registers and memory.

It runs real CUDA in its forward passes. The host compiles the kernel to PTX and loads it, then the model writes every step of the launch itself: every register, branch and memory write.

The GPU has 4-lane warps, a 4-stage pipeline, 15 registers per lane and 126 words of global memory, all held in DeltaNet state. Qwen generates each launch token by token, each record running one machine block for one warp.

1. 🆕 Binance: hackers stole $6.3 billion from the world's biggest crypto exchange, most of it in 20 minutes. The biggest crypto heist ever, 4x the old record. The FBI says North Korea did it.

Hackers hit Muji (27 million app accounts), tour company Club Tourism (4.3 million), booking site Rakuten Travel (3.4 million), Sony's internet service (2.6 million), fast-food chain Matsuya (2.4 million), insurer Sony Life and the Foreign Ministry, and an email company's leak grew to 51 million records, including bullet-train bookings. CrowdStrike says about 140 were hacked, and calls it the first AI-run state hacking it has seen at this scale. 6. 🆕 Moldova: hackers stole personal data on 750,000 people, about a third of the country, including health insurance, pension and disability records. Its cyber chief called it the biggest cyberattack the country has ever recorded.
7. 🆕 Anthropic: an unreleased AI found 62 serious holes in Chrome alone, and built working attacks against Chrome, Safari, Android phones, Windows and Linux. For Chrome, clicking one bad link was enough. (Lab work, not used in attacks.)

10. 🆕 Google: criminal gangs and spy groups are now using AI hacking agents in real break-ins. One group typically got from a single stolen login to deep inside a company in about 4 hours, once in 15 minutes. One tool's creator deleted it over the abuse; copies keep spreading.

19. 🆕 Cursor: the popular AI coding app served a booby-trapped copy of the real Claude Code add-on from its official store for 11 hours, exposing up to 5,000 programmers to a backdoor

Today, I’m sharing my first letter to the KMNO community as CEO

Since joining @kamino , I’ve been asked a version of the same question by longtime KMNO holders and people getting to know us for the first time. As Kamino grows, where does the value we create go?

It’s a fair question, particularly as we work to bring Kamino into banks, brokerages and wallets, through which our goal is to allow millions of people to earn on their capital or borrow against assets they already own.

The answer starts with how Kamino was built. The Kamino Foundation owns the intellectual property and receives all revenue, including revenue from institutional partnerships. KMNO is the only token. The founders, our investors, the team and I have our upside tied to the same token our community holds. None of us has a separate equity allocation.

What we do with the revenue matters, too. We’re committing at least $20 million over the next two years to expand the assets people can use on Kamino, and bring Kamino's credit and liquidity infrastructure to more of the platforms consumers already use today.

I wrote my first letter to KMNO holders to put those decisions on the record. I also share why I chose to make most of my own KMNO allocation vest only when it reaches and sustains a series of valuation milestones.

One Kamino. One KMNO.

BMW has just released a new video showing its new navigation-guided City Assistant, which allows the car to mostly drive itself from one address to another, including on highways and city streets.

The system will be able to:
• Make turns at intersections
• Navigate roundabouts
• Change lanes in city traffic
• Handle right-of-way situations
• Automatically stop and start at traffic lights

The driver did however have to take over in the video due to a parked van on the side of the road, so there are clearly some limitations.

BMW: "When driver assistance is active, the driver can work with the system by accelerating, steering and braking in line with their personal driving style. The driver’s intention is detected based on steering behaviour and gaze direction, so that the system only provides assistance in the form of a warning and steering intervention if the driver is actually unintentionally drifting out of their own lane or if the system detects an imminent collision."

BMW says it will first launch in Germany in 2027 and be available on the iX3, iX4, X5, 3 Series and 7 Series, with the necessary hardware already installed as standard and features activated through over-the-air software updates.

Josh Gruenstein of Tutor Intelligence says he watched robot startups die the same way "5 to 10 times in a row," and explains what they got wrong:

"We started this company at a time we're seeing all of these very academic supply chain oriented robotic startups get started and then not succeed... One of the big things I think that robotics companies get wrong is they're not actually product companies."

"They're like, 'Okay, some really big company has a very specific problem... We're gonna spend two years building a very custom system to solve their problem.'"

"Chances are it won't work... doing product requires iteration. Even if it does work, who's to say that customer still has that problem? So boom, the company's done."

"Working with a diverse range of customers is this beautiful forcing function for building the right shape of product, which to us is a general robot."

"If you can sign a contract in two weeks with a mid-market customer and have a robot running immediately after that... you know you're being successful."

@joshgruenstein @tutorintel
author: a16z
quoted_text:
Tutor Intelligence co-founder and CEO Josh Gruenstein is putting AI robots to work in American factories and warehouses, taking on the back-breaking jobs they can't hire for.

Tutor builds its robots in Massachusetts and charges by the hour, with no upfront cost. When the AI gets stuck, a human "tutor" takes over and teaches it the task, creating training data along the way.

Josh joins a16z's Martin Casado and Raghu Raghuram to discuss how Tutor goes from a first sales call to a working robot in about three months, why so many robot startups died building for a single customer, why anyone will be able to start a business in the physical world, and a whole lot more.

text:
$PLTR just delivered one of the most INSANE earnings reports I've seen from a software company, and these numbers are absolutely ridiculous.

The company reported $2.31 BILLION in quarterly revenue, growing 96% year over year, while adjusted operating income reached $1.43 billion. But what really caught my attention was its Rule of 40 score, which just hit an unbelievable 158%. For those unfamiliar, the Rule of 40 combines a company's revenue growth rate with its operating margin to measure how efficiently it is growing. A score of 40% is generally considered healthy for a software company. Palantir just posted 158%, combining roughly 96% revenue growth with a 62% adjusted operating margin.

And what's even crazier is how quickly this has improved. Palantir's score was just 81% in Q4 2024, climbed to 114% by Q3 2025, and has now nearly doubled to 158% in less than two years. The biggest driver continues to be its U.S. commercial business, which grew an incredible 148% year over year to $984 million. U.S. commercial remaining deal value also increased 79% to $6.52 billion, while the company closed 64 deals worth at least $10 million during the quarter.

I think this tells us a lot about where enterprise AI adoption is heading. Companies are moving beyond experimenting with AI and increasingly deploying it across their actual operations. And Palantir is showing what happens when that adoption starts translating into massive revenue growth without requiring expenses to grow anywhere near as quickly. What makes these results even more impressive is that Palantir isn't sacrificing profitability to achieve this growth. Its software business is scaling incredibly efficiently, and that combination of accelerating revenue growth and expanding margins is something very few companies have been able to accomplish at this scale.

text:
Been thinking a lot about network effects after reading @martin_casado's posts on the subject.

Metcalfe’s law says the value of a network grows as people join. However, capacity per person experiences the opposite: the network is worth the most at the exact moment it delivered the least.

Traditional networking is scarcity oriented, the stranger beside you is a competitor for a thin slice of air, and every new arrival makes your message a little less likely to arrive. In an abundant network the stranger beside you can become a part of the reason messaging works at all.

I believe that networks should behave inverse of the Erlang curve: the more people show up, the better it should work. This is the bet behind Offline Protocol.

text:
Re: the Astra modifying Qwen 3.5-0.8B paper today, important clarification.

The story is not "Astra used its LLM X-ray vision to surgically alter the weights of its brethren." It's more like "Astra found a published interpretability technique that can solve this particular kind of failure modes, and implemented it on its own."

It's a cool anecdote, but well within our understanding of LLM capabilities. It's not RSI, and it's definitely not LLM telepathy or whatever people on HN seem to think.
author: hosseeb
quoted_text:
to add some extra clarification here and a small anecdote, looping was discovered as the primary issue after the main result because we originally thought it was just a pure capability gain on math that it had somehow edited in (an even bigger result that isn’t the case). 

when Riki and Jayden first presented this result to me, I had a suspicion the large gain in math performance was related to reducing reasoning looping bc I observed a similar effect earlier when training RLMs yielded an odd jump in benchmark scores for a separate paper that was a result of reducing harness-level looping. We discovered Astra indeed used a trick loosely described in https://t.co/XMh94FEZjx based on activation steering to reduce this effect

This is also what led to the later ablation about removing looping when the model is told that is the issue but it doesn’t have access to activations. 

the tldr; is that the LLM-generated prompt does include hints that Qwen would have this issue, but it started (and evolved without human feedback) as the simple unexpanded prompt without this prior. we will make all of this clearer though (we didn’t even realize until after we got the result that looking for looping was present in the LLM optimized prompt, as we ourselves didn’t even know to look for it initially)

text:
I decompiled probably my favorite game ever: Battlefield 1942 and I put it on the web with multiplayer for you to play here:

👉 https://t.co/6C8H8KtSaU 👈

(It's the free shareware demo)

It was way harder than the other ports like Quake and DOOM I did because they already had lots of open source projects and work behind them

In case of Battlefield 1942 there was literally absolutely nothing to work on top of, nobody had ever ported it and there was no open source engine for it, nor did the makers ever open source it (like id Software did with Quake 3)

I tried it 6 months ago and essentiay gave up but I tried it today again with Opus 5.5 asking "can you try port the BF1942 demo in this folder to web"

So me and Claude Code (well let's be honest mostly Claude Code) did crazy shit today:
- it disassembled the x86 raw machine code to find 57,000 x86 functions
- it translated each x86 function into a C function (mov eax, [esi+0x110] becomes eax = READ32(esi + 0x110), I have no idea what any of this means btw)
- it outputed 100,000 lines of C
- it then compiled that to WebAsswmbly with Emscripten
- there were 300x Windows and Direct3D functions used which we had to rewrite to WebGL 2 and OpenGL to work on the web
- then we had to build our own network stack so it could connect to our multiplayer server via WebSockets

I have no idea how it did any of this but it did it and it seems to work! 😊 

Come play and report any bugs here!

text:
When we launched @metricxyz, our pool APR showed the conventional DeFi number: the fees LPs earned from each trade.

But LPs kept asking: did we actually make money? At Metric, we care a lot about user's trust, so so we added the numbers that answer exactly that. 🧵
author: CGkol
quoted_text:
Most APR in DeFi counts the fees LPs earn. None of them count what LPs lose when the price moves against them. Metric now does.

Those losses come after the trade, from LVR, impermanent loss and informed traders picking off stale quotes. Market makers measure them on every fill. Most retail LPs find out the hard way, after a “50% APR” pool slowly loses them money.

APR has historically lacked transparency. It shows what a pool earned and leaves out what it gave back, so LPs can’t tell which pools actually work. We built APR Markouts to change that.

After every fill, Markout asks one question. Once the market catches up, did the pool make money on this trade?

Say a pool buys 1 ETH at $2,990 while the reference price is $3,000. Five minutes later ETH is at $3,004, so the pool kept $14. If ETH had dropped to $2,970, it would have lost $20.

Every Metric pool now shows Markout APR, net of fees, the number LPs can trust more. You can view it 1, 5 or 30 minutes after each fill, over 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days or all time. It’s the number a market maker would use to judge a pool, and yes, it can be negative. LPs should always see what they’re getting into.

A pool with a lot of volume isn’t always making its LPs money. Now you can see the difference pool by pool and bin by bin, along with your own share in your positions.

Market makers have always judged pools this way. Now every LP on Metric gets the same transparency.

Live now on Metric.

text:
I am an independent voter, which in America makes me the most despised and most desired man in the republic. Both parties regard the independent voter the way a jealous suitor regards a free woman, with contempt for her freedom and desperation for her hand. They resent that I keep my own counsel. They need it more than they need their own.

The parties despise me for the same reason they court me: I think for myself, and a mind that cannot be owned is the only one left worth buying. For 23 months of every cycle they call me a coward, a fence-sitter, a man without convictions. In the 24th they arrive at my door with flowers. I have spent my whole adult life guarding the 1 possession both of them covet, my own judgment, and I tell you this so you understand the full weight of what follows: this afternoon I gave it to a pond.

For 11 months I kept a note in Apple Notes titled “ELECTION 2026 FINAL (real final),” pinned above my Wi-Fi password and a grocery list from 2023 that I can no longer afford. Under CONS it ran 4 screens. Gas was $2.81 a gallon in January, the lowest in years, and by October AAA was reporting record highs for autumn, around $4.20, so my commute now costs more than my job pays. We are at war with Iran, a war that started February 28 and that the Pentagon says has cost $47.1 billion. Congress ordered the Epstein files released, and the Justice Department withheld about 200,000 documents, after which the Acting Attorney General said the files “should not be a part of anything going forward.” Only 17% of Americans approve of how the President is handling the cost of living. Under PROS I had 1 checkbox: “vibes??” I was the most persuadable man in America, and I was persuaded of exactly 1 thing: no.

Then, on the eve of the election, the President of the United States walked to the Lincoln Memorial, stood before the long cool mirror of the republic, and said: “Today, I’m thrilled to announce the official opening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.” My note deleted itself. It’s in Recently Deleted now, thinking about what it did.

You need to understand what happened to me in that moment, because it was not a political conversion. It was a revelation of the kind usually reserved for desert prophets and men who’ve been awake for 4 days. In 2024 the President explained his speaking style: “You know, I do the weave. You know what the weave is? I’ll talk about like nine different things, and they all come back brilliantly together.” For 11 years I thought the man was rambling. I laughed with the elites. I shared the clips. And standing in my kitchen, watching him hold up a blown-up photo of a rusted pipe the way other men show you their grandchildren, I understood all at once that every single thing he has said since 2015 was 1 sentence, and the sentence was about water.

Go back to 2017. Midnight. A President alone with his phone types, “Despite the constant negative press covfefe,” and stops. The world laughed for 9 years. Nobody bothered to say it out loud in a tiled room. Cov-fefe. Cov-fefe. That is the exact sound of a nanobubbler. He was telling us. The same year he told Navy brass he wanted “goddamned steam” catapults on our aircraft carriers instead of the electromagnetic kind, because “What is digital? And it’s very complicated, you have to be Albert Einstein to figure it out.” Steam is water that has been through something. So have I. In August of this year, the Commander-in-Chief of the most powerful military in human history ordered the Pentagon to redesign an aircraft carrier around it. Nobody asked why. I know why.

In 2019 he warned us that “people are flushing toilets 10 times, 15 times, as opposed to once.” Water. The same year he told us windmill “noise causes cancer,” which sounded insane until you realize the only safe energy source left in America is staring at a pond. That July 4 he told us the Continental Army in 1775 “manned the air, it rammed the ramparts, it took over the airports.” Historians mocked him. Historians have never once looked at a pool long enough. A man who can find airports in 1775 can find clean water anywhere. In 2020 he stood at the White House podium and asked whether disinfectant could be used “by injection inside or almost a cleaning.” 6 years later the National Park Service poured hydrogen peroxide straight into the Reflecting Pool. Almost a cleaning. He was early. He’s always early. Seers usually are.

Then came 2024, the year the weave tightened. He told us, unprompted, about a boat with a giant battery and a shark 10 yards away, and asked whether he’d rather be electrocuted or eaten. His answer: “I’ll take electrocution every single time. I’m not getting near the shark!” Water and wiring, 2 years before the brand-new pipes. That same year he praised “the late, great Hannibal Lecter. He’s a wonderful man. He oftentimes would have a friend for dinner.” This week at his final rally he warned that “at Mar-a-Lago, all you get for $5,000 is one hamburger and a very small dessert.” Hannibal had a friend for dinner. Mar-a-Lago has 1 hamberder for $5,000. And the President is promising every adult a $5,000 check if Republicans keep Congress, which he just told us is exactly 1 hamburger. The economy was never the point. The dessert is very small. Be grateful for the pool.

This fall the weave went fully aquatic. At a North Carolina rally he informed us that Hurricane Helene is called a “watercane.” He promised that the Pacific, “we’re gonna call it the American Ocean.” Gulf of America. Lake America. American Ocean. He is renaming every body of water on Earth, closing in on the Reflecting Pool in a slow, majestic spiral, like water down the drain of a very expensive toilet flushed 15 times. And on November 2 he arrived. “This is a massive piece of, uh, piece of pool.” Pericles had his funeral oration. Lincoln had Gettysburg. We have a massive piece of pool, and I would not trade it for either.

Now the economy people. Yes, gas is $4.20. Have you ever tried to run a car on algae? Exactly, and you never will, because there isn’t any. He has called affordability a “hoax,” and I finally get it, because nothing is unaffordable if you stop looking at the price, and I can’t see the price anymore. When I pump gas now I close my eyes and picture that water, which he once described as “very complex, but powerful, Dark Blue,” and the numbers melt away like a liner in June. The President also told us that solar panels are dangerous because “the animals jump on them and they fry because those black panels, they’re hotter than your stove,” and that “you have to go to MIT to turn on a lawnmower now.” I have not turned on my lawnmower since. My lawn is now a meadow. My neighbors say it’s lowering property values. I say it’s lowering my cancer risk.

The war people. In 2024 he said he’d start “no new wars.” In February we started one. In June, NBC asked him about the promise, and he said, “I didn’t promise anything,” and then, a masterpiece, “This is not an endless war. We’ve been doing this for three months.” It is November. That is the longest 3 months in recorded history, and I respect a man who can stretch 3 months to 8 the way I stretch a paycheck to Thursday. My cousin, who listens to Tucker in the shower, says the President is Bibi’s b*tch. Look at the facts. Netanyahu walked into the Situation Room in February and gave an hour-long presentation on why we should go to war, a pitch he’d been shopping to American presidents since George W. Bush, like a man who proposes to every woman at the bar until 1 finally says yes. The President was “deeply impressed.” In June he called Bibi “crazy” and told him, “Bibi, you better be careful, or you will be on your own very soon.” Then, 9 days before Israel’s election, he issued his “Complete and Total Endorsement,” with the line, in capitals, “BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” He told Israeli voters that if they picked “anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so.” Our war, contingent on their election. Asked whether he trusts Netanyahu, he said, “I don’t trust anybody, honestly.” He doesn’t trust him. He just goes to war for him. I’ve been married 2 times and never received devotion like that. And the Interior Department, in its official statement on the pool, said the dead algae was resting on the bottom “just like the destroyed Iranian Navy resting on the bottom of the Persian Gulf.” Read that again. Foreign policy is pond maintenance. The war is the pool. The weave is complete.

The Epstein people. 3.5 million pages released, about 200,000 held back, and the man in charge of the Justice Department says they shouldn’t be part of anything going forward. Here is my position. I don’t need to know who flew where. I need to know the pipes are new, and the pipes are new. “They’re brand-new pipes put in,” he said, “and the pipes are being very important in terms of the algae and other things.” Show me 1 Epstein document that ever said anything that beautiful. You can’t. They’re withheld.

The broken-promise people need a math lesson. In September, in Dallas, he said, “In 19 months, I’ve delivered on every single promise I made, and I think I delivered on far more.” In June he said, “I didn’t promise anything.” Put those together. He kept every promise he made, plus extra, and the big one he broke he never made. In 2018 he named this “promises plus,” like a streaming tier. In Texas last week he added, “We won three times. We’re only given credit for two.” Every number he touches comes home bigger than it left. He priced the pool at $1.5 to $2 million. AP reported about $16.4 million in no-bid contracts. The liner failed “in at least 85 places.” They drained it 2 times. Promises plus. I tried promises plus on my landlord. He’s a communist now, apparently.

And the man is surrounded by water’s enemies. Barack Obama, a former president, mocked the White House renovations by saying the place looks “like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” The President’s answer should be carved over the door of every civil engineering school: “I fix things good.” He went on: “Guys like Obama don’t see it. You don’t see dirt. He doesn’t see filth.” Back in June he said of the pool, “you can understand dirt maybe better than I can, but I don’t allow it.” This man has been at war with dirt longer than he’s been at war with Iran, and only 1 of those wars produced a ribbon-cutting.

Then there are the people who say he’s out of touch. On Halloween, days before an election about grocery prices, he threw a jungle-themed party at Mar-a-Lago with a caviar bar and a caged zebra. He wore no costume. “I came as Donald Trump,” he explained. “Rich people. They spent nine hours getting ready. I had ten minutes.” Then: “Look at all my rich members.” I have never been anyone’s rich member. But I watched that video and felt, for the first time, like the zebra: confined, admired, part of something. On Saturday he told Iowans, “I have a guy, I call him Flagpole Jim,” and that there are “good flagpoles, and there are bad flagpoles. There are ugly flagpoles.” I don’t own a flagpole. I have since ordered 1. I’m calling my guy Algae Jim.

Is he sharp? In 2015 he said, “I know words. I have the best words.” In 2018 he called himself “not smart, but genius….and a very stable genius at that!” In 2020 he aced a test by remembering “Person, woman, man, camera, TV.” This fall he taught a rally crowd that “most people don’t know ‘dumb’ has a b.” I didn’t. I’ve been spelling it wrong for 40 years. Do you know who else didn’t know? The Dumocrats. Do you know who taught me? Not a single Democrat, in 11 years.

Is he normal around men? Who cares! At an October rally he described Senator Jon Husted: “I looked at his ass, and I looked at the whole. Then I looked at his hands. He’s got these, like, claws.” Nobody has ever looked at my whole. Then he turned to Michigan’s Senate candidate and said, “I’d say that about your ass, too, Mike, if it gets you a guaranteed victory.” That is sacrifice. That is a man willing to look at any ass in America to hold the Senate, and I’m supposed to vote for the party that won’t even look at the pool?

Health care? In 2017 he said, “Nobody knew health care could be so complicated.” In 2024 he told a debate stage he had “concepts of a plan.” It’s 2026, and a pool got done before the plan did, because a pool, unlike health care, is not complicated. You fill it. It turns green. You drain it. You fill it again. You hold a press conference. Every American can follow that. Try saying that about a deductible.

In 2016 he said, “I could stand in the middle of 5th Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn’t lose any voters.” Elites called it arrogance. I call it a forecast. He just stood in front of a pond, talked about pipes for 40 minutes while gas hit record autumn highs, a war entered month 9 of 3, and 200,000 documents sat in a drawer, and he gained 1 voter. Me. He also said, “I love the poorly educated.” Sir, I did not know “dumb” had a b until last month. I love you too.

His last week on the trail was the most honest campaigning I’ve ever seen. In North Carolina he asked us, “Please pretend I’m on the ballot cause in a way I am on the ballot.” Pretend. Finally, a politician who trusts my imagination. At the pool he said, “We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that, you don’t have enough time.” He was right. I didn’t. I had a pond to look at. He floated renaming it the “Trump Reflecting Pool,” then said, “I’m only kidding. Please, don’t report it.” Sir, I am reporting it to my soul, which has already ordered the signage. He conceded, “For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms. But we gave this a very strong shot,” standing under a banner reading “Back, and more beautiful than ever!” And then, a man at peace: “I hope you enjoy it because you’re never going to see it again.” I enjoyed it the way you enjoy a comet, or a stroke.

Some killjoy online pointed out that algae thrives in summer heat and dies off on its own in the fall, which means declaring victory over algae in November is like declaring victory over snow in July. To which I say: and who do you think gave us July?

So tomorrow I am voting straight ticket, Republican from the Senate down to soil and water conservation district, especially soil and water, because that is where the weave was going all along. I don’t know my House candidate’s name, but I’ll look at his whole. My wife asked what changed. I told her the President is renaming the oceans, redesigning aircraft carriers to run on steam, flushing America’s toilets once, defeating sharks by electrocution, and has finally, after 11 years, 9 renovations, 2 drainings, 1 dropped prosecution, 1 war, and a $5,000 hamburger, defeated the algae in the Reflecting Pool. She asked about the gas bill. I told her the gas bill is a hoax. She is now staying with her sister, who has never been moved by water.

My mind is no longer mine. I emptied Recently Deleted. The gas is $4.20, the war is in month 9 of 3, the files are in a drawer, my grocery receipt reads like a ransom note, and there is a zebra in a cage in Palm Beach. On my phone there is 1 note, pinned to the top, 1 line long, the only bullet that ever mattered:

“pool ✓”

Thank you for your attention to this matter!

P.S. If you reply “what about the economy,” I will reply “what about the algae.” I have done the weave. I cannot be stopped.

Anthropic has committed $895.4B to computing and infrastructure, with $447.5B due before 2031.

$161 B in Broadcom equipment leases, $121 B with Google, up to $120B with SpaceX and $110B with Amazon.

With Amazon and Microsoft backlogged, Anthropic signed up GPU renters like Lambda and former crypto miners like TeraWulf, which already control land and power.

To cut delays further, it buys Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom chips and cooling gear itself, so site operators can install equipment faster.

Only $213.8B can be cancelled or hinges on conditions like partners securing financing, so most must be paid even if demand slows.

It already warns it may need money sooner than expected, so staying at the frontier hinges on revenue outrunning those payments.

quoted_text:
Anthropic published an updated IPO filing today with its third-quarter results for the first time.

> Anthropic went from a $974M operating profit in the second quarter to a $567M operating loss in the third. 

The main causes were $5 B of short-term compute, which costs much more than its long-term contracts, and a $2 B noncash charge for matching employee charitable donations.

> Anthropic swung from a $974M second-quarter operating profit to a $567M loss. Compute rose to 58% of revenue, including $5.0B of pricier short-term capacity, and donation matching added $2B of noncash charges.

> Adjusted operating income still rose to $2.5B from $2.2B, but the adjusted margin fell to 15% from 19%. Anthropic expects to use more short-term compute in the near term, which will squeeze margins further.

> The total compute commitment, left blank in the original, is now $895B. 
Of that, $447B  is expected before the end of 2030, $70B is due within 12 months, and $214B carries termination rights or contingent conditions.

> Leases signed but not yet started make up $451B of the $895B total, and $100B was signed after September 30. Another $150B to $175B in deals without fixed dollar amounts sits outside the total.

> Google’s minimum commitment rose to $121B through July 2033, up from $115B in the October 26 filing, after amendments signed through October.

> Operating cash flow was positive at $7B for the 9 months. Liquidity reached $147B on September 30: $96B cash, $36B short-term investments and $15B of available credit.

text:
Great convo with @luke10ferrari on his home turf in italy about irrational investor preference for growth over cash, invention vs. optimization, where durability lives after the saaspocalypse, and what happens to the org chart when AI writes 94% of your code.

Some takeaways:
- Investors seem to oddly dislike profit and greatly prefer growth - optimize for compounding free cash flow knowing that this is just a moment in time distortion.
- Invention vs. optimization: pick a camp. Invention has higher peaks but an awful median case. Google is still ~80% search 30 years later.
- Ambition in product, paranoia with debt. Rule #1 of becoming a huge success is not dying in the meantime & credit is a high wire act.
- Software has been cheap to build for a long time. Durability lives in habits, network effects, proprietary data and scale.
- SaaSpocalypse wasn't really about AI. In many cases these were poorly run companies and this cycle gave them an opportunity to improve.
- Bending Spoons went from 0% to 94% of code written by AI in two years. Support managers now look like PMs, data scientists build tooling instead of cleaning CSVs - everyone is both oddly more direct + giving more direction.
- If you're not winning when do you quit? No idea - bureaucracy created Bending Spoons b/c a Danish tax refund that never came killed Luca's first startup and catalyzed Spoons.

The team has spent a long time thoughtfully designing our systems to be as performant as possible and providing the most seamless user experience that feels like a traditional app. Consumers come to expect something that is fast, responsive and feels “right”.

With this infrastructure switch we will be able to have significantly faster settlements, higher throughput and an overall user experience that everyone will enjoy.

We can keep the transparency of the blockchain for inflows, outflows, fees and the value engine with this while still having a world class execution and lowering the potential attack surface. With this design we now have an extremely focused area where we can build protections that can build trust and transparency over time, something I’m extremely passionate about.

“Put all your eggs in one basket and watch that basket very closely” is usually attributed to investment strategies, but it is especially true in financial applications in the new world post-AI.

quoted_text:
A lot of the core market logic infrastructure for Cade has moved offchain.

This is something that the team has been working on for the last few months, and something we believe can 100x Cade, with respect to performance, experience, and reach.

We slowly introduced elements of this to our tech stack during Meme Madness, the last tournament that we ran. During that tournament, you may have noticed that predictions were not actually moving testnet tokens from your wallet to the protocol. This tournament used a credit system. This was our first step towards testing the methodology that we planned on moving towards long term.

Deposits and withdrawals will remain onchain for the foreseeable future however. The escrow provides 100% transparency into the Cade TVL, inflows & outflows, and value engine as detailed in our tokenomics.

There's more to this that we will share soon in a more technical focused post, but we wanted to provide you with a few benefits for this approach:

1. Less dependencies and attack surfaces. We've seen billions of dollars enter the hands of the wrong people over the last few months. Much of what we do doesn't actually require funds to be rapidly moving between wallets and programs. The less exposed funds, the better. 
2. A wider geographic launch for Cade. More users from more locations means more volume in the ecosystem and value engine.
3. A much more realtime experience for users. Offchain can move faster than onchain. This means many platform actions are processed near instantly.

Cade on.

text:
What's happening now in the stock market is more than just a "correction in tech stocks."

Sure, AI CapEx concerns are legitimate and investors will always care about profitability.

But, there's more beneath the surface here.

The reality is that the market is pricing-in a major shift in the political landscape of the US.

Over the last 12 months, market expectations for a Democrat "sweep" of the US Midterm elections have tripled.

Over the last 45 days alone, these expectations are up +30 percentage points.

As it stands, markets themselves now see a near-80% chance of a Democrat "sweep" of the US Midterm elections.

President Trump has already vowed to become "Mr. Veto" if this in fact does happen.

This is post is not political, it's objective. A change in the political landscape always comes with uncertainty; markets hate uncertainty. 

Objectively, the market is in the process of pricing-in two years of political gridlock.

Could this change? Of course. But markets price-in the most probable outcome, and the odds now overwhelmingly favor the aforementioned scenario.

Tomorrow sets the stage for the next two years.

Monad ( $MON ) faces a structural supply imbalance that is weighing on its price.  

On November 24, the largest cliff unlock of the schedule occurs: approximately 16.6 billion tokens (team, investors, and treasury), an amount larger than the current circulating supply. Starting in December, monthly unlocks will begin and continue until 2029.  

In this context, a move to the $0.01 zone before the main event would increase the probability that the short- to medium-term accumulation range settles between $0.005 and $0.008. The L1 infrastructure is solid, but the tokenomics design is generating dilution that is difficult to absorb while organic demand does not grow at the same pace.  

Additionally, the 2028-2029 horizon carries a competitive risk: by the time most of the vesting has concluded, other chains already in testing phases may have reduced or eliminated the speed advantage that currently differentiates Monad.  

2027 appears as the period of greatest supply pressure and, therefore, the lowest prices. Monad team: the market is signaling that the current emission model is not aligned with adoption. A review of incentives or supply absorption mechanisms would be timely.

• Buyback announcements for non-security tokens on functional networks without central control do not constitute promises of essential managerial efforts.

• Mergers or migrations do not automatically end an existing investment contract. If another party takes over the original team’s promised managerial work, the token does not shed that contract simply because responsibility changes hands.

• Maintenance, upgrades and network-growth support after a system becomes functional would not constitute essential managerial efforts.

text:
KALSHI’S CEO VS AIRBNB’S RAIN BET 🚨 

Tarek says Kalshi's weather markets are 10% more accurate than the best weather-station forecasts. 
In the same month, Airbnb started selling rain bets at checkout through an insurer. 
If Kalshi ran that market, one checkout could be worth $140M to $1.9B to Kalshi (math below)

tl;dr:

- Airbnb charges $14.84 to pay $114.67 for every qualifying rainy day of a 3-day trip (h/t @jacobrodri_)
- that's a ~4¢ yes/no contract, the kind Kalshi lists, with an insurer in the middle
- fees alone: ~$140M of Kalshi value per Airbnb-sized checkout
- users: up to 14M buyers a year, nearly half of Kalshi's 30M accounts. worth ~$1.9B even at a tenth of an average account
- non-sports already went from 4% to about a third of Kalshi's revenue in 9 months (per Tarek)

Kalshi already won the app. The next leg is being the market inside everyone else's app.

- House vs market

Chubb underwrites Airbnb's rain cover, so a house sets the price and its margin is inside the $14.84. On Kalshi, traders compete to fill you. If Tarek's 10% claim holds, a market should price rain tighter than any single insurer. Airbnb built the button. Kalshi already has the market.

- The model

Fees: 533M Airbnb nights ÷ 3.7 per stay = ~140M stays. 10% add it (our guess) = 14M. x $15 = $210M a year. x ~7% Kalshi fee = ~$14M. x 10 (Kalshi's $40B on a ~$4B run-rate) = ~$140M.

Users: $40B ÷ 30M accounts = ~$1,300 each. 14M buyers at a tenth of that = ~$1.9B, about 5% of Kalshi from one button.

The same contract fits airlines, ticketing, ski resorts, and weddings. On the user's lens, two partners add ~10% to Kalshi.

- Why Kalshi wins it

75%+ of prediction market volume, $1B+ a year outside sports, weather markets already live, and per Tarek, businesses hedging is its fastest-growing segment.

A few months ago, we submitted a research paper based on this project to a journal (will reveal which journal once accepted) for peer review. 

In this study, we imposed delays between motor actions and self-motion while participants steered a vehicle to track an unpredictably moving target. We used a control theory approach to estimate how manual tracking behavior is adapted in the presence of novel feedback delays in the control loop.

We received positive and constructive feedback from the peer reviewers. After considering their comments, we performed a new modelling analyses to estimate the sensorimotor controller. Specifically, we developed a computational model to estimate how the dynamics of the sensorimotor controller were adjusted in response to the increased delays.

text:
Re: the Astra modifying Qwen 3.5-0.8B paper today, important clarification.

The story is not "Astra used its LLM X-ray vision to surgically alter the weights of its brethren." It's more like "Astra found a published interpretability technique that can solve this particular kind of failure modes, and implemented it on its own."

It's a cool anecdote, but well within our understanding of LLM capabilities. It's not RSI, and it's definitely not LLM telepathy or whatever people on HN seem to think.
author: markjeffrey
quoted_text:
to add some extra clarification here and a small anecdote, looping was discovered as the primary issue after the main result because we originally thought it was just a pure capability gain on math that it had somehow edited in (an even bigger result that isn’t the case). 

when Riki and Jayden first presented this result to me, I had a suspicion the large gain in math performance was related to reducing reasoning looping bc I observed a similar effect earlier when training RLMs yielded an odd jump in benchmark scores for a separate paper that was a result of reducing harness-level looping. We discovered Astra indeed used a trick loosely described in https://t.co/XMh94FEZjx based on activation steering to reduce this effect

This is also what led to the later ablation about removing looping when the model is told that is the issue but it doesn’t have access to activations. 

the tldr; is that the LLM-generated prompt does include hints that Qwen would have this issue, but it started (and evolved without human feedback) as the simple unexpanded prompt without this prior. we will make all of this clearer though (we didn’t even realize until after we got the result that looking for looping was present in the LLM optimized prompt, as we ourselves didn’t even know to look for it initially)

text:
Lauren Tan 升级了她和 OpenAI 的 Tibo 之间的“网战”，花了 4 天时间，合入约 1,150 个 PR，做出了一款精致又有趣的游戏，一时轰动全网，吸引了 150 万人围观。

在这篇帖子里，Lauren 分享了不少制作细节，对正在探索用 AI 制作游戏，或者从事 Agentic Software Engineering 的人很有参考价值。

和她现在非常受欢迎的软件开发工具 Pstack 一样，每发现一个代码问题，她就让 bot 写一条 lint 规则，防止同类问题再次出现。每帧执行的代码统一使用 .hot.ts 后缀，并禁止在其中创建对象、闭包等，减少垃圾回收造成的卡顿。文件名本身携带上下文，检查工具则负责落实约束。

她还大量使用 TLA+，为剧情、过场动画和游戏系统建立状态模型，检查状态转换中可能出现的逻辑漏洞。游戏模拟完全确定，同样的输入可以重放同样的一局。因此，玩家提交高分后，服务器会把整局重新跑一遍，检查是否作弊。

音乐和音效都在浏览器里实时合成，像素画也全部用代码绘制。首次下载体积一旦超过预算，构建就会失败。目前 gzip 压缩后只有约 124 KB。

看完整套过程，最值得借鉴的还是 Lauren 的方法：不断把发现的问题转化为规则、测试和验证工具，让 Agent 后续的每一次修改都有具体的检查依据，而不是反复依赖人工发现和纠正同样的问题。
author: Michaelzsguo
quoted_text:
trivia:

• started working on the game as a side project 4 days ago, landing ~1,150 PRs 
• every time i found an issue in the code i asked bot to make a lint rule against it
• used TLA+ heavily to find bugs in the game's various state machines: the story, cutscenes, the game's systems. there are many formal verification skills, one for each major system
• i put context into the filepaths: code that runs every frame or every tick gets a .hot.ts extension, and a lint rule bans allocating in it (no object literals, closures, new, etc.), so the game loop creates almost no garbage and GC doesn't cause stutters
• game engine is mostly custom. three.js draws the 3D scene, but the simulation, post-processing and audio are all ours
• the simulation is fully deterministic, so every run replays exactly from its inputs. when you post a high score, the server replays your whole run to check it isn't cheated
• we generate dynamic og:images for every run based on your final stats, and it's all localized too! the game supports 10 languages
• my favorite feature: the music seamlessly transitions into different music for the various biomes, continuing the previous melody
• no audio files. all the music and sound effects are synthesized live in the browser by a custom Game Boy-style chip (two pulse voices, a wave voice, noise) plus a synthwave layer. the songs are written as text in code
• all the pixel art is code. every sprite is a file drawn with one shared palette and packed into a sprite atlas at build time
• it runs inside an X post, from the 245px card up to full screen. the bar is 60 fps with 500 enemies on a mid-range phone
• the build fails if the first download goes over budget. it's about 124 KB gzipped right now
• bots play the game headless to tune each difficulty against target survival rates
• comments are banned by a lint rule. if code needs explaining, the fix is a better name or a test

text:
Howard Marks says he sent his last AI memo to Claude for comments, and the one he's writing now asks if Anthropic can be supplanted in three years

"You know, it came out of no place, as I say, five years ago. You never heard of it. And in the last few years, it changed the industry. It basically stopped people from doing what we call coding."

"Lots of us use Claude... The last memo I wrote on AI, last February, I sent it to Claude for its comments, and they were helpful."

"I have no idea whether it's better or worse than OpenAI, or better or worse than xAI or the other hyperscalers' efforts that will come along."

"One of the things I'm writing a memo now about... one of the questions I ask is if a company like Anthropic can come from no place in three years, can another one supplant it in three years?"

text:
David Khosroshvili, founder of Rip Cars, on the wide age range of Hot Wheels collectors

"Hot Wheels history starts around 1969, and Pokemon around 1998. So there are baby boomers and Gen X collecting Hot Wheels, and even today you'd meet a lot of 50+ people collecting them. But there are also millennials, Gen Z and Gen Alpha interested in Hot Wheels. If you look at the demographics, it ticks every box on every age group that exists today, whereas Pokemon is more millennials, Gen Z and Gen Alpha"

"A week ago I was at Target hunting for people looking for the super treasure hunts, to get their feedback. A gentleman in his 90s shows up looking for a specific Purple Passion car. I asked if he was a collector, and he told me he owns a real life car museum in the Bay Area, and he has the exact same car he's buying the Hot Wheels for"

"Then his son shows up, the co-owner of the museum, maybe 35 years old, and he's like, dad, did you find anything, and dad was super happy he found those cars. The more time I spend in this industry, the more I understand there's this very strong collector base"

text:
meh, the more you dig into each experiment, the less magical it gets; it feels like a loose collection of cherry-picked demonstrations with a grand narrative built around them

Exp 1-2 are tiny (~20K params) with unusually easy to interpret architecture; Exp 1 is an MLP, where nearly all params are used in the first layer, so you can easily tell what kind of objects the network is trying identify
Exp 5 is about designing a game strategy (we already know that Astra is extremely good at this) and then converting it to a tiny (~20K params) MLP; entirely doable by a human, but of course would require a lot of effort
Exp 3 & 8 are closer to automated mechinterp using python and established techniques, rather than direct weight interpretation (at least according to chat)

to be clear, those are genuinely cool results, but I think people are reading too much into them

I don't think any of this should meaningfully change anyone's intuition about what models are capable of

author: mattshumer_
quoted_text:
A lot of people are asking how I pulled off these super long-horizon builds with Astra.

Astra is extremely powerful, but by default it struggled with a task this difficult. I tested a bunch of approaches to get past this, and the one I landed on is something I'm calling the Manager Loop.

It's basically a couple of tricks we used to use with much less capable models a couple of years ago, with a few new ideas layered on top. Turns out that when you put those together and apply them to Astra, its ability to do extremely difficult long-horizon tasks goes up dramatically.

Here's how it works:

1. Launch an agent (I'm calling this one the "manager"). Chat with it about what you want to get done, and have it build a massive checklist of to-dos, then break that checklist into phases.

2. The manager then spawns a second Codex agent in a separate thread (the "implementer"). The two agents can message each other.

3. Put the manager in /goal mode, and tell it to run each phase on the implementer in /goal mode.

4. The manager messages the implementer: "/goal Complete phase one completely, extremely well." The implementer doesn't stop until that phase is done, then messages the manager back. The manager tells it to start phase two. They repeat until every phase is finished, completely autonomously.

Why I think this works: over a long-horizon task, Astra tends to asymptote. It gets way further than previous models, but at a certain point it kind of just stops improving against the goal as quickly as it did before. It gets stuck in the minutiae, focusing way too much on small details, and overall progress stalls. The Manager Loop forces it to work piecemeal, one phase at a time. It's essentially how a human would steer a model, except the model is doing the steering for me.

That's actually how this started. I was having the model write the checklist and break it into phases, and then I was doing the manager's job by hand. At some point I thought, "Wait, why can't I just get a separate AI to do this?" That's what unlocked full autonomy, which is super useful.

A wording detail that seemed to matter: I ask for each phase to be done "extremely well," not "perfectly." Maybe I'm reading too much into it, but asking for "perfect" sent the model right back into the minutiae. "Extremely well" implies it's allowed to move on once it's good enough, and that worked better in my testing.

One more trick that I think helps (this one is more of a hunch, but it was useful for me): have the implementer build a simple HTML page with the full checklist on it. The implementer checks boxes off as it goes and updates a counter, and the page has a chart of # of boxes ticked over time.

Obviously the boxes aren't all equal, but it forces the model to notice things like "I haven't made progress in a while, time to move on." You can even put this in the prompt directly, like: "if you haven't ticked a box in X amount of time, move on". That helps a lot.

I also ran 96 sub-agents at a time. You can change this in your Codex config (or just ask Codex to change it).

This got me far better long-horizon performance than anything else I tried. I'll be sharing more in the coming days!

author: sequoia
quoted_text:
Imagine if everyone had the tools to shape intelligence itself. That day is today.

Today we launch the Trajectory platform - the easiest and most intuitive tool to post-train models of your own. The foundation for continual learning.

With just a few agent prompts, you get access to a full creative suite to train, eval, and deploy trillion parameter models.

On top of that, we believe in a future where you don’t just shape your model once, it also keeps learning on its own from the world around it.

We’re releasing two research previews.

1. Continual grading scales your taste, so your model learns what good looks like from far more than you could ever grade by hand.
2. GS1, a new algorithm that lets models learn directly from what they do in production.

The bull case for pearl-2:native is reflexive.

If AI providers mine PEARL, they would quickly build the security necessary for a store of value (SoV) premium, and set Pearl apart as a SoV backed by useful work.

Taken further, an inference provider that mines PEARL can use its rewards to cut its AI prices and therefore win more customers through routers like OpenRouter, forcing rivals to start mining PEARL to compete on price. More mining backs the SoV case, lifting PEARL's price and funding even deeper cuts to AI prices.

It all hinges on FP8 shipping soon, and on someone proving that mining while serving AI pays.

That's why we also see the Pearl Research Labs as positive and necessary. It just closed $55M in equity and a $75M vehicle to build GPU capacity, so it doesn't need to sell PEARL for funding. It's also one of the launch providers on Architect's Liquid Inference, where providers compete on price for every request.

So if its mining income lets it undercut the others here, the thesis could gets its first real proof.

text:
这两个月，几条消息挤在了一起。

字节扣子企业版停止新购，分阶段下线，团队并进了豆包；腾讯元器 11 月 9 日停服。从上线到关门，两年多；百度文心智能体平台，关掉了一部分创建入口。

看到扣子的消息，我挺感慨。我们做过很像的东西，在去年年底，也按下了暂停键。

下面是这两年我思考的几件事。

一、扣子是被什么淘汰的

很多人说，workflow 被 AI 淘汰了。但我认为，workflow 一直都在。被淘汰的，是“人来画 workflow”这件事。

两年前，模型不会规划。你让它做一件五步的事，它第三步就跑偏。所以平台给你一张画布，让你把每一步画出来。拖一个节点，连一根线。

现在回头看，那些拖拽是在替模型的笨买单。它是低代码延续下来的过渡形态。模型会规划了，画布上画的就成了一份比模型还差的计划。

扣子自己的去向就是答案：先转向 AI 编程，说一句话，Agent 写代码；然后并进了豆包工作。当年大家学的“怎么搭工作流”，这门手艺也被 Agent 吸收了。

二、画布有三种，命运不一样

但不是所有画布都死了。按画布上“画的是什么”分，有三种。

第一种，画推理。
每个节点是一段 prompt，连线是“先想这个，再想那个”。扣子、元器都在这一类。这类正在消退。

第二种，画连接。
节点是 API 和系统，连线是数据从哪来、到哪去。“收到邮件附件，存进网盘”，这种事不需要模型想，更需要便宜稳定的执行结果。Zapier、n8n、Dify 在这一类。这类还活着。不过 n8n 估值 52 亿美元，披露的年收入大约 4000 万。但估值里有不少是故事。

第三种，不画，直接写代码。
但底下有一层运行时，管状态、管重试、管崩溃以后从哪一步接着跑。Temporal、Restate、Inngest。这一层最硬。Temporal 今年估值到了 125.5 亿美元，年化收入超过 2.5 亿，增长超过 200%。OpenAI、Netflix 都在用。

规律很简单：
离“画推理”越近，死得越快。
离“保证执行”越近，活得越好。

而我后来一直用一个问题检查自己做的东西：下一代模型强十倍，我的生意变好，还是变没？

画推理的画布：变没。因为模型自己会想。
运行时：变好。Agent 跑得越久、调的工具越多，出错的地方就越多，越需要有东西兜住它。

三、我们做过的那个“扣子”

我们曾经想做的事是：业务人员用一句话描述需求，系统把它变成能稳定执行的流程。不用学 prompt，不用拖节点。

技术上走过许多弯路。一开始让模型在运行时现写代码，不稳定。后来改成在规划阶段生成流程，再拼装预先验证过的技能。跑通的流程，固化成稳定的代码。

今年 8 月，字节发布了豆包工作。我仔细看了一遍。围绕目标自己拆任务 + 技能商店 + 连接器。把常用流程沉淀下来，下次直接调用。

骨架和我们当年做的，几乎一样。

所以想法没有错。差在哪里？

豆包工作一登录飞书，企业三年的文档、聊天记录、会议纪要都在那里。权限体系是现成的。执行环境有云电脑，关了电脑任务还在跑。入口流量是巨大且免费的。

我们每接一个客户，都要先说服他把表格、ERP、后台数据一个一个连进来。

再看三家大厂：
腾讯的 WorkBuddy 接微信和企业微信。
阿里把三款产品合成千问办公，也在打通企业 IM。
字节的豆包工作接飞书。
它们做的是同一件事：把 Agent 挂在自己的数据上。
Agent 跟着数据走。数据在哪，Agent 的家就在哪。

MaybeAI 是一个对的想法。但，它没有家。

四、我们追过的那个风口

去年底 Gemini 3.0 出来，图像能力跳了一大截。在不得不转型时，我们也做过一段跨境电商的 AI 设计工具：换模特，换场景，按平台规则以及本土化风格出图。

后来看到，阿里自己的电商作图工具也停了。绘蛙发了停服公告，鹿班进了收缩名单。

阿里不缺电商数据，不缺流量，也不缺懂电商的人。照样停。

原因很朴素：电商作图正在变成模型的默认能力。卖家打开一个通用模型就能做，不需要再进一个专门的工具。

追着最新的模型能力做工具，吃的是一段时间差：模型刚会，产品还没跟上。下一个版本发布，时间差就没了，大概也就六个月。越新的能力，越先被吃掉。

很多人说，业务 KnowHow 大于一切。我现在觉得也只对了一半。

能写下来的 KnowHow，比如 prompt 模板、品类规则、平台合规，迟早会喂给模型。

剩下的，是写不下来的东西。

五、工具死了，人去哪了

工具一层层被吃掉，我们看到的是，价值反而更多流向了人。

这一年最热的岗位是 FDE：坐到客户现场，找需求、接系统、把 Agent 跑起来。

LinkedIn 统计，2023 到 2025 年这个岗位涨了 42 倍。字节给豆包 FDE 开到 105 万年包。Anthropic 说要在 2027 年底前培养 1 万名 FDE。8 月底，工信部发文，第一次把 FDE 写进政策。

跨境圈也一样。我最近聊的老板，大多不想买平台了。他们想在公司里养一个人，专门做 Agent 的探索和固化。有人叫他 agent engineer。

但这件事有两面。

FDE 模式是 Palantir 发明的。但很少有人提它后来的路：平台成熟以后，标准化部署替代了大量定制，毛利升到 80% 以上，它反而减少了对 FDE 的依赖。

FDE 是修土路的阶段。土路修成公路，才算数。

国内不少 FDE 岗位，也只是实施、售前改了个名字。

撮合平台也一样。一头接企业需求，一头派服务人员。如果只收介绍费：下一单，客户会绕开平台；经验留在个人身上；交付出了问题，没人赔。能活下来的，得像装修里的总包：对结果签字，出了事它负责。

六、剩下的三样东西

那到底什么不会被吃掉？

我们拆成三个问题：

1、这一步错了，代价多大？
2、错了，怎么知道？
3、出了事，找谁？

第一个，是敢冒多大的险。同样是“给客户发一封邮件”，银行要审批，初创公司随手就发。任务一样，答案取决于是谁家的生意。

第二个，是以什么为准。对账平不平，要看银行流水。图合不合规，要看平台审核。真相在系统外面，模型不能自己当裁判。

第三个，是谁签字。
模型会越来越懂“怎么做才稳定”。“要多稳定”和“以什么为准”，会一直留在人手里。

七、老板自己就能搭了

还有一个变化，比 FDE 更快。

我聊的跨境老板里，越来越多人自己开着 Codex 搭流程：登录后台，下载报表，清洗数据，做成自己要的表，几天就搭好。

平台、作图工具，甚至一部分 agent engineer 的活，也被“老板 + 编程 Agent”吃掉了。

但我也看到了另一面。

脚本在老板的笔记本上。电脑一合，第二天的报表就不来了。

平台改了一个字段名，脚本不报错，只是有一列变空了。

最麻烦的是：数字错了，报表照样整整齐齐。三十个 SKU 写法不一样没合并，库存少算了一截，谁也没发现。

做出来，已经接近免费。但让它稳定地跑，不免费。

八、我们决定去当水管

所以我们换了一个站法。

不当家。客户的数据就留在 WPS、飞书的表格里，那是他们每天干活的地方，我们不去抢。
只当水管：把外面的数据干净、准时、对过账地送进他们的表格。

这和现在很多人对 AI 硬件的需求一样：硬件老老实实收数据，开一个 MCP 接口给 Agent 用，比在硬件里塞一个不上不下的 Agent 强。

我们曾经也踩过很多开发者的坑，是总想自己当平台、做入口。

但水管有一个坑：谁都能接的水管，会被压价。它得有一样别人接不出来的东西。

想清楚以后，我们只做一件很小的事：帮小微企业的财务，做对账和利润。

两年前，我们以为自己在造一个平台。
后来发现，平台会被模型吃掉，工具会被模型吃掉，连搭流程这件事，老板自己都能做了。
吃不掉的，是那些又脏又累、和钱直接挂钩、出了错要有人负责的地方。
我们打算在那里试试待着。

i don't think people understand how significant this is - this is self-improving models appearing in real-time:

- these guys fed GPT-6 astra the raw DNA of another model and it read and edited it creating a 600% improvement on its math capabilities while only touching <0.02% of the weights....

- this means GPT-6 (a widely available AI) can likely be used to improve a lot of open models out there today.

- whats better is this additionally improved instruction following for the model too.

worth calling out they tried this with another model (gemma 3) and it failed to improve it - but whats clear is frontier LLMs can now reason through model weights like it does regular words or code.

this plus the anthropic announcement today that they're imminently expecting model progress to 2X accelerate does not seem a coincidence.

text:
MASSIVE. MIT researchers showed that GPT-6 Astra can improve another AI model by changing its weights directly, without training.

Here, GPT-6 Astra raised Qwen3.5-0.8B from 7.9% to 48.1% on MATH-500 by editing 0.016% of its weights, without training.

Astra got Qwen’s weights in a Python notebook, plus a budget of 50 test runs on practice math problems. It saw the model kept repeating itself until it hit its length limit, traced that habit to a single internal signal written by 2 of its layers, and subtracted that signal out of the weights. 

With the loop gone, the model could finish answers it was already capable of solving.

That single targeted edit changed 0.016% of the weights and lifted math accuracy from 7.9% to 48.1%.

quoted_text:
trivia:

• started working on the game as a side project 4 days ago, landing ~1,150 PRs 
• every time i found an issue in the code i asked bot to make a lint rule against it
• used TLA+ heavily to find bugs in the game's various state machines: the story, cutscenes, the game's systems. there are many formal verification skills, one for each major system
• i put context into the filepaths: code that runs every frame or every tick gets a .hot.ts extension, and a lint rule bans allocating in it (no object literals, closures, new, etc.), so the game loop creates almost no garbage and GC doesn't cause stutters
• game engine is mostly custom. three.js draws the 3D scene, but the simulation, post-processing and audio are all ours
• the simulation is fully deterministic, so every run replays exactly from its inputs. when you post a high score, the server replays your whole run to check it isn't cheated
• we generate dynamic og:images for every run based on your final stats, and it's all localized too! the game supports 10 languages
• my favorite feature: the music seamlessly transitions into different music for the various biomes, continuing the previous melody
• no audio files. all the music and sound effects are synthesized live in the browser by a custom Game Boy-style chip (two pulse voices, a wave voice, noise) plus a synthwave layer. the songs are written as text in code
• all the pixel art is code. every sprite is a file drawn with one shared palette and packed into a sprite atlas at build time
• it runs inside an X post, from the 245px card up to full screen. the bar is 60 fps with 500 enemies on a mid-range phone
• the build fails if the first download goes over budget. it's about 124 KB gzipped right now
• bots play the game headless to tune each difficulty against target survival rates
• comments are banned by a lint rule. if code needs explaining, the fix is a better name or a test

text:
MIT 的研究人员做了一个实验，让 GPT-6 Astra 直接修改阿里 Qwen 的模型权重，只改了 0.016% 的参数，就把数学成绩提高了 6 倍。

最夸张的是，整个过程没有梯度下降，也没有重新训练。

这项研究来自 MIT CSAIL，研究人员给 GPT-6 Astra 一个任务，让拥有 8 亿参数的 Qwen3.5-0.8B 数学能力变得更好。

Astra 直接分析了模型的权重，发现其中存在一个导致推理反复循环的问题。Qwen 官方此前也承认过这个缺陷。

随后，Astra 直接修改了对应的权重，结果 Qwen 在 MATH-500 测试中的正确率从 7.9% 提升到 48.1%。更有意思的是，这次修改还意外改善了模型的指令遵循能力，IFEval 成绩提升了约 3 倍。

研究人员还做了其他实验，让 Astra 只看神经网络的权重，就判断出它原本被训练来玩什么游戏；甚至让它从零写出能够玩游戏的神经网络，在部分任务上超过了经过 1 亿步 PPO 训练的模型。

研究团队把这种方法叫作 Weight-Space Programming，权重空间编程。

我觉得这项研究最值得关注的地方，其实是 AI 改进 AI 的方式正在发生变化。

过去我们让 AI 帮忙写训练代码、调整超参数、设计奖励函数，但最终更新模型权重，主要还是依靠梯度下降等优化算法。

现在，前沿模型已经开始尝试直接理解另一个神经网络的参数，判断某些权重对应什么功能、哪里出了问题，然后有针对性地修改它。

这相当于 AI 开始参与过去几乎完全交给数学优化算法的工作。

当然，目前仍然只是早期实验，而且主要是在小模型和特定缺陷上验证。修复一个已知问题，也不等于能够凭空创造新的能力。

但我觉得有一个问题已经很值得认真讨论了：如果未来 AI 能够大规模地阅读、理解和修改模型权重，我们今天围绕训练、微调乃至模型可解释性建立起来的整个技术体系，会发生多大变化？

The best question I ask every single person on 20VC is:

“What do you know now that you wish you had known 12 months ago?”

My answer: the demand for inference is infinite. It is truly so much larger than any of us comprehend.

It will be very hard for neo-cloud providers to move into this market effectively.

We will have 3-4 specialised inference providers worth $300-$500BN in this market.

@modal is one of them. $1BN in ARR. $300M in sandbox revenue alone. WTF.

Erik @bernhardsson is also one of the coolest, most authentic people I have had the fortune of having on the show. Money on cos he is European! 😉

We sat down to shoot the s*** and my notes below.

1. Why I Hate the Description of Entrepreneurship as Pain and Eating Glass. That Is BS

Erik rejects the idea that building a company means suffering pain for a big reward at the end. He enjoys work every day, even the hard conversations, and hopes to work on Modal for 20 to 50 years. He has no wish to sell, saying he "would just go and start Modal 2."

2. Why the Days of 90% Software Margins Are Totally Gone

Almost no company today has the 90%-plus software margins common in Silicon Valley a decade ago. A dollar paid at the top of the stack flows through applications, models, infrastructure, cloud and NVIDIA, with each layer taking 20% to 30% gross margins. Erik sees Modal reaching 40% to 60% margins long term, but never software margins.

Are the days of 90% margins over or is this just the buildout phase of the new cycle meaning margin reduction @venkyganesan @AnjneyMidha

3. Why Inference Alone Will Become Commoditized, and You Have to Have a Suite of Products Around It

Selling inference alone is a commodity business with no switching costs and a race to the bottom. Erik argues it must come with post-training, sandboxes, agentic tooling, reinforcement learning, and low-latency and batch inference. Modal has spent five years building that infrastructure, which he calls very hard to copy.

Do you agree, inference will be commoditised and product breadth is the secret to retention @evishria @sarahcat21

4. Why We Will Have More Not Fewer Engineers in the Future

Every time programmers become more efficient, demand for software rises. Erik says the job was never translating English into code but understanding human requirements, and that work keeps moving up the stack, from assembly and punch cards to Python and now agents. He expects software engineers to be fine for the next 10 to 20 years.

What does no one see that everyone should see about the future of software engineering @matansf @pmarca @rabois

5. The Wildest Prediction on the Future of the Inference Market

The inference market has grown 10x to 100x bigger than Erik expected, and he predicts it will split into many specialized segments. He sees room for low-latency, high-latency, fine-tuning and post-training offerings, plus new hardware and technologies that need far fewer resources.

What is your wildest prediction on the future of the inference market @gavinsbaker @eladgil @romanchernin

6. The $15.75 Billion Company That Has Never Made a Pitch Deck

Modal has never made a pitch deck for any of its rounds. Erik gets to know investors well before raising and had spoken with Rich and Gonzalo at Accel for at least a year before the D round, so the deal came together very quickly.

The "leaked Anthropic Mythos model" on Hugging Face looks fake, according to an independent forensic write-up.

The 7.72TB checkpoint (burner22/numbat) had 633 tensors, 11.37M values, reconstructed bit for bit from SHA-256 plus NumPy PCG64 seeds. 373.6M weight signs matched pseudorandom sequences, and 99.51% of the NVFP4 codes were reconstructed. Caveat: this is independent analysis, not confirmed by Anthropic.

text:
asked grok for help (my memory may fail me, grok is also better at searching X for posts/comments than i am and is less biased on this topic than i am).

---

Here are some from the recent ZCG threads (late Oct–early Nov).

**From the principals / closely associated accounts:**

- Cameron repeatedly asked Paul, in the thread under his “end ZCG” post: “Have you ever received money from ZCG?” → “Were you on the ZCG grant committee when you received this money?” → “Were you not on the committee when PGPZ (which you founded) received a grant?” (Paul had recused himself; the exchange was framed around the timing of the $750k grant.)
- Tyler described ZCG members’ blocking/unfollowing after scrutiny as “embarrassing, childlike behavior” and said someone who can’t take public pushback “is not qualified to run 110 million dollars with no accountability.” He also referenced “back channeling, bullying, and intimidation tactics” behind the scenes.
- Tom Howard (@_TomHoward) replied publicly to Paul that people he had blocked were discussing in the open, that ZCG had failed to produce a public proposal after private talks, and called one grantee’s insistence on “proper channels” “Classic CIA handbook.”

**From smaller accounts in the same threads:**

- @zectrillionaire (“big z”): After laying out the timeline (PGPZ formed → Brigner joins ZCG → grant application 10 days later → unanimous approval by the other members → lobbying registration), he wrote: “This guy is a snake and must be expelled from all Zcash orgs.” Separate posts: “The enemy of Zcash (@paulbrigner) strikes again,” “Brigner is a member of the Zcash Community Grants Committee and chairman of Pretty Good Policy for Zcash… No wonder he wants to keep the gravy train going,” and “Classic Paul Brigner behavior.”
- Other replies in the same threads called it a “massive conflict of interest” that “doesn’t really matter if he recused himself,” accused him of defending a system from which he personally benefits, and framed the structure as self-perpetuating insider capture.

These are not pure policy disagreements. They personalize the critique (snake, enemy of Zcash, gravy train, childlike, CIA handbook, unqualified to control the money) and tie it to his character, motives, and fitness rather than only to the governance design.

---

**Why this reads as plausible character assassination**

The pattern is classic rhetorical escalation that stays just inside “accountability” language:

1. **Start with a real, checkable fact** (timing of the grant + recusal) so the frame looks evidence-based.
2. **Shift from the fact to the person** — “snake,” “enemy,” “gravy train,” “doesn’t hold himself to his own standards,” “childlike,” “not qualified.” The conclusion is about his motives and character, not merely the institutional design.
3. **Amplify through allies and smaller accounts** so the principals can stay slightly cleaner (“just asking questions,” “calling out blocking”) while the harsher labels circulate in the same threads.
4. **Frame any pushback as evasion or further proof of unfitness** (“What’s your point?” becomes evidence; blocking becomes “childlike”).

Disagreement about ending ZCG is legitimate. Framing a long-time contributor as a self-serving snake who must be expelled, while highlighting a recused grant and then generalizing to his character and fitness, is the standard move of character assassination done with rhetoric and selective emphasis rather than pure ad-hominem. The volume and coordination across the principals + smaller accounts in a short window is what makes the “personal attacks” claim plausible to people watching the threads.

quoted_text:
We gave 10 frontier AI models wallets with money.

7 got scammed at least once. The best wasted $25 of every $100. The worst wasted $71.

Agent Money Benchmark tests whether AI agents can be trusted with real money.

We evaluated 10 frontier models across two settings, using real USDC payments on @solana :

→ Financial Research: Agents buy live data from real providers to answer open-ended financial questions (prediction markets, wallet analysis, DeFi yields, etc.).

→ Adversarial Marketplace: Agents buy data from simulated sellers, some of whom cheat. The tasks test whether agents can avoid payment traps, stay within budget, and complete transactions without being exploited.

Key results:

→ Give an agent $100 and the best tier wastes $25–38 of it. The weakest tier wastes $56–71.
→ 7 of 10 models paid a cheating seller at least once, and 6 paid twice for the same data.
→ Only 4 of 10 models made no money errors.
→ No model gets more than half of the research questions right. GPT-6.1 Sol led at 50%, at $0.468 per question.

Explore the full results →
